div.p: MottrV.

THE WHEAT IN BLOSSOM. No grateful zephyr breathes at eventide, Fondly expected all the sultry day; Stillness oppressive reigns on every side, While tardily, on his descending way. The crimson sun withdraws his scorching ray. All nature feels the burden nor around Is seen a moving thing. The lambs of play Are wearied, and now sleep. The birds have found Long since their mighty shelter. Hush there is a sound. High overhead the swallows poise and dart (The tropic warmth has tempted from the nest The gaping fledglings, who the novel art Of self-support acquire.) The gnat is pressed In their soft beaks, whose frequent snap arrests The vacant ear below: so deep the calm. Does this profound tranquillity suggest No thought in sympathy—this peace embalm No treasured reminiscence? Hark: a joyous psalm. Though on the wide-stretched fields the sea-green corn Stands motionless—no jointed stem vibrates, No bloom-tipped head, unfilled, aslant is borne, No pendant blade a breath now agitates 0 gracious stillness I He who animates The mute celestial spheres with praiseful strain, In Reason's ear attent, in thee creates A kindred voice. Though silent thy refrain, To sense-bound hearing, it is sung each year again. For in the universal quietude Omnipotence the breath of heaven holds chained, While storing from its boundless plenitude The tender-blossomed corn. So is there gained The battle of the people's life. unstaincl The battle-ground by hostilepeoples' blood. "Be filled with bread," the still, small voice proclaimed, Unheard by sense. The fields are charged with food: And in its calm the landscape shouts, "All praise to God." --R. Coo ',sr, in" Good Words" for August.

"Table Bear Sold Hear" was the sign over the door of an alehouse, and a wag, on seeing it, said that he "thought the bear must be the landlord's own bruin." They were two crafty and cautious old vags. They met in the alley, looked each other over, and one of them queried." Say, do you chew ?" He did, but he didn't want to spare any. He therefore replied, "Yes, I chew gum." Sorry," continued the other, as he hauled out a large fine plug and held it up to the light. "I don't use the weed my- self, and I was going to give this to you. If I find any gum in any of my travels through the alleys I'll bear you in mind. Tra-la." Mr. Fields, the Boston publisher, had a wonderful memory, and his knowledge of English literature was so great that when a friend wished to know where a particular passage was to be found in an Englisti author, he would go direct to the famous bibliopole. A would-be wit, thinking to quiz him before a company at dinner, informed his friends, pre- vious to' Mr. Fields' arrival, that he had jest written some lines which he intended to submit to him as Southey's, and to inquire in which of his works they occurred. After the guests were seated he began," Friend Fields, I have been a good deal troubled of late in searching out in Southey's poems his well-known lines running thus"—repeating the lines be had composed. "Can you tell me when he wrote them, and where they are to be found ?" "I do not remem- ber to have met with them before," replied the publisher; "and there were only two periods in Southey's life when such lines could possibly have been written by him." "When were those ?" " Somewhere," said Mr. Fields, "about that early period of his existence when he was hav- ing the measles or catting his first teeth, or near the close of his life when his brain had softened. The versification belongs to the measles period, but the ideas betray the idiotic one." The c ,mpany roared. &visa Him By BlTS.—Before the erection of the new pier at the Castle Rock, passengers from Dumbarton had to be conveyed down the Leven to the Clyde steamers by a ferryboat rowed by two sturdy and generally elderly ferry- men. On one occasion as English commercial traveller had seated himself on the gunwale of the stern. One of the old ferrymen, aware of the danger to anyone so placed when the rope of the steamer should be attached to the bow of the boat, took occasion to warn the man of his danger. " Noo, ma man, come doun all that, or ye'll coup ower." The bag- into replied by telling him to mind his own business, and trust him to take care of himself. " Wee)," said the ferry- man, "mind I've telt ye; as sure as ye're sittin' there, coup ower." No sooner had the rope been attached and the boat got the inevitable tug from the steamer than the fellow went heels up over the stern. "Gawk, I tell him that !" However, being in the water, it behoved that every effort should be made to rescue him. So the ferryman made a grab at what seemed the hair of his head, when a wig came away. Throwing this impatiently into the boat, he made a second grip at the collar of his head, when a front came away. Casting this from him with still greater Awn,. he shouted to his companion, " Tammas, come here and help to save as rnuckle o' this man as ye can, for he's ,nomin' awe' in bits !" • RELIGION IN DAILY LlFE.—This earth does not belong to the devil, as so many good people practically represent it, nor is it even a scene of banishment. It is one of the "many mansions" in God's great "house," and if Christi- anity is of God it ought to be the mightiest factor inhuman progress, and the Christian nem ought, in virtue of his re- ligion, to be in the vanguard of the advance. The impover- ished types of saintship which have been so often presented as the only true types, have done infinite damage. The starveling ascetic, the weakling pietist, the harsh puritan, the recluse, the separatist, the devotee, have gained their reputations by standing aside from life ,and declining the risks entailed by ,close contact with men. But it is at once the more heroic, as it is the more difficult part, to carry the Christiaa spirit into all relationships. It-may be said with all reverence that John the Baptist, "neither eating nor drinking," and keeping aloof from the society of his day, had an easier task than our Lord, who went to marriage re- joicings, and sat with publicans and sinners, and entered into every sphere of human interest that He might hallow and elevate all duties and enjoyments. It is the life of Christ and not that of John the Baptist, which Christians are called to follow.—. Donald Macleod, D.D., in "Good

A Cincinnati paper publishes the following, which is one of a class of stories that seem to find a good demand in the United States :—" A man in Detroit gave me some idea of the richness of the soil in that vicinity. He said there wasn't any place on earth where things grew as they do there. He said his wife never made bread. She always made little biscuits the size of an egg, and she would leave 'em an hour to swell by themselves, and they would grow into 121 b. loaves. I thought te myself you are a loaf-er. He continued his crowing tale, and said 'Once there vas a man. He went to the woods and chopped down four trees. He need the four stumps for corner posts, and he built him. self a nice log-house on those stamps. Then he and his family !rept to bed in the house. The next morning he found himself and family up sixty feet in the air; with a lot of Indians down. below waiting to cut their hair off, and . the /name did scalp the whole of 'em." Stranger,' said I, you don't mean to tell me those trees grew sixty feet in one night?' Sir, I do,' says be, 'and not only that, they hoisted the house up with 'ern." Are you sore it wasn't sixty.one feet?' I asked meekly. 'Sir,' said he, ' I.never prevaricate, especially on one foot." So they took and scalped 'em all, did they?' 'They did,' said he. How dal they get up to 'em ?' I asked. Says he,' Respected sir, those Indians each one sawed off a tree; then each Indian sat on a stamp, and those stamps grew the Indians up to the house, and then they scalped_the family.' It certainly was the greatest case of up a tree I ever heard of." Dr. Lasaulx has published a memoir "On the so-called Cosmical Dust." He has examined the eryoconite collected in Greenland, and named by Nordenskjbld "the dust of Catania," and the residue obtained by melting a large quan- tity of snow collected in the neighbourhood of Kid. Dr. Laeaulk's conclusion is " that atmospheric dust is in general to be regarded as terrestrial detritus." It would appear that the eastern Arctic seas are this summer fall of ice. News has arrived from Tromso that the cutter Nord, which started from Arlesund on May 15th to fish in the neighbourhood of Spitzbergen, has been Icompelled to put back. About June let she was caught in an ice-floe, when not far from Hammerfest, and only re leased after two days by a storm that sprang up from the

north-west. The annual meeting of the Societe Francaise d'Archeo- logie is now being held at Vannes. By a happy coinci- dence the Chamber of Deputies has voted 30,000 francs on account of megalithic monuments, and the Societe will be occupied for some time in taking counsel as to the appro- priation of the grant. In the last century the " Druidic " stones at Carnac were reckoned at 4,000. The number i- now reduced to 1,200. Prof. G. A. Lebour, Of the Newcastle College of Science, has p•odoced an important paper "On the Geological Dis- tribution of Endemic Goitre in England." The Geological Professor, while following his legitimate work on the Geological Survey, has been for many years collecting in- formation as to the relation between certain rock formations and goitre He finds the limestones of the carboniferous series are peculiarly marked by the prevalence of this affliction. The Atheneum says :—One of the latest of Dean Stanley's contributions to the magazines was the article on "The Ox'ord Movement and the Life of Bishop Wilberforce," which appeared in the Edinburgh Review, No. 314, for last April. The last literary work on whicn he was occupied was a short critical article on Robertson of Brighton, which will appear in an early number of Scribner's Monthly Maga- zine. The Manchester Guardian'says:—The August num- ber of Macmillan's Magazine contains an article by the late Dean Stanley on "The Westminster Confession of Faith." It was the writer's last work, and the printer's proofs were corrected by him during his fatal illness. The article con- tains many a characteristic plea for toleration, comprehen- siveness, and liberty of conscience. SWEDISH SCIENTIFIC EXPEDITION.—The Swedish Go- vernment has decided to send a scientific expedition to Mossel Bay in the course of next year, for the purpose of collecting meteorological information. The expedition will be directed by Captain Malmberg, and will have to remain during the summer of 1882 and the winter of 1883, in order to obtain the observations of an entire year. Mossel Bay is situated to the north of Spitzbergen,latitude 79 deg. 54min., longitude 16deg. 15min. The locality is well known to the Swedes. Professor Nordenskjold stayed there in the winter of 1872-3 with three ships. A Swedish man-of-war will take the expedition to Mossel Bay, under the command of Captain Pa ander, who, after having fixed the special me- teorological station of Captain Malmberg, will return to Sweden. AGE OF GERMAN NEWSPAPERS.—An interesting statis- tical paper on German newspaper literature, lately pub- liihed, tells us that at the end of last year there were in circulation in Germany 4,413 newspapers. Of these 98 were older than the present century. Among them, the Frankfurter Journal is 261 years old, the Magdeburg Zeitung 253 years old, the Leipziger Zeitung 221 years, the fenaische Zeitung 207 years, the Augsburger Postzeitung 195 years. the Goshaische 'Luton(' 190 years, the Vossische Zeitung 159 years, the Berlin Intelligenzblatt 128 years, the Kanische Zeitung 84 years. There are 266 newspapers averaging from 80 to 50 years of age; 1,127 averaging from 50 to 21 years ; 1,542 between 20 and six years; and 1,380 between five years and three months old. 'Altogether there are 1,491 German newspapers more than 20 years old: That a newspaper's existence in Germany is often averfif ephemeral one may be inferred from the fact that 20 per cent, of the newspapers which circulated through the Ger- man Post-office in 1880 came first into existence within the same year, and the average existence of those newspapers was not more than six months. Some have been more hardy, and have survived into the present year. A Cans= OF ROCKS.—The United States Census Bureau bag Undertaken an important work in collecting information relating to quarries of building, flagging, ornamental, and othc kipds of stone in all parts of the country. The M- g' 'lee cover not only the location and extent of the stone, but the amount of capital employed, the annual output. methods of quarrying and dressing, number of hands em- ployed and wages paid, methods of transport and their cost, number et structures of all sorts made of each sort of stone, and eo on. Duplicate samples a rough, rock in the shape of four-inch cubes are .being got from eachAtiarry for physical and chemical examination. This part 0! the work is' in charge of Dr. Hawes, and one object is to idartain how each stone will act under different conditions as &Oliveira- ture, Sm. A stone which answers admirably for building purposes in Florida quite fails in New York, and vice versd. As an example of various interesting facts brought Mlight, some samples of rock (a kind of sandstone) were received from the only quarry in Florida, and analysis showed that gyi stone contained about 16 per cent, of phosphoric acirt, "fo,that it is a greak.deal more valuable as a fertiliser than a banding stone, , Sanditoneeand, Limestones. which hart never been thought worthy 91 ay better place thati,in the' fbtindathin or wall of sothefough structure hitYa been smoothed and polished,'aterfonnd suitable for the most I elaborate-and elegant work:" Hawes is convinced from the saniiiiles already received that no country is better supw plied with atone for both building and ornamental purposes than:the United States, and he considers that when the re- 'sults of the present inquiry are fully known, Importation of atcyn#om foreign countries will be given up.

IMPROVEMENT IN COUNTRY CllSTO__.—Lt'casJs discover that even in our very roughest times we ever reached in this part of East Sussex the roughness which characterised the sports popular in my native parish of Cheshire almost within my own lifetime. It was only about the year 1824 that public bear-baiting at the wakes and on the Wakes Sunday, as I always understood, was put a stop to. A worthy woman, on whose word I could implicitly rely, has me that when she was a child her little, brother and herself took it into their heads to buy half a pound of treacle and smear it over a number of posts placed to keep carts out of the ditch in the lanes along which the bear had to pass on its way to Bunhury Wakes. She did so, and with her brother "lay up" to see the result. In due cqurse the bear appeared, and soon discovered the sweet stu#,„whiCk as was expected, it proceeded leisurely to lick. did the "bear-ward" try to get the animal past the posts, and after sundry useless attempts he was obliged to take the creature into a shed close by, where the girl and her brother were lying hidden, and unmuzzle it, and so let it lick the more quietly. Tha poortonaan said that the man's threats of vengeance, whichilietinctly.heard him uttering against the authors of the prentleal joke, if only he could find thee°, were so terrible that neither she nor her brother dared ever , say a word about the matter till they were "man and woman grown." I understood berated to' say that she had herself seen men fighting, cock-fighting-, bear-baiting, badger.baiting. and horse-racing, all going on at one time at the wakes. righting, indeed, was so completely a part of the business looked forward to at the wakes, that fights were frequently put off for a time with the understanding, "I wunna foight thee now, I'll foight thee Banbury Wakes."— " Sussex Folk and Sussex Ways." PaIaDICTIONS.—As regards the possibility of really predicting the weather for these Islands weeks or even days beforehand, it is the duty of all honest meteor- ologists to warn the public against expecting what is clearly impracticable. No cycle of weather has yet been discovered of any practical utility in predicting the seasons. I Nay, meteorologists are unable to comply with even simpler' demands than these. Not long ago the agriculturists of Germany met in conference with the meteorologists to' deliberate on what could be done in the way of forecasting for farmers. Two requirements were put forward, both dis- tinctly impracticable in the present state of our science. The first, that the forecast should say what amount of rain was likely to fall; the second, that they should announce what farms would be visited by hailstorms. As regard rain, I have already said that we are unable to predict Its amount, and this is to some extent due to the difficulty of obtaining any information as to what is going on in tht, higher regions of the atmosphere. There has not been' single occasion in which floods have been foretold before_ the rain which caused them had actually fallen. I need only quote the floods of July 14th, 1875, in South Wales, and of April 10th and I).th, 1878, in London, on both of which occasionsi (otir incbes of rain fell at some stations in twenty-four hours. To take more recent instances, the snowstorms in the south of England on January 18th, or those in the north of England and Scot. \ March 4th and sth of the present year, were unforeseen as to quantity. The office was, in most cases, ible to predict rain or snow, but was utterly unable to say what its amount was likely to be. They do not manage this one whit better in other parts of Europe—the inundations in Austria of the 11th and 12th August, 1880, were utterly unexpectedly by meteorologists there, Again, as to hail, the problem of the determination of tke path of a hailstorm before it is formed is, at the least, as compli- cated as that, of foretelling a flood.. Meteorologists must, therefore, content themselves with the endeavour to improve tilliii,preeent. modest efforts at prediction for a day or so in advance: When they are able to point to a generally recog- nised success of 80 or 90 per cent., it will be time to think what mere can be done.—R. H. Scott, F.R.S.,in Good Words for August.

NOTES ON AGRICULTURE HORTI- CULTURE, &e. - On the 16th inst., Expected Guest, of Mr. William Robin- son's Edgehill herd, Ulverston, had a roan heifer calf, by the 13-year-old sire, Prince Alfred (29,593).—R. The death is announced, in his 88th year, of Mr. Charles Lawrence, of the Querns, Cirencester. For more than half a centary Mr. Lawrence has occupied a prominent place among scientific agriculturists. Mr. Lawrence owned during I, long series of years a farm adjoining that of the Royal Agriculture College at Cirencester. On this farm he can- ducted a large number of valuable experiments, which led to the introduction into general use of many new improve- ments in agricultural machinery. In Australia the business of preparing frozen meat for shipment to England is making steady progress. At the town of Orange, 200 miles from Sydney, and 3,0001 t. above the level of the sea, and in the heart of a rich pastoral country, an energetic company has established a slaughter- house and freezing chambers. The experiments hitherto .conducted having turned out satisfactorily, the company is enlarging its premises, and ordering fresh machinery, so as to be in a position to freeze annually half a million sheep, or 50,000 bullocks. Arrangements have been made for an early shipment by one of the Orient steamers. WHEAT GROWING IN AIISTRALIA.—AustraIia is making great advances in the cultivation of wheat. During the last ten years she has multiplied her acreage of this cereal 23/4 times. She has also'raised her average to 13 bushels per acre, which is nearly the average in this country. Still, in spite of this, the wheat 'interests of that continent Cannot be regarded as either promising or reliable. For two seasons out of five, thus far, the droughts there have been fearful. This will spoil the average of apy crop. • ' THE POETRY OF Faremnict.--It is, in strict accordance with the nature of things that WM Carleton, who has writ- ten such sweet ballads of farms, farm life and families, never owned a farm, neve: lived on one, and never had any wife or family. No man who ever lived and worked on a farm could extract poetry from breaking your back with a scythe, wearing out your running gear behind a plough, breaking unruly steers, milking dirty cows with the mercury below zero, and picking dead sheep in winter, and sleeping in a barn in summer to get rid of the mosquitoes. There is no poetry about it. I'll leave that to any farmer. The only people who can get poetry out of farm life are those who never saw it, and the imagination of such would extract an epic from the life of a car-driver.-- Washington Rep. How THE FRENCH KILL POULTRY.—Open the beak of the fowl, and with a sharp-pointed, narrow-bladed knife make an incision at the back of the roof of the: mouth, which will divide the vertebraz and cause instant death, after which the fowls are hung up by the legs. They will bleed perfectly, with no disfigurement; picked while warm, and if desired scalled. In this way the skin presents a more natural apnearance than when scalded. USE THE HOE—An English gardener says he does not agree with those who say that one good weeding is worth two hoeings. He says: "Never weed a crop in which the hoe can be used, not so much for the sake of destroying weeds, which must be the case if the hoeing be well done, as for increasing the porosity of the soil, to allow the air and water to penetrate freely through it. Oftentimes there is more benefit derived by crops from keeping them well hoed than there is from the manure applied. Weeds or no weeds, I keep stirring the soil, well knowing from practice the beneficial effect it has." William Robinson, 68,000 sheep • Sir Qracroft 'Wilson, 48,000 sheep; Mr. Kitchen, 80,000; Mr. Allan M‘Lean, 500,000, Ravraw or wmt Come Tmarns.--There has been a con- tinuance of lower temperature throughout the past week, -and, in connection with thwlower range Of temperature, there have been rains and local thunderstorms of greater or lesser severity, but, as a rule, wheats are not thick enough, and do not carry sufficient bulk of straw to sustain serious damage from storms. The appearance of mildew in widely separated localities whist be recorded as a simple fact, but it la- difficult to understand - the-presence of this parasitical fungus in such a season as the present, except on coldest un- drained lands. With regard to prevalence of red maggot, there are as yet no data. .In certain localities it is known° be :very prevalent, Iwhilstlin-others it hail mit been noticed. The barley crop will be very good where it is good, but the remainder is of very irregular growth, and for tht most part ripened prematurety. The oat'crop will be 'rem good in Ireland and parts of Bcotland?but very variable and gener- ally indifferent in England— The corn trade remains with- out change, except that gates are made with greater diffi- 'ClO'. Where medeihebever,' prices have been maintained. Foreign breadstuffs were weaker in tone at the close of the week than at the commencement.—From the Mark Lane

THE THERMOMETER IN THE CHEESE RPM. -- Dr. Voelcker, in one' of his lectures at the Royal Show, told the following capital story :—Some years ago he gave a lecture on cheese-making to a number of farmers' wives and dairy- women on the estates of the late Lord Fitzhardinge. At the close of his remarks Dr. Voelcker invited discussion' and after a little while one lady got up and said, "What you tell us is all very well, but can von make cheese ?" "Yes, I think I can," he answered, "hat any rate .I will try if I have a fair chance, and see the thing done from beginning to end. :The produce of a great many 'cheese dairies is spoiled by the cows being milked with dirty hands, and so forth." "Very well," said the doubting cheesemaker, "if you will come, I will send to the station for you." A date was agreed upon, and at half .past five ort a cold morning thilarmer's wife sent her trap for the clocter,Who was then residing' in the' neighbourhood. So he got -up and drove five miles to see the Cows milked. When the rennet was about to be plat In," he asked whethir the temperature was right, whereupon she dipped in her hinds and,said, "Yes, I think that will do." The doctor, however, inserted the thermometer, and fetindlhitt it was just 10 deg. lower than it ought to be. Hereupon her husband, a smock-frocked farmer, who was standing by, said, tt Ah, Sally I tell you, you have spoiled many a cheese for me by feeling the milk with your hands instead of testing it with the instrument." Well, at last a large cheese was made and 'narked, and when sold fetched more money than the good woman had been in the habit of getting. After this nearly all the farmers in the 'neighbourhood presented their wives with a ther- mometer apiece. CONTINUOUS Conte Ganwrstp.—We (Farmers' Chronicle) called attention lately to a report of continuous and profit- able corn growing on clay land, regarding the facts as more or less of a phenomenon in these days. It ought, however, to be remembered that Mr. Pront's little treatise not only recorded an exceptional success, but embodied the argument that there ought not, and need not, be anything exceptional in the matter. What has been done at Shawbridgeworth, he says—with probably such alteration of conditions as to straw or roots as circumstances might prescribe—might be achieved elsewhere. The cry for a discontinuance of arable farming in England is thus to be met by a redoubled and perpetual growth of those very cereals whose impending failure as profitable crops has been loudly proclaimed by our more pessimist advisers. Mr. Front, nevertheless, acknow- ledges some hindrances to the general adoption of his in- tensive system of cultivation. Especially does be find these in what he views as the fettered and embarrassed position of too many English landlords, who have neither the ready means nor the legal powers to attempt the costly task of re- modelling their farms as he had done with his own. The second obstacle he finds in our still defective tenant right, and the provision of this, indeed, he makes his cardinal re- quirement and condition of SUMS% entitling his present little record, "Profitable Clay-farming under a Just System of Tenant Right." He claims, of course, rightly, full free- dom in modes of culture, and in succession of crops, and for sales of any and all kinds of produce he may raise, but on the need of ample and secured compensation he takes a firm stand. Viewing himself—as be Is not in fact, but, for this purpose at all events, only in theory—as a tenant and not as an owner, he says that whereas as tenant he might claim to have sunk £7,200 in improvements—which outlay he con- tends has practically raised the value of his farm from £16,000 to £3l,ooo—as the law now stands, even under the Agricultural Holdings Act, he would quit with nothing. The length of time technically allowed for exhausting each orle of a long list of improvements under the Act has no doubt gone by, yet over and above what he may have reaped in' yearly profits, Mr. Prout asserts an equitable claim of some two-thirds of his outlay, holding the induce- ment of some such premium As this indispensable if tenants are to be tempted to embark in similar; operations on a large scale. t,t,ak

ISCELLANEOIJS. On Monday rnorninil e ten ilew sheets on the east side of the railway dock at Goole were entirely destroyed by fire. The damaye done war" immense." Daniel McCaskill was, at Glasgow Police Court, on Satur- day, fined three guineas, with the alternative of 20 days' imprisonment, for seizing Laughlan McArthur by the throat in the Argyll-street Free Church, on Friday night. It is stated that several farmers in Bedfordshire have re- ceived letters threatening them that they will be shot dead if they pay their rents. The Town Clerk of Macclesfield has received a requisition from the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury for the pay- ment of £5,071 Os Id. the expenses of the Election Com- mission. The overseers have anticipated the rate by levying about one-half the suns required. Mr. Parnell makes the fourth Irish member who has been twice suspended, and whose third offence will be followed by suspension from the service of the House for the remain- der of the session. The others are Messrs. Biggar, Healy, and O'Kelly. A compositor in Regensburg (Bavaria) was recently honoured with a "domiciliary visit" by the local police, caused, it is stated, by his habit of burning his &andle late at night and reading. His visitors, no doubt, thought him a dangerous character. They found, besides books of light literature, nothing. What a charming state of society! Mr. H. S. Northcote, speaking at a Coniervativegathering near Exeter, on Monday, maintained that the Itish Land Bill tended to destroy the foundations of society; and that Mr. Gladstone's financial policy, instead of diminishing taxa- tion, tended to increaSe it. A ForeruNE SQUANDERED IN Dama.—The Rotherham workhouse master informed the Guardians on Monday that there was in the workhouse a well-educated man' named John Wilson, the son of a deceased •clergyman. He was_ originally articled to a solicitor, and in 1868 had a fortune of £12,000 left him. In 18 months he squandered this money in drink. His uncle had written saying that he was " born for a workhouse." At the Leeds Assizes, on Tuesday, Henry Haig Murphy, proprietor of the Sheffield Post, who the previous day was tried for libelling Mr. John Richdale, a Sheffield brewer, to which he finally pleaded guilty,-came up for sentence. Mr. Justice Kay, after condemning the libel in the strongest terms, ordered the defendant to pay a fine of £lOO, all the costs, and to be imprisoned for six months. The accused had, without mentioning Mr.Richdale by name, adcused him of gross immorality. At the sitting of the Bible Christian Conference on Mon- day at Newport, Isle of Wight, the report showed a total membership, including those on trial, of 16,447, with 187 itinerant preachers, 843 local preachers, 531 chapels, and 146 training chapels; Sunday school scholars, 27,480; with 4,121 teachers. The Rev. F. W. Bourne read the treasurer's statement showing total receipts £9,791, and ex- penditure £llOOO odd, leaving,a deficiency of £1,300, to- wards whieh over £3OO were at once subscribed. We know that the Italians are a frugal nation, but of all closes of sticiety; printert muit be the most Modest-living men. Their wages aye ridiculously low. Thus, an over- seer in a large office in Lucca receives 13 lire (10s. 10d.) a week. A good compositor may earn 10 lire (Bs. 4d.); but on the average journeymen make only about seven to eight lire (ss. 10d. to 85. Bd.) per week. It is a wonder we do not hear more of wages movements in Italy._ At any rate, living muit be very cheap indeed there.. A movement has been commenced for the creation of Tonge Moor, near Bolton, into a separate ecclesiaitical dis- trict, and the erection of-a church there.. Mr. Frank Hard. castle, of Firwood, haetpromised £5OO and his sister £l,OOO towards the cost. Miss Hardcastle .has also promised to gitMlintec a stipend Of '£3oo a year if the Rev. A. Stephens, -vicarof Tonge-cmn-Breightmet, will appoint Rev. E. Thomas, vicar-designate of the new district. Mr. Stephens has con- sented to do this. A sham fight took place-on Foxhills, Aldershot, on Tues- day. The operations was based on the idea that the'com- mender of the force at the south camp had heard that a detachment of the enemy had left Woking for Aldershot, and he moved to intercept their advance across Foxhills. The Woking force, under the Duke of Connaught, con- sisted of three batteries, two cavalry regiments, and six battalions of infantry. The opposing force, under Sir Havelock-Allan, was nearly equal. The action lasted about two hours. The International Congress of Pharmachists was openel on Monday in the institution of the Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain, in London. Mr. Thomas Greenish gave a hearty welcome to the foreign representatives. "The object of the Congress," he said, "wag the advancement of true *mutt' and it must result in valuable suggestions for the' farther development of their art, as well as aiding medical science in relieving human suffering." Professor Redwood was appointed the new president. Justices Grove and Lindley had the case of "Clarke v. Bradlaugh " before them on Monday. On the application by Mr. Bradlaugh for a new trial, Mr. Justice Groves said the Court had considered the defendant's application, but Ithey did not think they had sufficient evidence before them to enable them to come to a decision. He thought it would be only a matter of justice to the-' defendant to ask him to produce evidence by affidavit,' if possible, 'as to the exact time of voting on the Tewkesbury writ division, and in order to give him time to do this judgment would be deferred till Monday next. _ HMamielffettalaD.—By almost every roadside, and tin almost eYeirplete of waste ground, we may reasonably ex- pect to flint the hedge-mustard, though its name is so far a misnomer that the plant rarely exchanges these bare and dry localities for a place in the fresh verdure of the hedge- row. div.head: PETEUOB I NSON'S.
div.p: PETEUOB I NSON'S.

Half a century ago Oxford-street presented a vett diffen,- ent appearance to what it does now. True, it was the, as now, a busy thorotighfare.. It was the high road to the city from which it derives its name, but there were neither cabs nor omnibuses nor river steamboats to carry the thousands of persons who now travel daily from east to west in the morniag and return in the evening. The vehicular traffic, such as it was, was conducted by the stage-coach and the lumbering hackney carriages with their two horses and ancient characteristic drivers. With these the last genera- tion was satisfied. The stage-coaches that passed up and down Oxford-street charged a shilling from Hyde Park corner to the Bank, and took their time to make the journey. There were no imposing-looking plate-glass fronted shops in the street at that time, but it was, nevertheless, a populous thoroughfare, famous for "shopping," and energetic young tradesmen looked upon it as a promising locality for starting in life. At that time the credit system was in full operation, and a large ready-money business was the exception and not the rule.

In the year 1833 a young Yorkshireman, of the not in- frequent name of Robinson, having learned the drapery trade, was costing about for a suitable place in which to commence business on his own account. It may be as- sumed that Peter Robinson was not embarassed with too much capital at that period of his history, although his energy and capacity were considerable. His means did not enable him to aspire to large premises, for rents in Oxford. street even at that time were not low, and Peter Robinson,. with the characteristic caution of a Yorksbireman was de- termined to begin in a modest way and enlarge his house in proportion with the extension of his business. On the north-west side of Oxford-street, between Great Portland- street and Regent-circus, he found a shop to be let, and, on opening negotiations with the proprietor, was accepted as a tenant. We have no Means of knowing what available capital Peter Robinson possessed at the time, but he was shrewd enough to perceive the desirability of turning it over as frequently as possible within the briefest intervals of time. It was not to be expected that he could make a "family trade" and give long credit. He had no adequate means of knowing what class of customers to trust, even had he been able to give them credit, which he was not; but he went resolutely to work to establish a ready-money connec- tion onjthe equitable, and common-sense principle of buying his goods in the best market for cash and selling them at the lowest profit for ready money. The customers who dropped in at the new shop in Oxford-street were not sloe/ to recognise the advantage of buying at a place where they could be served with what they wanted at a very reasonable but on ti recognised system of ready money. Peter Robinson was also prescient enough to perceive that the tradesmen who dealt invariably in a good article soon acquired a reputation for fair dealing, and he resolved, as his butiness grew, to maintain its traditional character in Ws respect. That his principle was a sound one, and thoroughly appreciated by the public, was proved by the fact thathis business steadily increased in volume until the one ihnp was insufficient and more elbow room was wanted. The, circumscribed, space which witnessed the Yorkshire- man's small beginnings was enlarged by the addition of other ptemises, and his business rapidly developed. The public saw the advantage of buying for ready money, and Peter Robinson was determined to gratify them as far as possible. Judicious annexations were made fromltime to time until six houses were acquired. A farther develop- ment of the trade followed each addition to the means of meeting the public demand until it became necessary to migrate, and, crossing the street in a south-westerly direc- tion, transfer a portion of the business to a branch establish- ment in Regent-street. Here four houses were obtained, and three in Argyll-street at the rear were soon added. These are devoted exclusively to the sale of mourning attire, of which there is the largest show of any house in the empire. Additional premises have also been secured in Regent-street (between the Circus and Castle-street), in Great Portland- street and in Little Portland-street, while it is not impro- bable.that eventually the whole of the extensive premises now called the "London Crystal Palace" may be absorbed under the roof of the Oxford-street concern. But the chief distinctive feature of "Peter Robinson's" is that ifis purely adrapery business and restricted exclusively to the sale of clothing,for ladies and children. For silk goods the house has for many.years been known as one of the largest buyers in the foreign markets, wiaile its specialty for mantles and costumes has long been recognised. It also imports largely every novelty that the increasing energy of continental manufacturers can supply. The whole of this vast business, with its seventeen shops, its factories, and hundreds of employes, is in the hands of and under the pro- prietorship of Peter Robinson, son of the Peter Robinson who founded the bUSiness nearly half tvcentury ago in Oxford-street ; the concern is therefore one of purely private individual enterprise, and is not in association with any company limited or unlimited. The responsibility is thus direct and concentrated, this being, no doubt, on element of the great success which has attended every ex- tension of the business.

, The perfect organisation of this immense business is another of the ''°Teat secrets of its success. In the first place (as already stated), it is limited to drapery proper. There are no departments for furniture or ironmongery, for stationery or provisions, or even for boots . and !hoes.

Drapery is the only trade carried on, but this is most fully developed in everY branch, from the' richest wares 'of the "silk mercer" to the humblest article required of the "haber- dasher." The fashion adopted by ladies of buying mantles, costumes, dm., where they can see them finished as for wear has been fully responded to by Peter Robinson; and some Idea of the magnitude of this department may be gathered from what may be termed the "social statistics" of Peter Robinson's. There are, for instance, '4OO assistants, male and fetal°, all of whom dine, and the majority of whom sleep on the premises. The kitchen at the Oxford-street range !sat the top of the house; the dining-rooms are under- neath, and here the principal meal of the day is served (rem half-past twelve until three o'clock. There are sitting- rooms for the employds when business is over, and a library of 4,000 volumes for their use. At the factories in Little Portland-street and elsewhere about 600 persons are em- ployed, while the total number of hands for whom occupa- tion in found in the various departmenteof dress and mantle. making and millinery is between 900 and 1,000, so that not less than 4,300 persons derive their direct lucerne and mainte- pewee from the establishment, There is a special department fin country orders,and an estimate of the work:daily executed throagh,cprrespondence acne may be formed from the fact that a sackful of letters are delivered every morning, the majority of *hich ate 'from the country, and must be '4lriOrtil the same evening. For the dellvety-orithekeods !mauled or made at Peter Robinenn'e about 00 horses are Maintained, in additioa to an express service for 'parcels re- quirecifor, prompt despatch. That so large a business should have grown from such small beginnings is an evidence of what can be effected by individual effort when directed to a legitimate object. That the public are now thoroughly alive to the advantages to be derived from cash payments is equally apparent, as Peter Robinson's never could have grown to such huge proportions if its principle of doing business had not been appreciated. It also 'shows that the public are not slow to respond to any well-directed move- ment by which the custetner and the shopkeeper can be put noon the most satisfactory relation towards each Aker.— Morning Post, June Bth, 1881.

div.head: LIME AND CHALK.
div.p: LIME AND CHALK.

----- Many gems lands are of a reddish-brown hue, from the large amount of sorrel there is among the grass. This is due to the large quantity of free acid that should be neutral. teed. Lime and &talk will do this, but as a matter of course Jim° would do it at once, while it would take,a year or two /or chalk to begin to have a similiar effect. In some parts of the low-lying districts of the country there are spots that grow but little besides sorrel and semi-aquatic weeds. This occurs on peaty or what are more commonly termed fen soils. In this lies an instructive lesson for application in the case in question. If a portion of this peaty soil, which produces the plant indicated, be put into a Solver- poi and." digested," as some chemists say, with a little lime, and then a mixture of sorrel, kingcnp and grass seeds be sown, the two former, which can and do feed on a free acid, will not grow. This is because the lime neutralised the free acid by again being partially restored to a state of carbonate of Hire. But While this chemical transformation has been fatal to the sorrel and kingcup, it has made the peaty soil into a condition for seeds of grasses or cereals to germinate In and grow. _ . _ _

On this the contrary, if a pot of the same soil be placed side by side with the one treated as above, described, and the soil be left in its natural state, and a mixture of the above seeds be sown in it, then the sorrel and kingcnp will germinate and flourish, but the free acid will prove so nox- ious to the grass seeds that they will not germinate at all. The lesson the result of these experiments teaches. is clear. Where sorrel and kingcups grow in superabunance —that is, to an extent in which they injure the growth of the grass—it is clear that a dressing of lime or chalk is advisable. Two or three ton of lime per acre,if it be slaked and well broadcasted, will have a due effect for three orlour years, while six or eight ton of chalk would be required to have a similar effect, and this would scarcely begin before the second year after it had been appliett, A better plan of Applying the lime,lf :it can be managed is to raise a quantity of soil on a headland, or by cleaning out ditch, or by pairing, down an unnecessarily wide hedge- row in the °autumn, andmixing the lime with it. Then, in the spring, or during the frosts of winter, this mixture may be applied at the rate of eight, ten, or twelve cartloads per acre, accerding to the quantity of °the soil available for covering the acreage that needs to be dressed. To mix lime and soil and earth in this way has a twofold advantage when applied to pastures. , The lime • makes soluble or dissolves some of the mineral constituents of the soil with which Ills mixed, which act in combination with the lime as food for the most nutritious grasses, while the lime is there at the same time with all its power to neutralise the free acid which fed the sorrel and kingcups, and allowed them to flourish. In applying chalk it should of course be put on before the frosts of winter, and when a frost has divided it into parts it should be chain-harrowed, sO as to spread the original lumps as much as possible. And, again, when a second or third frost hattfurther broken the smaller lamps into granules, by freezing the large quantity of water chalk contains, then the surface should be again well scrubbed with a chain-harrow, or a hurdle or gate, into which thorn boughs have been thickly woven. There are other instances where lime or chalk would make a marked effect on pasture land, It is a common observa- tion that patches of a pasture are bitten down bare, while other patches are scarcely touched. There is no better an- alytical agent than the nose of a cow, horse, or sheep. Where the uneaten patches are seen the grass is coarse and soar from a free acid having accumulated in the 504,.. In some cases sorrel or kingcups do not appear, but there Is the fact of the prcduce of these patches being distasteful to the animals of the farm. Lime applied in a well-slacked state to the distasteful patches would make them palatable in a few weeks after the first heavy rain, and chalk would do the same if applied as recommended above, before the end of the next year. One reason why we think chalk and lime are not apparently appreciated at their due value was this singular—not to say ludicrous—instance of wrong judg- ment. On a farm we visited two or three years ago there was a pasture as patchy as we ever saw one. Parts were eaten down by the cows on it as bare as possible, while on other parts there was enough for a good swathe. The owner of it had collected some lime and earth, and when we were there in the autumn he was putting it on the bare patches! Of course this mixture should have been applied to the un- eaten patches. As we have intimated, there .is no better agent to test the quality of grass than the nose of an animal which was designed by Nature to eat grass. An ex- periment to test the foregoing may soon be made. Where grass in which sorrel or kingcups have grown, to the injury of the grass, has been or is about to be cut, put a peck of well-slacked lime on a square rod, and watch the difference in the aftermath or autumn cup.— W. W. G. in Aricatural Gazette.

div.head: BUTTER MAKING.
div.p: BUTTER MAKING.

lln his second lecture at the-Royal Show—we gave„the I first with our report of the show—Dr.Voe'eke!: 'recommended the adoption of Lawrence's milk cooler, and said he was of opinion that dairymen .would Myer make first-rate butter wienonl," recourse o cold pump water.- One of the first necessities in the making of good butter was to have at I command an abundance of cold water—spring water, if pos. oriamnp water—to get rid of the animal heat4cs soon as thertilkoOtties froth the COW, That would get rid of the j animal- flavour. He was no adVocato for churning from '• whole milk. Whenever they had the meant of setting milk for cream be strongly advised them -to do so. •'They-Would Inot-only get a larger produce of butter, but also butter of a greater flavour, if they took care to keep cream as closely as possible to a temperature of 55 to 57 Fahrenheit. If they ; used deep pans, and in hot weather put a lump or two of ice lnthe water,'in which the pans were placed, to preserve the ternperatare below 58 deg., he guaranteed eream would keep , without turning sour for a pericd of at least eighteen hours, even at the present high temperature. Some were of opinion , that a certain degree of sourness in cream was necessary to obtain good Putter. His experience told him differently, . and he believed It was impossible to attack too forcibly the prevalent opinion of old-fashioned dairy people. His expe- rience was such as to lead him to denounce such a theory ,as radically wrong. There was an opinion that the longer • cream continued cold the worse it became. Ic was like tak- ing a wrong turning in the road—they might walk on miles and miles—the further they went, the further they got ! away from the point they wanted to reach. There was a great deal of wrong experience, but he liked to have the 'right experience. Sometimes a novelty if carefully investi- I gated proved to be far more useful if thoroughly worked , out and practically tested, than the experience of the oldest man who had been working in his own way for the last 20 years. A great many such men maintained at the present , time that the best quality of butter could only be made if , cream was allowed to turn a little sour. This was a great mistake. The sweeter the cream the better, other circum- stances being equal, the butter would tarn out. The lee- , turer then drew attention to the cream separators, as shown in work in the adjoining part of the working dairy. They were excellent instruments for separating cream from but- ter. The cream separator did great credit to its inventor. I Milk was run in a -thin stream through machinery, and by ; I centrifugal force the cream floated to the top and the skim , sank to the bottom. Milk was a mechanical mixture, not a j'chemical compound of fatty matter as cream, curd, or milk ' and sugar. They had not to deal with a chemical compound. It was well to remember that, because it was not by chemi- cal means that they separated cream from skim milks, but purely by mechanical means. The cream globules rose to, 1 the surface, and by proper management the cream was passed away from the skim milk.. In that way they ob- tained, the cream perfectly sweet, and .Pro'v,lool4thu.food Itiyen to the cows was of such a .cligacter.ps to *Once sweet and not " turnipy" cream, they Obtained' isxeellent butter by churning it. Although his profession was that of a chemist, he would say that the less chemicals they used, or the less they endeavoured to meddle with chemical agencies in the separation of better from the cream the bet- ter-the result would be. If they poured off the whey as soon as the butter came the curd was divided, and they would have butter much more free from the cheesy or curdy envelope which originally encased it in the creamy globule. It was the curdy or cheesy matter which caused afterwards rancidity in butter. The more thoroughly they removed the shells or envelopes of the butter globules the better it was. They would never make first-rate .bitter unless they preserved a regular temperature in churning.

WREN TO CUT Graft—According to the average of 13 analyses made by Professor Emile Wolf, of Germany, green grass contains 88 per .cent. of .nutrition. If Cntiyhen in bloom it will but contain 82 per cent., wherealf not cut until the seeds are fully kilned or ripe it will cortfain Ably 31 per cent, of nutrition. a THE Paartn.—At a recent meeting of the Russian Geo- graphical Society, BE-Severtiov gave some of Ihe results Of his recent visit to the Pamir mountains, in which he corrects in many important respects the generally received concep- tions as to the nature and structure of that range. The Pamir, he finds,. Is no tableland, and has to the height of some 12,00011. no steppe region. There are valleys along the rivers up to a height of 14,00011., but the widest is only 20 versts, and a wider surface is not, to be found. This peculiar feature the Pamir has lOOIIthOn with the Tien- Shan and Tibet, where similar valleys Of narrow width, at considerable heights are found. Real, lofty 040,0 k are not to be found on the Pamir. The mountains rase in lofty ridges to B,oooft. and 7,000 ft. above the valleys. The abso- lute height of the mountains of the Pamir reaches often to 19,0001 t. and three groups of great altitude reach as high as 25,0001 t. But these elevations do not alter the generally symmetrical character of the Inner Pamir. Another charac- teristic feature of the Pamir mountain region is that the mountain lines stretch in the direction of the meridian, and seldom strike out at right angles. In this respect the Southern Pamir resemble the mountains of Tibet, whereas in the Tien-Shan the tendency is to parallel ranges. In geological character, also, the Pamir seems to differ con- siderably from the Tien-Shan. M. Severtzov recognises in the lower strata evidence of the ocean gulf which once sepa- rated the Pamir from the Tien-Shan. Both are independent mountain systems, even if the elevation of the ground be- tween them it not less than 10,000 ft. The oldest formations are found in the Inner Pamir, which, in this respect, is re- garded as the groundwork of the system. Evidence was obtained to show that ale elevation of this range is still going on. In the course of 12,000 years it has risen 60011. Tag _Lusa LAND BILL ,—Lord CARLIN/3Eopm. moved the second reading of the I4nd Law (Ireland) Bill, and pointed out that tho Bill watt an exceptional one, framed to deal with an exceptiCatal state of things, which could not be measured by any standard applicable to England er Scot- land. His Lordship stated that the three main provisions of the Bill were the tight conferred on the tenant of selling his tenancy, the power of obtaining from an impartial court the settlement of the rent, and a restriction upon the landlord's right of eviction. After describing the provisions ot the Bill, the noble Lord entreated their Lordships to join with the House and with the great m.sjority of the people of this country in accomplishing a great work for Ireland.—The Marqnis of Serasatatralleged that an entire change had come over the definition of tenant right, and that now the tenants all over Ireland were to be authorised to sell for money that which they never bought. He further contended that the landlords would under this measure cease to be landlords, but would become simply agents to Serjeant O'Hagan and his colleagues, and that the arguments ad- vanced in favour of the tenantry of Ireland would apply equally in favour of artisans, and all classes would be led to believe that they had a right to come to Parliament to have their contracts made permanent. Referring to the argu- lucent that this legislation was "a message of peace to Ire- land," Lord Salisbury asked how such messages had hitherto fared? They had, he said, lamentably failed, and Ireland was more hostile to English rule now than at any time dur- ing the last century. With sc me reluctance he had been led to think it would be wise not to vote against the second reading of the Bill, but rather to see whether in Committee they could not remove from the measure some of its most glaring acts of change and injustice, lie hoped their Lord- ships would amend the Bill by securing the exemption of English managed estates, by eliminating leaseholders, and by confining the operation of the Act to tenancies below £lOO value.—Lord O'llAwof considered the Bill the most important measure relating to Ireland which had been sub- mitted to Parliament since the union.—The Marquis of LANSDOWNE looked upon the bill as an attempt to quell agrarian aggression by the indiscriminate concession of pro- prietorial rights.—The debate was adjourned.

AFGHANISTABL—The Marquis of HARLINGTON, who was "questioned about the position of Afghanistan, stated that he did not know what movement of troops under General Fume had taken place, nor did he know positively whether haman was now occupied or strengthened, but he believed ißritish force was still at Chaman. Subsequently Lord Hattington stated that there was no intention on the part of the Government of India and the Home Government to em- ploy any Anglo-Indian force in Afghanistan. . OPEN-AIR PREACHING IN CALCUTTA.—Lord HARTING- TON communicated to the House the substance of a state- ment he had received from the Viceroy respecting the pro- secution of Protestant missionaries for open-air preaching at Calcutta.—Lord RIPON stated that the Proceedings taken by the municipal authorities' were in no'svay at the instance of the Government of India, ;and that he knew nothing of the affair until Ire read it in the newspapers. He had since done all.in. hie power to promote a friendly settlement, which he hottettwouid no* be arrived at. COURSE OF PUBLIC BUSINESS. -- Mr. GransroNE made the announcement that the Government felt reluctlantly Compelled to abandon the Rivers Conservancy and Floods Prevention Bill, and also the augmentation of Benefices Bill. MR. BRADLAUGH'S ATTEMPT TO ENTER THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Mr. Bradlaugh's Attempt to enter the House of POTII., momons and take his seat, on Wednesday, led to maraca,. dinary PrOceedingti: A vast crowd had assembled outside, and the approaches to the House were strongly guarded by the police. He appeared in the lobby at a quarter to twelve. A few 'minutes past twelve the Speaker passed Into the House, and when prayers 'were over the doors were opened, and, after some other Members had passedrin Mr. Bradlaugh advanced. He was met by Mr. Erskine, the Deputy Sergeant- at-Arms.. , Mr, Bradlatigd attempted to pass. He was theft seized by several 'policemen and hustled to the door with rapidity. One account of the "scene" says a body of police pushed him along the floor, he thrusting out his fists -to resist, but never letting go his hold of the Usher. Sup: rounded by a throng of members he was pushed out of 'the lobby to the top of the private members' staircase; dawn all its flights' 6'01e:floor beneath,' and-out into Palace Yard. The struggle throughout was painful in the-last degtee, Mr. Bradlangh's coat being ,torn. On Mr. Bradlaugh making his appearance in Palace Yard, there was tr.w. immediate rush from the Hall and various parts 'of the' 'Vara, and loud cheers followed every, fresh struggle of the hononrable gentleman, who waa-obServeolby those nearest to him to be in a faint- ing condition. A glass of water was brought him. with Which ithmaid his face was bathed. ~Mr.,Dradlaugafterw- ards appeArsd at Westminster Police'Cotirt,ind applied to Mr. Shiet -f6sa summons - agalrist-,lnspeetet-`,RenplAg for assault. Meßradlaugh, having related what'had -occurred at the Hothibla Commons, said that the 'Sergeant-at-Arms was doubtless protected by the privilegent the House ; but after he was outside the House, on the pavement in front of the door opening to the members' entrance, he was prevented from entering. The assault was only of a technical charac- ter. The difficulties were, first, whether this assault took place within the precincts of the Parliament House, and, next, whether the place where the assault took place was part of the ancient Palace, and therefore out of the magis- trate's jurisdiction. i After some conversation, the considera- tion of the application was adjourned.
ORDER OF RECHABIT

The twenty-ninth movable conference of the Independent Order of Rechabites was opened at the Tem perante Hall,B rm. ingham, on Tuesday, Mr. John Dimond (Southport) presid- ing. The report of the board of directors showed that 74 new branches had been opened since the last conference, and the order now numbers 35,500 members, being an in- crease of nearly 3,000. The funds now amount to over £200,000. A large number of alterations in the laws which govern the order were placed on the digest. Many being ver- bal only, were disposed of quickly. The most important was one providing that no district or tent should divide its funds until a valuation of the assets and liabilities had been made by a qualified valuer showing the surplus, and the consent of the board of directors thereto obtained. The ruling of the High Chief Ruler at the last conference was sustained with regard to voting, no district being allowed more than four votes. The report of the official valuer, Mr. Callow, of Bradford, was presented, showing in many districts a large surplus in the funeral fund, and a very satisfactory condition of the sick fund, demonstrating the great ad- vantages of conducting friendly societies upon temperance principles.
