The executive committee of the Blackburn Weavers' Association resolved to bring out on strike the weavers em- ployed at mills, eight or ten in number, where broad red headings are woven in the cloth without extra payment. It is alleged these hands earn less wages than weavers of plain cloth, although they have much more work; and great dis- satisfaction prevails in consequence. There is already a strike at one mill on this ground.

div.head: TIP!: WESLEYAN CONFERENCE.
div.p: TIP!: WESLEYAN CONFERENCE.

At Saturday's session it was resolved that a committee should be appointed to consider the future of Mr. Garrttt's mission in Liverpool, and to report to the next Conference. The Allocation Committee reported on the number to be allotted to each district to attend the Pastoral Conference next year; the total number being 400. The report of the Memorials Committee was • brought, and the Conference agreed to the following:—" That a fresh text be printed on each new quarterly ticket for the junior society classes, that a list of theological books be prepared suitable for the read- ing of candidates for the ministry." A discussion arose upon the question of making collections in the Sunday schools for the Children's Home, in which the Pevs. G. Dickenson, H. W. Holland, W. Arthur, Dr. Stephenson, M. C. Osborn, and others took part, the latter observing that he proposed to send out circulars to the superintendents in October, asking when it would be convenient for them to have a col- lection for the orphanage, though he did not think it would be needful to trouble the superintendents with circulars for them to send to the Sunday schools. He said that the work in which he was engaged was not merely philanthropical, it was religious. The Rev. R. Roberts said he could prove that the foreign mission cause had suffered through the collections which were made for the Children's Home. It was finally agreed that the collections should not be made for the Children's Home without consulting with the superintendent of the circuit, who should fix the time for making the collection. It was I agreed that the revised baptismal service should be referred tack to the original committee, and that the com- mittee for the revision of the catechism should prepare a re- vision to submit to the original committee. After some brief conversation the recommendations of the Revising Committee for the morning service were unanimously adopted by the Conference. 'The result of this vote is, that where the Church of England service is used, it may be used still ; and when the prayers are proposed to be introduced for the first time, it will be optional to use Mr. Wesley's abridgment, the revised form now adopted by the Con- ference, or the form used by the Church of England.—The Rev, H. W. Holland's resolution, asking the President to publish a letter on the importanceof studying John Wesley's writings, was unanimously agreed to.—After the passing of the resolution, the President said he regretted the in- difference of too many Wesleyans on Mr. Wesley's writings, especially those of his writings which shed light upon their standards. The juniors did study these standards, but neglected other portions of his writings.—Tha Rev. Marshall Rarrdles was at the last Conference nominated for the Divinity Chair at Richmond College, but Dr. Osborn engaged to continue at his post another year, and in conse- quence of the continued improvement of his health he has been again appointed to the Professorship of Divinity. The Position of Mr. Randles was discussed in the Conference, and it was decided that he was freed from his nomination. The result is that for the next vacancy in any of the divinity chairs a fresh nomination and election will have to be made. The afternoon session was occupied with the reading of the Conference journal. At five o'clock strangers were admitted to witness the signing of the journal, and the Conference adjourned. 'The stations, as fixed for the Liverpool district, are as follow :

Warrington: John Eglinton, Joseph Agar Beet, Thomas Rippon ; Francis S. Hagen, supernumerary. Runcorn: John Nowell, George Hack, John Bateman (Halton). Frodsham : John M. Bamford, who shall change on one Sunday in every six weeks with the ministers of the Run- corn circuit ; Frederick F. Edmunds, supernumerary. Widnes: James H. Cummings, John Tesseyman. St. Helms and Prescot : John M. Wamsley, W. Gluyas Pascoe, Richard Crozier (Earlestown, Newton-le-Willows) ; Samuel Taylor (Rainhill), supernumerary. THE REPRESENTAITVE SECTION. The s,..ssion of this section of the Methodist Conference commenced on Monday in Brunswick Chapel, Liverpool. Dr. Osborn took the chair, and allayed the fears which had been aroused by his absence from the pulpit through indis• position. The Conference is composed of 240 ministers and 240 laymen, most of whom have been chosen by the district meetings throughout the country. The representatives of the Liverpool district are :—Revs. George Mather, J. Chal- mers, M.A., W. G. Pascoe, W. H. Tindall, Zadok Robinson, David C. Ingram, J. A. Beet (Warrington). Laymen : Dr. Dale, Messrs. J. Mack, E. Healey, S. Hough, E. Hutchinson, Lloyd Jones (all of Liverpool); G. S. Hazlehurst (Runcorn), H. R. Bowers (Chester), Joseph Meek (Wigan), T. W. Stead (Southpert), and R. Lloyd (Newtown). The President, in openingeverytii ntgh eh andu vs irnoecsese, dreedf el ar rsetdw et oe kth eHhea rtmr uosnteyd wt hi t h elly which not lose sight of their spiritual work in the msideration of the temporal.

MEMORIALS AND SUGGESTIONS. Rev. F. W. Greeves, secretary of the Memorials Com- mittee, brought up several memorials from districts includ- ing-.--Bolton: That the Conference use its influence in favour of Wesleyan ministers performing the marriage rite without the presence of a registrar. Sheffield: For the amalgamation of the children's and schools' funds, and the reduction of the number of connexional collections. Hull : Concerning; the expense incurred in the removal of ministers from one circuit to another. ECUMENIC AL CONFERENCE. This question was introduced by the Rev. John Bond (secretary). Eighty-seven representatives from English Wesleyanism were to be elected, 44 mincsters and 43 lay- men. Out of 43 laymen, it was agreed that six, who have been appointed to read papers before the Conference, should be elected ex-gficio, viz. :—Messrs. T. M. Banbridge, F. G. Osborn, M.A., G. J. Smith, M.A., R. W. Perks, H. T. Atkin- son, and R. W. Allen. The reinaining 37 laymen were to be elected by ballot after nomination. It was decided that, as ministers only had voted for ministers, laymen only should vote for laymen. Nearly 100 lay gentlemen were then nomi- nated, the following being the result of the voting :—The Lord Mayor of London, 150; Mr. H. 11. Fowl er, M.P., 132; Mr, S. D. Waddy, Q.C., 131; Mr. Mewburn 127; Mr. James Wood, 124; Mr. A. McArthur, M.P., 121; Mr. T. F. C. May, 121; Mr. Sguance, 114; Mr. W. W. Pocock, 113 ; Mr. Bick- ford Smith, 108; Mr. J. W. Gabriel, 105; Mr. John Dyson, 104; Mr. F. Howard, 103; Mr. J. Beauchamp and Mr. P. W. Bunting, 100; Mr. Warrington and Mr. Isaac Hoyle, 98; Mr. James Barlow, 94; Mr. S. Cole, 93; Mr. J. H. Mason and Mr. H. Mitchell, 91; Mr. T. W. Pocock, 90; Mr. S. Rathbone Edge, 88; Mr. James Sutcliffe, 87; Mr. Joseph Edge, 86; Mr. J. S. Budgett, 83; Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst, 82; Mr. E. Healey, 79 ; Mr. Geo. Lidgett, 73; Mr. Alderman Barlow, 72; Mr. W. H. Budgett and Mr. J. R. Hill, 71; Mr. John Dingley, 70; Mr. Holden, 68; Mr. J. Jenks, 65; Mr. Lewis Williams, 63; and Mr. J. J. Flitch, 61. HONE MISSIONS. Rev. A. WAulay moved the adoption of the report of this fund, and that an abstract be printed in the minutes of the conference. The ex-President seconded it, and it was carried unanimously.—Rev. J. W. Greeves read the financial statement of the fund. The total income during the past year had been £33,766 19s. 4d., while the expenditure was £33,404 2e. 2d. Grants were made to circuits to the amount of £10,431. It was resolved that the following resolution of last Conference be repeated :—" The Home Missionary Committee has authority to employ, in addition to district missionaries, ministers and lay agents for general evangelistic work in different parts of the Connexion. During the next year all the arrangements connected with the employmeet of such evangelical agents shall be left to the discretion of the Home Missionary Committee ; and the committee shall report to the next Conference as to the regulations which they judge advisable in regard to the employment of such agents."—lt was stated that the fund was in a better condition this year than last by about £6OO. - WORU IN THE ARMY. In the evening session the Rev. R. W. Allen introcLiceci this subject. Some time ago the Wesleyan Home Missionary Committee applied to the War Office for payment for seats occupied in Wesleyan chapels by soldiers who are marched to the Wesleyan tninistry. The War Office declined to pay in that form, but consented to give the ordinary capitation grant, as in the case of other religious denominations.—The Rev. A. WAislay moved "That the Conference accept the offer of the Government, and instruct the committees con- c,rned to take such steps in relation to the money that tu ty be received as will secure fair remuceration for provision for Wesleyan soldiers in our chapels, and at the same time the . utmost efficiency of our work in the army." He said they bad originally asked the War Office for pew rents only. Now they had offered more. Why should they decline? Some thought it wati concurrent endowment, but it was not. The Government compelled soldiers to go to worship somewhere, and many of them chose to go to Wesleyan chapels. Why, 1 then, should their trustees be compelled to decline what was , practically payment for the seats they occupied 2—Mr. Dawkins (Pembroke) seconded the resolution.—Mr. Alder- man Rees (Dover) moved an amendment to the effect that the offer of the Government be declined. He believed if the principle were adopted it would tend to officialism in the re- lation of the War Office to their Church. He had had some
was i

- experience in reference to mili:ary affairs in Gibraltar and China, and he would deprecate, through such a grantas that, that the freedom of the Methodist minister. should be lost. —The Rev. R. Hardy said if it were simply a question of pay to ministers they would oppose it. But they asked only for pew rents. He supported the resolution. The original resolution was carried by a large majority. The following resolution was passed: —"That all ap- pointments of additional ministers to the cir- cuits made at the Conference nf 1881, 1882, and 1883 shall be subject to such financial arrangements relating to con- nexional funds as may be made during the three years." Also the following :—" That whenever a minister shall be withdrawn from a circuit, in the receipt of an ordinary grant, unless used for aggressive purposes within the district under the direction of the District Home Mission Sub-corn- mittees it shall revert to the general fund." The commit- tee was reappointed, and the officers thanked.

div.head: FERNLEY LECTURE.
div.p: THE FERNLEY LECTURE.

The Rev. F. W. Macdonald delivered the Fernley Lecture last evening in Wesley Chapel, Upper Stanhope-street, before a very crowded congregation. Its title was "Dogma," and the preacher delivered a brilliaM anl exhaustive elucida- tion of the subject.

div.head: SESTEN'TATION FUND.
div.p: THE SESTEN'TATION FUND.

_ The Secretary read the report of the Sustentation Fund, the object of which is to raise every married minister's stipend t o £l5O, and that of every unmarried minister to £BO. Since the establishment of the food £lB,OOO has been raised, and £15,000 in the circuits in response to the grants; and the total amount raised is £33,744 ; 31 out of the 33 dis- tricts contribute to the fund. From the report of the Chapel Committee it,appears that 141 new chapels have been com- pleted, at a cost of £299,912 ; 13 ministers' houses, £13,205; 26 schoolrooms, £12,324 ; 89 alterations and enlarelnents,

£55,087; 14 organs, £5,326. The average cost per sitting of the 141 new chapels is £6 12s. 90. Of these new chapels 43 have been erected in places where there were previously no Wesleyan Methodist chapds ; and 98 supersede former erections, which, according to the returns, provided 19,312 sittings. The total additional accemmodation provided in the new chapels is, thetefore, 25,852 sittings. The chapel enlargements provide 1,817 sittings, making the total addi- tional accommodation represented in these returns as 26,669 sittings. The report of the committee of the fond for the Relief and Extension of Methodism in Great Britain was read and adopted. During the year grants for chapels and sites from this fund have been made to the amount of £4,749.

METROPOLITAN CHAPEL BUILDING FUND. This business had been postponed to Wednesday to meet the convenience of the Lord Mayor of London, the treasurer, who occupied a place on the platform during the review of the work of this department During the year the com- mittee have inspected eight sites in the different metropoli- tan circuits. Chapels have been opened at Greenwich and at Old Ford, while several are in course of erection. Forty- one of the proposed 50 chapels have now been commenced, and five projected schemes are still under consideration by the committee. £2,050 has been paid as loans for sites, £1,657 as loans and grants for new erections, and £2,750 as grants from the special fund. The ordinary subscriptions, donations, and collections amounted to £1,315, a decrease of , £B2, loan instalments repaid £1,561. The sum of £2,604 Os. 6d. has been received during the year on account of the special provincial fund. Eleven commodious chapels have been commenced during the year, the largest number recorded for any one year since the establishment of the fund. On the motion of Dr. Pope, a resolution, expressing deep sorrow at the loss occasioned by the death of Sir Francis Lvcett was adopted, and a letter of condolence was ordered to be sent to Lady Lycett. Votes of thanks were accorded to the officers.

THE SCHOOLS FUND. For some years the condition of the schools for the chil- dren of Wesleyan ministers has occupied the most serious attention of the ministers and laymen, and been discussed in the conference, district meetings, and specially appointed committees. The funds have not increased in proportion to the claims, and the yearly deficiency makes it absolutely necessary that something should be done. There are now two schools for the sons of ministers (one at Eingswood and the other at Woodhouse-grove), and two for the daughters of ministers (cne at Southport, the gift of the late John Fernley, Esq., and the other at Queenswood, near London), the education of the children not being regarded as a part of the ordinary circuit income of the minister. It appeared that an annual saving of £2,300 would be effected by con- centrating the two boys' schools on one site—a proposition favoured by 10 districts and opposed by 21. The financial statement, by Mr. T. C. Squance, showed a present debt of £4,048 18s. Bd. • .

The Rev. G. W. OLVER, 8.A., moved a resolution in favour of immediate concentration on the site at New Kings- wood.—A long discussion ensued, which had not concluded when the conference adjourned. The members with their hosts and hostesses were enter- tained at an "At Home" in the Town Hall by the Mayor of Liverpool. This day was chostn on which to do honour to the Lord Mayor of London who could only attend the con- ference on Wednesday. The Lord Mayor of London, the president and secretary of the conference, the chairman of the district, the Rev. F. W. Briggs, M.A., and others, pre- viously lunched with the Mayor. At the Wesleyan Representative Conference, on Thurs- day, the debate on the proposed concentration of the schools for ministers' SODS at New Kingswood, Bath, was resumed. After a protracted discussion, in which Dr. Rigg. the Rev. Henry W. Holland, and others took part, a vote was taken, when it was agreed, in the proportion of three to one, that the Conference direct that the scheme for the immediate concentration of the schools at New Kingwood be carried out by the general committee. It was subsequently arranged to meet the deficiency in income by a levy on ministers and circuits.

CONFERENCE OF CFPISTIAN CHURCHES. The annual meeting of representatives of churches of Christ in Great Britain and Ireland, "pleading for an Un- reserved return to Christianity as taught by Christ and his apostles," was commenced on Tuesday, in the Co-operative Hall, Manchester. The proceedings began with a conference of Sunday-school workers, presided over by Mr. W. M‘Lin- took, of Glasgow. Statistical reports and other items of interest were presented and discussed. A considerable ex- change of thought took place on the relation between the faithfulness of teachers and the success of schools, as regards the number of children, the retention of elder scholars, and the a 'ditions to the churches. A system of examination of teachers and scholars, which bad been in force for some years, was under consideration, and it PM resolved to con- tinue it, subject to improvements to'be introduced by the committee representing the schools during the year. During the afternoon session, a paper was read by Mr. James Grin- stead, evangelist, Wakefield, on "The duty of the Church of Christ to the young and how to perform it." The paper was well received, ano ordered to be printed in the Ecclesiastical Observer and the Christian Advocate, the organs of the body. One prominent feature in the treatment of the subject was the contention that it is the duty and privilege of the churches to encourage and receive into their fellowship young disciples at whatever age their intelligence enables them to understand the truths and requirements of the gospel. In the evening the delegates met in augmented numbers to receive reports and schedules from the churches id co-opera- tion. Mr. T. T. Wallis, of Huddersfield, was called to preside over the meetings, and delivered an interesting opening address.

On Tuesday morning, the report of the Evangelist Com- mittee was received and discussed, and a resolution was carried, calling upon the Churches to develop all the avail- able talent in the membership in order that they may realise the apostolic intention of an effective mutual ministry, leaving the evargelists to assist weak churches and break up new ground. During the afternoon session the Cenference paper was read by Mr. Gilbert Y. Tickle jun., of Liverpool, on the subject: The duty of the churches in relation to the drinking customs of the country." The psper dealt with the ravages of drink in society and the churches in a most comprehensive and able manner, and a long and important discussion followed. There was almost perfect unanimity as to the duty of members and churches in relation to the use of unfermented wine at the Lord's Supper, to personal abstinence from intoxicants, and on the legislative aspects of the drink question. At six o'clock there was a conference of Sisters, at which a consultation was held upon the best means by which they might further the work of the Lord in their respective churches, and at half•past seven o'clock Mr. David King, nf Birmingham, editor of the Ecclesiastical Observer, preached upon the authority,of the Apostles tb legislate for the Church of , Christ, in connection with the giving of the keys of the kingdom to Peter, and the sole right of the Apostles to bind and loose in relation to the things of the kingdom. Mr. King, in a brilliant and exhaustive discourse, which was received with breathless attention, dealt with his subject in a masterly manner. He dwelt at length upon the admissions of the late Dean Stanley on the practice of the early Chris- tian churches, especially in regard to baptism, showing that infant baptism was unknown to the Primitive Christians. The speaker contended that the Apostles legislated once for the Church of Christ, and, though dead, yet they now ruled through their words and the laws they had promulgated under Divine inspiration, and that it was the duty of all Christians to yield implicit obedience to their commands.

_ The above conference was continued on Thursday, in the Co-operative Hall, Manchester, when the sessions were occu- pied in making arrangements for the labours of the evan- gelists in response to many and urgent calls for help. •At seven o'clock in the morning a meeting of temperance friends attending the conference was held in the Grosvenor-street Chapel, belonging to the body presided over by Mr. W. E. Knight, Huddersfield. A. memorial was adopted calling on the Government to redeem, at the earliest possible moment, their pledges on the licensing question. During the day a resolution was passed appealing to the Government to amend the law that forces the opium trade on China, also one expressing sympathy- with . Pivaident— and Mrs. Garfield in their affliction, and joy at the favourable reports of his condition that have reached us; the President being a member of the religious body now represented in I Manchester. It was resolved to hold the next conference at ' Leicester. The meetings were brought to a close by a social meeting in the Co-operative Hall, under the presidency of Mr. Alexander Brown, of Glasgow, when stirring addresses Were delivered by Messrs. Shepl4td(of Canada West), B. Ellis (London), P.Staphen.(Chester),Leavesle,y (Leicester), Adam (Ireland), D. King' Pirmingham ), and' others. Dele- gates were present from St. Helens, .Watrington, Liverpool, Wigan, Golborne, Smithport,'Preston Blackburn, Oldham, kc. It should be stated that th e dele;rates ea members of '- churches assembled disclaimed all Power•to enact laws, or to intermeddle with the affairs of individual churches, and that the conference -was exclusively a co-operation for
evangelization.

• THE DISCOVERY OF In-wait CHINII:IS' AT LLYTRPOOL. CONFESSION OF T,HE„__,B44XER. CHICAGO, JULY 31.—The Chicago Inter Ocean publishes intelligence from Peoria, Illinois, asserting that Mr. F. W. Crowe, the Irish Nationalist;e.Oknowledges having manu- factured the cases in which the infernal machines recently seized at Liverpool were packed, and that he had the in- teriors made in New York, where more machines of similar kind were being constructed. Mr. Crowe is further represented as having declared that the oronisation which he represents believe that they are not liable to proseca. ,tion, and will continue their work until England does justice to Ireland.

At a meeting of the Welsh Calvinistic Methodist Associa• tion at Dowlsis, on Tuesday, resolutions were passed deprt. eating the attempted murder of President Garfield, and approving of the Welsh Sunday Closing Bill. div.head: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL
div.p: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL

The quarterly meeting of this Council was held on Wednesday, the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) presiding! There were also present Aldermen Mcßryde, Johnson, and Gamble, Councillors Twyford, Baxter, Hanson, Bishop Belsher, Wilcock, and Brook.

div.head: VISIT TO THE VYRNIVY WORKS.
div.p: VISIT TO THE VYRNIVY WORKS.

The MAYOR: I have no formal communication to make, but I may say that since our last meeting I accepted an in- vitation from the Mayor of Liverpool to accompany him and the Corporation of Liverpool on a visit to the new waterworks at Vyrnwy to see the first stone laid by the Earl of Powis. The town clerk was also invited, and he accompanied me. I mention this because St. Helens is SO deeply interested in a good supply of water, and, as you are aware, St. Helens will be supplied ultimately when Liver- pool get their gupply completed, which will be probably in three or four years. We were very much impressed with the suitability of the site, and we all considered—and there were 180 present—that the waterworks would be one of the finest in Europe. (Hear, hear.) Whilst on this subject, I may say that within the last few days I had the pleasure of dining with the Lord Mayer of London, the Mayor of York, and many mayors and mayoresses in the country. I say this because I consider it an honour to the town as well as to myself. (Hear, hear.) MATTER OF MANAGEMENT. Mr. WilkoCa said he had been told by several ;arties that the 7nen in the water department, such as turneocks and others employed out of doors, waited in the yard every morning for the arrival of Mr. Gaskin, the water engineer, before they turned out. He thought this a waste of time.— Alderman GAMBLE promised to bring the matter before the Water Committee at their next meeting.

GAS COMMITTEE. The following minutes of the Gas Committee were con- firmed :—Resolved, that Mr. Dyson obtain tenders for the supply of 300 Peebles and Borradale's gas governors, and that the chairman have instructions to accept one of such tenders.—The Manager produced a quantity of old gas ser- vice pipes recently taken up, which were completely des- troyed by corrosion.—The Manager reported that during the past month 4,427,600 cubic feet of gas had been produced at these works, of an average illuminating power equal to M 1 sperm candles.—Resolved, that the Manager have in- structions to remove the partition wall between the com- mittee-room and the old laboratory at the Gas Works, so as to enlarge the committee-room.—Resol red, that the gas main in Cross-at. be extended to Henry-st. with a three-inch pipe. —Resolved that the offer of Mr. Ralph Betley, of Wigan, to make a quarterly test of the gas produced at these works, for the sum of £8 per annum, be accepted for 12 months; and that Councillors Wilcock and Twyford be authorised to buy a horse for this department.—Mr. Dyson reported that he had invited tenders for the supply of 30 lamp tops.—Re- solved that the Chairman be authorised to accept one of such tenders when received.

HEALTH COMMITTEE. The minutes of the Health Committee having been sub- mitted, and proposed and seconded for confirmation, Mr. Wrizocx asked if it was the duty of the Health Committee to take any notice of a paragraph which had appeared in a local paper iq reference to the weighing of bread to the people? ("No, no.") I heard It came within the province of the Medical Officer.—The MAYOR: I don't think we can recognise newspaper reports.—Mr. WILCOCK : But the mean- ing is, according to the statement of that, that we are not working according to the Act of Parliament.—The MAyoR : I don't think we can deal with reports in the newspapers.— The minutes were confirmed. THE CLOCK.—THE COVERING FOR THE MARKET. Mr. Wrizocx moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Parliamentary Committee from which it appeared that Mr. W. S. Blundell, of Liverpool, bad attended the com- mittee on the subject of the Town Hall clock, and after the subject had been discussed and the committee's feeling of dissatisfaction of the clock had been expressed, it was- resolved that Messrs. Blundell furnish a full report as to any requirements necessary in the clock to make it a correct time keeper and to work satistactorily.—The Market Sub-- Committee resolved that the Parliamentary, Improvement, and General Purposes Committee be requested to conskler the question of paving or asphalting the streets leading to. the Market-place.—That the Treasurer be instructed to look through the books of the late St. Helens Improvement Com- missioners with the abject of finding the date of the erection by them of a wall in the passage near.the fish market, at the point now visited. That he subsequently see the chairman, who should summon a special meeting ef the committee, to consider the matter if he deems it necessary.—Mr. BAXTER seconded the motion.—Mr. BROOK: I should like to ask the Chairman of the Sub-Committee if he knows anything about the covered market? I think it is time something was done. It is a shame to see people standing outside in the wet and cold in the winter time.—Mr. BEISHIM : With regard to this question I can only say that we are not yet in a posi- tion to snake a statement which we consider will be satis- factory to the Council as regards the Ifit and loss of the undertaking. We want to show that Ws c * make an- additional profit on the market income .to pay t,.r the ad- ditional outlay. The matter is not being lost sigh: ; have it still under condition, in fact there is a notice of a special meeting to be called previous to the next Parliamen- tary Committee when we hope to make a statement to that committee.—The MAYOR: Then it will come forward at another meeting. Is that satisfactory, Mr. Brook ?—Mr. BROOK : Quite satisfactory, Mr. Mayor.—The minutes were confirmed.

COMPENSATION POR DAMAGES : DISPUTE BETWEEN COM- MITTEES AS TO RESPONSIBILITY. The minutes of the Paving Committee contained the following:—" The Surveyor submitted a letter from Mr. Tipping, of Bold, claiming compensation in respect of damage alleged to have been caused to a mare belonging to him by falling into a hole in Sutton-road, near to the pump- ing station. After consideration of the matter, it was resolved, but without prejudice, that the chairman with the surveyor, have authority to settle the claim with Mr. Tip- ping upon the best terms they can; that this committee consider that, under the circumstances the Water Com- mittee account be debited with one-had or any sum that may be paid to Mr. lipping in the matter."—Alderman• JoussoN moved, and Mr. BEtswEn seconded, the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Bnoox : It appears you are allowing compensation to Mr. Tipping, and that you have declined it I to Mrs. Lyon, whose horse was injured in a similar manner in Boundary-road. I should like to know the difference between the two accidents.—Alderman JOHNSON said that in Mrs. Lyon's case the contractor engaged in putting down the sewer was responsible, as he had charge of the road.—Alderman GAMBLE said it was proposed to charge one-half of the com- pensation to the water account. He hoped the Council would not sanction that, as it was quite clear that the Water Committee had no more to do with that accident than had the occupier of a house in Church-street if a sewer fell in where he was living. He moved that the minutes be con- firmed with the exception of that part of the clause which proposed to debit the Water Committee with one-half the cost.—Alderman MCBRYDE seconded the amendment, and said the Water Committee went thoroughly into the matter, and came to the conclusion that they had nothing to do with it, but that it was muter the supervision of the Sur- veyor.—Alderman Jowsrsow said from the statement made at the Paving Committee, the steam from the Water Com- mittee's pumping station had caused a subsidence of the soil, which gradually crumbled in, so that there was only a small covering of earth which fell in when the horse stepped upon it. That was the report given to them, and he believed it was very likely to occur again unlees there was some altera- tion in the blowing off of the boiler. The Paving Committee I would be very sorry indeed to charge the Water Committee, 1 but under the circumstances they thought only reasonable. —Mr. BISHOP said there was nothing said at the Paving Committee about the boiler, but what Mr. Hart said was that a pipe after having been approved by him had been broken by somebody; and there was evidence that the pipe had been broken before being filled in. Mr. Hartsaid nothing about steam, but that it was simply the drain that had broken in; the water then wastedlaway the soil naturally.— Alderman JOHNSON was aware that the pipe had been broken I but Mr. Hart supposed that the man after laying the pipe, I and making it solid must have broken it, and covered it over with a piece of flag. The flag then had given wiy-bi the action of the steam, andocaused the subsidence.—Alderman MCBRYDE : It is just as likely as not that the steam roller I did it. (Laughter.)—Mr. BELSRER : Nay, nay, don't lay on the steam roller that which he is not guilty of. Idon't think he is blameable for anything of this sort. (Laughter.) Mr. Hart did not suggest that the pipe had been broken in consequence of the steam ; it came from some members of the Paving Committee, and it was ascertained' in the course of the discussion that this was the drain that con- veyed the water from the boilers. In his opinion the ordinary drain pipes were not of sufficient strength to resist the pressure brought to bear upon them in that sewer. That drain should have been of iron.—Mr, BAXTER suggested that the matter be referred to a joint committee of the Paving and Water Committees to inquire further into the facts of the of the case.—Alderman JOHNSON had no objection to that course.—Alderman GAMBLE said he knew nothing of the transaction beyond what had been told him by the deputy chairman, and he had no objection in withilravring his amendment in order that the matter might be ref el red hack to the Paving Committee.--On being informed that Mr. 13a.t• ter's suggestion was that the matter be inquired into by a joint committee.—Alderman GAMBLE objected as he did not see why the members should be put to the inconvenience of assembling to discuss the matter. He repudiated a 1 liability on the part of the Water Committee.—Alderman Jormrsow I don't understand Mr. Alderman Gamble'cargument. He was not at the meeting; he hears the statement of one per- son in favour of the Water Committee, but attaches no im- portance to the other statements made now, and I don't know the' reason unless is that he feels more intere,st in the Water Committee and that the Water Committee should not pay the bill. (I,aughter.) I certainly cannot see any valid reason, and I think it is a very good suggestion on the part of Mr. Baxter. If the surveyor is to blame, let him be blamed, but here is the expense caused by this accident, and I think these things ought to be inquired into.—Alderman Gamble's amendment was then put, when four voted for it, and five against it. It was declared lost.— Alderman GAMBLE: I beg to move that the minutes be ap- proved with the exception of the clause referred to, such to be referred back to the joint meeting of the Paving and Water Committee. (Laughter.)—Mr. Harrsow seconded, and the motion was carried.
The minutes of the Finance -Committee, recommending the payments of accounts—£3,243 18s. 3d. in aeneral ac- count, £982 9s. 7d. on water account, and £3,736 6s. sd. on , gas account—were confirmed.

LOU ‘l, NOTES.

Runcorn has not proved an exceptionally fruitful soil for the plant of Congregationalism. Perhaps this may be ac- counted for by the strength of the Wesleyan and Church of England sections of the religious community in the town ; but Jam glad to be able to report that Independency is now decidedly looking up, as will be admitted when I state that the church and congregation at Bethesda Chapel have decided to erect the Rev. J. D. Thomas, the pastor, a manse, at a cost of about £650, to- wards which about £3OO has already been sub- scribed. The plans of the building, which will be bituate in the new street immediately above the cemetery in Green- way-road, have been already passed by the Board of Com- missioners. Whilst upon this subject I may add that an effort is being made to secure a sermon from the Rev. Dr. Parker, of the City Temple, London, to b 3 preached at Bethesda Chapel; and also that a Flower Queen service of song isto be given this year after the style of the one which proved so successful last year, when it was held in the Public Hall. It was stated at the Wesleyan Conference at Liverpool on the 24th ult. that "in consequence of the long-continued commercial depression the funds of Methodism have seriously suffered, and owing to the too rapid multiplica- tion of ministers in years of prosperity many circuits are in financial difficulties, and instead of applying for addi- tional ministers are in some cases diminishing their num- bers!' The Runcorn Wesleyans may be congratulated on the capital financial position of thecircuit, but of course, the town has for many years been exceptionally situated owing to the chapels having been presented to the denomination by the late Mr. liazlehurst.

The meeting of the Runcorn Commissioners this week was a very tame sort of affair, probably on the principle that a calm always follows a storm. The two members who have made themselves so conspicuous at late meetings were present, but white-robed peace appeared to have descended upon their spirits, and not a solitary syllable was uttered that might not have been heard at the quietest Local Board in the kingdom. Jr. Curzon, who has made himself famous in the local struggles of the past, has thrown himself into the breach, like another Horatius,„,who, in classic story kept the bridge so nobly. He is apparently determined that the contract, which it is proposed to make with Mr. Cliff for the cleansing of the streets for a period of several years, shall not be entered into if be can prevent it. He presented a petition on the question, signed by some 300 ratepayers, who are of opinion that it would not be for the good of the town economically or otherwise that the work should pass out of the hands of the Commissioners. Mr. Curzon's eloquence is generally distinguished by some striking metaphors, but when he went so far as to say that these who had spoken in favour of Mr. Cliff having the contract, on the ground that it would be a saving to the town, had repre- sented that if the work were entrusted to that gentleman the ratepayers would be enabled to walk about in silver slippers, whereas they were likely to each have to purchase top boots, he was drawing the long bow with a vengeance. Possibly Mr. Curzon has what the Yankees call "an axe to grind," or he would not have used such extreme language in dealing with the matter. Without going into the ques- tion of whether Mr. Dobson is justified in calling the action of the supporters of Mr. Cliff revolutionary, I may say that I am of opinion that Dr. McDougall and the chairman of the Board (Dr. Steele) seem to have a good foundation for their remarks to the effect that the Commissioners had not treated the contractor in a business-like manner, and that they ought to decide one way or another what course they intend to pursue. Mr. Dobson's proposal that Mr. Cliff should be asked what he will take to free the Board from any liability, appears to admit that the Commissioners have gone so far as to enable that gentleman to sue them for breach of contract if they come to the decision that the agreement shall not be completed. It seems very strange that Mr. Cliff should have been permitted to commence work before the document was signed. Certainly such a course is also a most singular one for some of the members of the Board to have sanctioned.

I may state that there is certainly a pretty strong feeling in the town against the old men who have previously been employed as scavengers being left to the tender mercies of the workhouse officials after they have worked so many years fer the Commissioners.

There was a bright bit of colour, so to speak, in the meet- ing of the Runcorn Commissioners this week, and it re- lated to literature. The number of columns of matter which have appeared in The Examiner since it was first published, on the desirability of Runcorn having a public library, must have been enough to call forth the "Prodigous "of Dominic Sampson, if he yet visited these glimpses of the moon. It appears that at last there is a slight hope that the rate- payers of Runcorn may ultimately have a public library, thanks to the indefatigable perseverance with which this ob- ject has been followed by Mr. W. Handley and other friends of the movement. The Commissioners have decided, on the motion of that gentleman, to appoint a committee for the purpose of opening up communications with the managers of the Literary Institute with a view to acquiring the public library possessed by them fof the use of the town. Mr. Hand- ley expressed himself as confident that the committee of the institute would do all they could to forward any movement which had for its object the intellectual advancement of the town. Dr. McDougall, who is becoming quite an old resi- dent in the town, gave a brief and interesting history of the subscription library which existed in the town some four- teen years ago, and which was afterwards removed to the Literary Institute, and forms, I believe, the greater portion of the books possessed by that association.

The Rev. George Hack, formerly of Sherborne, is the gentleman who will succeed the Rev. Henry Valentine as minister in the Wesleyan Methodist circuit. Mr. Hack is spoken of as a very popular man in the pulpit. The friends of the Rev. W. Robinson, lately of Trinity Church, Runcorn, will be pleased to hear that the gentle- man speaks in very pleasant terms of his new sphere of labour.

Several ef the principal thoroughfares of Runcorn are at present in a most disagreeable state. They are sprinkled liberally with rather large stones which have not been fixed in the ground, but have, in the primitive manner common to some towns of the same size, been thrown on the road and allowed to take their chance. The result is that several of the roads are left in a state which is most irritating to the tender feet of ladies. I feel sure that this matter only needs to be brought under the attention of Mr. Barker, the town's surveyor, for kim to see that his subordinates do their work in a different manner. FLACCUS.

Ix RE Thos. BEASLEY.—At the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court on Tuesday, the public examination of this bankrupt, a solicitor at Widnes and Runcorn, was further adjourned to the 12th inst. Mr. Seger appeared for the creditors, Mr. Copeman for the bankrupt, and Mr. W. Morris for Mr. Rolland, the trustee. MErirory Maslow TO SEAXEN.—On Sunday, the anniversary sermons in connection with the branch of this mission at Runcorn, will be preached in the Public Hall, and addresses delivered by Mr. Roberts and Mr. Pearson, of Liverpool. On Monday, the annual excursion will take place, the steamer leaving Duke's Pier at ten in the morn- ing and returning from Liverpool at half-past seven. The excursionists will have the privilege of visiting the training ship "Indefatigable," the fire station, one of the large Atlantic steamers, and the Sailors' Home. The fares for adults are Is. 3d. each.

Bowriwop RuNco—On Saturday afternoon, George Jones and R. Hatbbone, played a game of bowls on the green attached to the Norton Arms Hotel, Halton. The game was 21 up, and resulted in favour of Jones by 14 points. - - -- WIDNES PROPERTY OWNERS' AND RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIATION.—The sixth annual meeting of this associa- tion was held on Wednesday evening, at the Market Hotel, Widnes, Mr. James Rimmer in the chair. The business of the past year having been discussed, the committee were congratulated on the work accomplished during the twelve- months. It was unanimously resolved that the association retain the services of those members who have so ably ful- filled their several offices during the past year. Also "that vigorous efforts be put forth during the coining year for the accomplishment of the objects of the association. and that the voice of the ratepayers shall be made heard—and their votes recorded when the time comes—both at the election of the Local Board and School Board against those who now refuse to hear them." If was also resolved "that a number of gentlemen belonging to the association be appointed to examine the estimate for the new rate, and, if necessary, to I oppose it ;—also that a careful eye be kept on the new sewerage scheme, so that it may be done for the benefit of the town and not for the benefit of a certain portion only." Several new members having joined, the proceeding termi- nated with a vote of thanks to the chairman.

div.head: SATILitDAY, A_FGU-ST* 6, 1881.
div.p: SATILitDAY, A_FGU-ST* 6, 1881.

M. PIERPOINT, OP RUNCORN, AND THE ROYAL ACADEILY.-Mr. Bantock Pierpoint, of Runcorn, was suc- cessful in obtaining a bronze medal at the late examination in connection with the Royal Academy of Music, London. This, we understand, is the highest prize he could gain, owing to the short time which he has been connected with the Academy.
WARRINGTON CEIIRTRRY.—Returns of interments in the Warrington Cemetery during the week ending yesterday : Adults, 8; children, 9 ; total 17.

THE FOOT-AND-MOUTIT DISEASE.—There are now 47 farms affected with foot-and-mouth disease in Lanca- shire, of which number 40 are in the Blackburn Hundred. Thirteen fresh farms were infected during the past week, and 98 fresh animals.

WIDNES AND BANK HOLIDAY.—MOSt of the trades- men in Widnes closed their places of business on Monday last, but many of the works were not closed. About 500 people left the London and North-Western station for Llandudno, in connection with the trip organised by the Catholics. Great numbets went to Liverpool and Man- chester, and a fair proportion to Knowsley. The weather was of a most delightful character. A STACK FIRE AT RIINCORN.—Very early on Mon- day mcrning, a stack of hay was found to be on fire upon the premises of Mrs. Simpson,Sea-lane, Runcorn. Informa- tion was sent to the Fire Brigade, who were on the ground in a very few minutes, and commanded by Mr. Wright. They were successful in saving a considerable amount of hay from being destroyed. The damage done, which i* covered by insurance. amounted to about £3O.

COLLEGE OF PRECEPTORS' EXAMINATIONS.— In the Class List, just published in the " Educational Times," the name of W. Duncan, from Cambridge Schbol, Sale (Rev. T. W. Gibson, M.A.), appears second in order of merit in music, amongst all candidates in England. St. Peter's Band will play the following selection in the Park, on Wednesday, August 10th, at seven p.m. : March, " Sir Garnet Wolseley," De Lacy; quadrille?, "Songs of the day," Coote; selection, "Beatrice di Penal,' Ballini ; grand march, "Triumphal," Herold; valses "Royal Caledonian," De Lacy; selection, "Popular airs,'' Newton ; "God save the Queen."

BANK HOLIDAY AT RIINCORN.—SIT Jail Lubbock's festival was very well observed in Runcorn, nearly all shops and places of business being closed during the afternoon. The Sons of Temperance had a pub`ic demonstration, which attracted considerable attention. Thousands left the town for Liverpool, Manchester, Overton, and Helsby, and the railway station presented a very busy appearance all day. The weather was of a charming description.

ORCHARD ROBBERY AT BEWSEY.—A boy named James Fallow was charged at the Occasional Court House, yester- day, before Mr. George Artingstall, with stealing apples from the orchard of Mrs. Warburton, Bewsey Hall farm. Mrs. Warburton found the prisoner in the orchard at five o'clock that morning, and in his pockets were about 41bs. of apples.—He was tined 2s. 6d. and costs.

On Saturday, the Master of the Rolls had before him a petition for the reconstruction of the Southport and West Lancashire Banking Company. The scheme included the creation of a new company, and the proposals for recon- struction had received the assent of the shareholders and creditors of the company. His lordship approved the scheme.

CLUB WAVES, OVER.—On Saturday last another of those clubs or friendly sccieties, of which Winsford and Over have several, paraded the streets of tine district, pre- r Iratory to having their annual dinner at the Red Li on, Over. Arrayed in the style of Robin Hood and his merry men, they presented a very grotesque appearance, which alone was calculated N draw the attention of the hundreds who flocked out to see them. We understand the lodge is in a capital working condition.

On Saturday, Mr. Superintendent Barker, who has been at the head of the county force in Barrow for nine years, and who is about to enter on similar duty at Prescot, was presented with a purse of £260, and an illuminated address, subscribed for by magistrates, property owners, tradesmen, and others, as a mark of appreciation for the very satisfac- tory manner in which he has discharged his duty during this period. BANE HounAY AT Wiatarnorox.—The Bank Holi- day of Monday last was observed by nearly all the trades- people of Warrington except a few grocers in the vicinity of Market Gate, and as the sun shone brilliantly during the greater part of the day, the holiday-makers had an enjoyable time of it. The railway companies did a large passenger traffic as many hundreds of persons left town for the neigh- bouring holiday resorts, the city of Liverpool and the vil- lage of Frodsham, where a Conservative demonstration was held, proving the chief attractions. During the day the streets presented a very dirty appearance, and the few per- sons to be met with were all dressed in holiday attire. BRUTAL MURDER AT PRESTON. —Early on Wednesday morning a most atrocious murder was comtnitted in Preston. A girl sixteen, named Ratcliffe, was about to be married to a young clerk named Simpson and met him on Wednesday in order to proceed to the Church. Simpson persuaded his bride-elect to enter a public-house, and • there deliberately cut her throat with a razor which he appears to have recently purchased. An alarm was raised, and the murderer handed over to the police. The poor girl's head was almost severed from her body. Simpson was afterwards remanded by the magistrates, and later in the day a coroner's jury re- turned a verdict of "wilful murder' against him. The surgeon who saw the body said that death had been, lie should consider, instantaneous. Before and after the mur- der Simpson maintained a cool and "jaunty" demeanour, and frankly admitted that he bad done the deed, giving, however, no reason for his detestable conduct. MILITARY FUNERAL AT WARRINGTOIC-A very large number of persons assemblA at the Warrington Cemetery, on Wednesday last to witness the interment of the late Colour Sergeant James Chubb, son of the highly respected Sergeant Major of the 3rd battalion South Lancashire Regiment. For a considerable time the deceased had been ailing and he gradually grew worse, and succumbed on Mon- day last to consumption of the bowels. As above stated, the funeral took place on Wednesday, when the remains of the deceased sergeant were followed to the grave by the whole of the troops in the Orford barracks, and the staffs of both militia regiments, who were accompanied by their bands. The funeral service was impressively read by the Rev. E. 0. Coleman, superintendent Wesleyan minister, and at the conclusion the usual volleys were discharged over the grave.

RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.— The half-yearly meeting of this society was held at the Co-operative Hall, Church-street, Runcorn, on Tuesday, when there was a large number of shareholders present. Mr Robert Royle pre- sided. The report presented by the Secretary (Mr. Gleave) showed that the total receipts for the half-year amounted to £29,208 78. 30., and the payments to £27,540 Gs. 2d. The profits of the half-year were £3,008 15s. 5d., and a dividend of 2s. 4d. in the pound was declared. The report was adopted.
INSPECTION OF RUNCORN POLICE.—The annual inspection of the members of the Runcorn county police force was made on Wednesday, by the Hon. Captain Legge, govern-

ment inspector for the northern division. There were present Superintendent Williamson, Inspector Hollingworth, and Sergeants Morris, Walley, McMichael, Blair, Booth, and 18 constables. After the inspector had put the men through a number of movements in the large yard adjoining the police court, he examined the accoutrements and the books. We are glad to be able to report that Captain Legge expressed himself as well satisfied with the appearance of the men and the state of the books.
RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.—The monthly meeting of this Bohrd was held yesterday (by spzcial arrangement). The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and there were also

present the Rev. W. Fennolly, and Messrs. Simpson, Nor- man, Pritchard, Lea, and Briscoe (clerk). The Chairman read a letter from the mistress of Mill Brow school (Miss Helsby) resigning her situation.—Canon Barclay remarked that he had received a communication from Mr. Brookes, secretary to the Runcorn Board of Commissioners stating that the members of that body had under their consideration the Canal Boats' Amendment Act. Seeing that the new Act contained clauses relating to boat children, Mr. Brookes said the Commissioners would be glad of the co-operation of the School Board with a view to considering the clauses of the enactment. The speaker proceeded to say that he had acknowledgel the receipt of the letter, and stated that Mr. Rigby, the clerk to the School Board, was of opinion there was nothing in the proposed legislation which could in any way interfere with their policy. One or two sections of the Act having been read over, the subject dropped.—There was no return from Mr. Bowyer, the attendance officer, owing to the midsummer holidays taking place.at the pre- sent time.

A CAPTAIN DROWNED AT Ruxcoax.—Mr. Ridgway, county coroner, held an inquest on Monday, at the Lion Hotel, Greenway-road, Rune,:mn, on the body of Enoch Hat- ton, boatman, of Barnton, near Northwich, who was found
SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE LIBERAL ASSOCIATION .-A

drowned on Saturday morning in the 011 Basin. De- ceased was 32 years of age, and captai; sf the Olvia, having for his assistant a young man named John Carter, his cousin, who also lives a' Barnton. On Friday night, as the boat was lying in the Old Basin, waiting for the morning's tide, the captain and hand retired to their cabins. Between one and two o'clock on the following morning, Carter was called by the lock tenter. He then got up and awoke the captain. Before Hatton left his cabin Carter went ashore, opened the lock paddles, and pulled the boat into position for going through the gates. As Hatton did not join him, and did not appear to be anywhere about the docks, Carer reported to the foreman that he was missing. The canal was dragged, and about three o'clock the same morning the body of deceased was found by Jos. Cooke, of Gilbert-street. In reply to the coroner, the man Carter, who was called as a witness, said he supposed that deceased must have met with his death through attempting to run ashore when he awoke out of sleep, being under the impression when he did so that the vessel was in the position as when he went asleep, whereas it had been moored. illen the poor fellow fell into the water the paddles were up, and he would im- mediately be drawn under the boat. Deteased was a steady man, but he was unable to swim. The jury returned a ver- dict of " Accidentally drowned." The body was the first which has been placed in the new mortuary. RUNCORN MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN.—Mr. SRAW, the missionary stationed in Runcorn in connection with the Mersey Mission to Seamen, is a man with an exceptionally large family, and the maintenance of them is no doubt a heavy responsibility. It appears to have occurred to him— whether from reading the advertisement of the building societies or not we cannot say—that it would boa great help if he could be placed in the position of Wesleyan Methodist and other ministers in the town, and have a house at his disposal. He brought the matter under the notice of Mr. Meadow- croft, the general agent for the Bridgewater Navigation Co. at Runcorn, and stated he thought the dwelling, when erected, might be conveyed to him. Mr. Meadowcroft said he felt sure that many of the friends of the missionary in Runcorn would not subscribe to the proposal unless the house was made over to trustees, so that any official of the-missions who filled the position now held by Mr. Shaw in days to come, might occupy it. Mr. Shaw consented to waive his first suggestion as to the house being vested in him; and the pro- posal next appears to have been submitted to several gentle- men, and favourably received. A meeting to consider the matter was called for Thursday, at the Mission Roorn,Bottom Locks. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, but there were only about half a dozen people present, including the secre- tary of the fund, Mr. George Howard. It was stated that about £3OO would be required to carry out the proposal, and Mr. Shaw expressed himself confident he could raise the money in Runcorn alone. It was resolved, on the motion of Mr. Meadowcroft, seconded by Mr. Johnson, organist at the Parish Church, that the committee of the Mersey Mis- sions to Seamen at Liverpool should be communicated with to ascertain whether they would be willing to undertake the trusteeship of such a house, in connection with other Runcorn trustees, and whether they would contribute to- wards the scheme in order to show their approval of it. HARVEST PROSPECTS IN NORTH LANCASIIIRE.—A

meeting of the Council of this association was held on Thursday, at the Reform Club, Liverpool; Mr. Thomas Brocklebank, J.P., in the chair. Among those present were Messrs. Nicholson, J.P., Tyrer, H. B. Gilmour, J.P., H. W. Meade-King, J.P., Kenworthy, H. Roberts, J. L. Booth, Blackhurst, E. Brownbill, T. G. Best, G. J. Whittaker, A. Billson' S. G. Godfrey, A. Eccles, Alderman Robinson, J.P., W. Bulcock, A. Hanson, R. G. Brooke, Joseph Atherton, P. M. Campbell, W. Tyrer. C. Wade, W. Roxburgh, Alder- man Wilde, A. Sinclair, J. Taylor, J. Harrison, B. Bleakley, and George H. Powell (secretary).—The Secretary read a report of a lengthy and interesting character, which, on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. H. B. Gilmour, J.P., was adopted and ordered to be entered on the minutes. —The other business was of a routine character, and the meeting closed with a vote of thanks to the chairman, which was duly acknowledged. KtraAD BY FALLING DOWNSTAIRS AT ST. HELENS. On Tuesday morning an inquest was held on the body of James Bellaugh Vass, 35 years of age, at the house of Mr. Naylor, Kirkland-street. It appeared that on Wednes- day morning at half-past one deceased, who resided in Napier-street, got out of bed for the purpose, as was his custom, of seeing if his children were all right in the next room. Having to pass the top of the stairs for this purpose it is supposed that through stupor occasioned by sleep he staggered and fell downstairs. The noise of his fall and the screams ot his wife roused the neighbours, several of whom flocked into the louse to see what was the matter. I Decetaed was at the bottom of the stairs in a pool of blood, and on examination it was found that one of his legs was broken, the bone having pierced through the flesh, causing the blood to flow freely. A doctor arrived in about an hour, and the wound was dressed. Deceased also sustained other injuries to the head and body, and died on Friday night. A verdict of "Accidental death "was returned. A MAN FOUND DROWNED AT S. HELENS.—On Sunday, at about ball-past one in the afternoon, a man was found drowned in Hughes Delph near the police station, at Sutton Grange. The body was taken to the Griffin Inn, at Peasley Cross, kept by Mr. John Fairhurst,and a description taken. The man appeared to be about 35 years of age, and five feet five or six inches in height. He had whiskers round the chin, and his hair was turning grey. His trousers were of brown corduroy, and he had on a soft hat, a sleeved waistcoat, and laced clogs. A pawn ticket was found upon him, bearing the name of John Harrison pawn- broker, Heath-street, Golborne, and the name of Mallet of Lawton. An inquest was held on the body of the man at the Griffin Inn, Peasley Cross, by Mr. Driffield, coroner.— William Maddocks, residing in Liverpool-road, St. Helens, said he had seen the body and he identified it as the body of his father, who had been missing since the previous Friday afternoon, when witness's wife saw him. Deceased had been working for some time at Sutton, and it is supposed that while making his way across the field to his work, he accidentally fell down the quarry, which was partly tilled with water, and was drowned.—A verdict of accidental death was returned. ORDER OF SONS OF TEMPEIII3NCE.
DEMONSTRATION - AT RUNCORN.

On Monday afternoon, the thirteenth annual demonstra- tion of the Life-boat-crew Division of the above Order was held at Runcorn, in charming weather. The members formed in procession at Bethesda Schoolroom, and paraded the principal streets of the town, attended by the Widnes. Star of Temperance bress band and the Weston Sons Of Temperance drum and fife band. At the house of Dr. Robin- son the bands played a salute. Proceeding over Delf Bridge, and a little way down Halton-road, the procession turned back and crossing Mill-brow went up Cawley's-lane to the Heath. Here, for a short time, games were indulged in, after which the procession returned to the schoolroom. The number of members in the procession was about 80 adults, and about an equal number of juveniles' but it must also be taken into account that the Weston fife band was formed by those associated with the juvenile department. Tea was providcd in the schoolroom and about 200 persons were present. • After tea a public meeting was held over which, in the unavoidable absence of Mr. Thomas Norimin, Mr. J. Withington presided There were also on the platform:— Messrs. R. Clough (Rochdale), W. If. Hughes (Crewe), D. Bisbrown, J. Jones, T. Cooke, T. Faulkner, and T. Heesoin (Runcorn). The CHAIRMAN said he was proud to belong to a society which had been the means of clothing many people and raising them to a good position in the world. He expressed his conviction that the meeting would prove a success, as though Mr. Norman was absent they had with them Mr. Clough, of Rochdale, who was a host in himself—(laughter and applause)—and quite capable of occupying the whole of the time they would be together. Mr. HUGHES, of Crewe, said he thought the committee had a twofold object in view in getting up the demonstra- tion. The first of these was to bring together all who belonged to their order, and try to infuse a friendship amongst them; and secondly, to endeavour to induce others who were not members to join the association. The princi- ple of total abstinence was a noble one, and it was one of which be never felt ashamed. Ile had found the pledge a great help to him, for all his acquaintenances knew his principles now, and never thought of trying to persuade him to take intoxicants. He regretted to have to state that many people, when asked to join the older, expressed an opinion that the pledge they were expected to take was one of too stringent a nature, but he did not consider it at all too strict considering the great work they had to do in trying to de- stroy the liquor traffic and build up a nation of total ab- stainers. The way in which the society was conducted was a great help to many men, for as the Sons of Temperance never had any drink in their club rooms, there was not the same temptation to take it which there was in connection with some associations of a somewhat similar character. The motto of the order was "Purity and fidelity "—purity from the unclean thing and fidelity to pledge. Temperance was a good thing for a man not only as regarded his health, but also in a pecuniary sense. It was only a few days ago that one who was now a member of the order, had told him that he might have been a wealthy landowner if . iad not spent his money at a certain public-hous, called the Big Duck. The society also gave them the means of providing for a " rainy day," and he thought that any right-minded man, when laid aside by sickness, would be comforted with the thought that his wife and children were not left utterly des- titute. Theirs was not an association where they paid all in and got nothing out, for they were allowed as much as from any other similar organisation. He appealed to the parents present to give up the use of drink, not only for their own sakes, but for the sake of their child- ren, who were often subjected to strong temptation by see- ing the drink freely used at home. In conclusion, he urged upon the members the necessity of doing their utmost to persuade others to join the order and he sincerely hoped it would prosper. Mr. CLOUGH said that he had noticed that total abstainers were looked upon as persons who gave up a great many of the pleasures of life, and they were thought to be very self- sacrificing; but it was not his idea to be a martyr to any- thing. The reason he became a teetotaller was because it suited him and that he thought it was the best thing for him, and not because any one else thought so. It had been Wged against him that he had no right to judge the evils of drink as he, never having tasted it, was not in a position to speak about it; but lie answered that before trying anything he liked to see the effect of it upon others and as the effect of drink on others had not to his mind ;lad a satisfactory effect, he declined to try it upon himself. When bethought tofe ptd the ravages made by drink, of the homes it had desolated, h pits it had robbed of the best of their ministers, and Vie noble minds it had destroyed, he felt it was his duty, not only to abstain from the use of it pers:nally, but to do his best to effect the downfall of such a heinous traffic. He had been in many a rich home that bad been desolated through the indulgence in drink. A case which had come under his own notice might be mentioned. A very respectable gentleman, who was always partial a glass of beer, and who had attained the age of 60 years without ever being the worse for liquor, was the father of two sons and one daughter. The eldest son went out one evening to get something for his wife who lay sick in bed, called at a public-house, where he got drunk, and in a drunken brawl he was knocked down. No one noticing him, he was left in the bar room all night, and in the morning, on being carried home, he expired. The second son, being one night intoxicated, stayed out all night. A storm coming on, he was drenched with rain and took the ague, and sub- sequently died. The daughter, a young woman fair to look ripen, acquired a liking for drink, and although repeatedly, told by her medical attendant that it would be the cause of her death, she persistently took large quantities of it, often rising at night to obtain it. One night she awoke, threw the coverlid over her, and with no other covering she went to a public-house, where she was supplied with the liquor she craved, and went home and died. As be eaw the old man bending over the corpse of his daughter, be (the speaker) carsed the drink in his heart. They must not think they could play with intoxicating liquor without receiving any harm. He could not see that they had any right to expect God to answer their prayers for health and prosperity, when they were doing what they knew to be injurious to them- selves. When they prayed for the success of their children, their prayers should be backed up by their own efforts in the shape of taking all obstacles out of the path of their off- spring. When all that lay in their power to do was done, then was the time to ask Divine assistance. He always felt a pride in doing the cause any service he could. He was happy to be able to say that he had been the means of turn- ing a few men from the error of their ways. Fourteen years ago that day, a temperance association to which he belonged walked through certain streets in Rochdale—streets they were told they dare not enter. He spoke a few words to the people, which were the means of influencing one man to take the pledge. That man he had met driving his own horse that very morning. That was only one proof among numbers he could give of what temperance would do for them. Another individual who had heard him speak determined to cease taking drink, and one day, some years after forming this re- solution, he presented him (the speaker) with a little trinket with his photograph inside, and the inscription," Presented to R. Clough by one whom he reclaimed." He knew the principles of temperance were good ones, and trusted that all would see their way to adopt them. To illustrate one of his points, yiz., that teetotallers were not so silly as they were supposed to be, Mr. Clough sang a song of his own composition, and requested the audience to join him in the chorus. Great amusement was caused by a well-known character in Runcorn very vociferously joining in the singing, but out of tune, and continuing his efforts after everyone else had stopped. During the evening, the proceedings were diversified by the fife band playing selections, and recitations were given by Mr. W. H. Hughes and Mr. T. Faulkner. Mr. George Lacey also sang a song entitled "The herring." After the passing of various votes of thanks, the proceed- ings were concluded by the singing of the Doxology.

- LIVERPOOL coas.—The market opened quietly for wheat. Indian corn is firm, and quotations are better than on Tuesday. —Second report: A fair trade was concluded in wheat, and a firm tone prevailed, Tuesday's rates being fully maintained. Flour in fair demand, and prices very firm. Beans and peas steady. I tdian corn advanced 2d per cental owing to specula- tion, and a fair business was done; new mixed American 5s 2d. MANCHESTER COTTON.—Things are not really better here as regards turnover, hence business remains very slow and difficult. Prices are unaltered, but are tending a little towards ease, while offerings are sufficiently numerous, but fer the most part wholly out of the quest ion. The most satisfactory feature of the market lathe quiet tenour of Cotton reports.

LIVERPOOL COTTON.—Spot: A quiet feeling has ruled in the market'all day, and only a limited business has been done. Prices are weaVfor tt e lower grades,and barely steady for good classes. Bales 8,000 bales, including 1,000 on speculation or for export.
