At the meeting of the Finance Committee, held on the 18th ult., a list of persons in arrears for rates, kc., was sub- mitted, to whom frequent applicatios for payment had ben made, and it was °reined that proceedings be taken for the recovery of same by the collector. Accounts amounting to £396 7s. 7d. were examined, and cheques signed for pay- ment—The minutes were agreed to on the proposition of Mr. WOOD, seconded by Mr. WINSTANLEY.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. A meeting of the School Attendance Committee was held on the 18th July. The Clerk (Mr. Brierley) submitted a contribution order for £l2O, which was duly signed and made upon the oversec-s to meet the expenses of the department for the current year —On the motion of Mr. BIRLEY, the minutes were confirmed.

THE BOARD AND THE BANK HOLIDAY. Mr. WINSTANLBY drew attention to the postponement of the Board meeting in consequence of their day of meeting falling upon bank holiday, and remarked he did not see any reason for the business to be posponed.—After some conversation, Mr. PENNINGTON gave notice that he would move at the next meeting that the bank holiday be not observed by the Board.

MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. Dr. WATKINS, in his report for the quarter ending 30th June last, stated there were registered 63 male and 55 female bit the, total 118; and 16 male and 14 female deaths, total 30, the excess of births over deaths being 88. The birth 'rate was 44.28 per thousand of the population estimated to the middle of 1881. The death rate was 1125 per thousand of the estimated population. This was the lowest death rate he had ever had the gratification of reporting to the Board. A table of deaths classified according to diseases and ages briefly showed the causes of death were as follow :—Scarlet fever, 3 under 5 years, 5 years!and upwards 5; 5 years and upwards; croup, 1; chronic dysentery, 1 ; phthisis, 1 ; bron- chitis, pneumonia, and pleurisy, 2; heart disease, 2; sudden death 1, suicide 1; other causes 6, and under 5 years 7. Scarlet fever (which had caused 14 deaths in the first quarter of the year) caused 8 deaths in the last quarter. The disease was fatal 'in 4 cases in January, 4 in February and in March. A single death only in the month of April seemed to promise the disease was disappearing, but the deaths from it rose to 6 in May, and the number again fell to 1 in June. Thus the months of March and April were precise parallels ! to May and June. The marked decline in , the rate of the infantile mortality was a matter for sincere congratulation. Although scarlet fever in children under five years accounted for exactly 10 per cent of all the deaths in the quarter, the total number of children I dying under five years from all causes was just one third of the whole number of deaths. This, compared with the pre- vious quarter, was a fall from 50 to 33 per cent. The corn- ' pletien of the arrangements for sending cases of infectious disease to the special hospital had already been taken ad- vantage of. In one instance no less than four children were sent in one week from one lodging house. Thus a focus of concentrated infection was swept away by the prompt adop- tion of measures now at their command. In conclusion he advised the periodical and complete flushing of the sewers for promoting the security of the public health and pre- venting as far as possible the invasion of an autumnal epidemic.—The CHAIRMAN remarked that it was very satis- factory to find that the death-rate was so small.—Mr. BlB- i.av could not help rising to thank Dr. Watkins for a.much more moderate and temperate report than ever he had read since be had been a member of the Board.—Dr. WATKINS : The report speaks for itself. The CHAIRMAN : We had better send it to the Committee. Mr. Wins-norm : I should like to ask Dr. Watkins if, within his knowledge, any waste steam is turned into the sewers.—Dr. WATKINS : lam not aware of any. There was some a long time ago, but it was stopped; and I have not observed any since, and have heard no complaints.—The report was then referred to the committee.

APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICER. Applications for the appointment of medical officer were received from the following :—MeJsrs. Watkins, Newton Goran, Anston, Itotheiham ; Handyside, Earlestown ; and; Hannah, Ashton-in-Makettield.—The Law Clerk having read the applications and testimonials, Colonel McConQuO- DALE proposed the reappointment cf Dr. Watkins. He believed that gentleman had most efficiently and fearlessly discharged his duty to the Commissioners.. Some people might say, and have the opinion,tlaat he was not sufficiently delicate with the language he used. But he was glad to hear Mr. Birley say that day that he thoroughly approved of the tone of the report which had been read. Personally, he thought the medical officer should be an independent man and say exactly what he liked, and it was for the Commissioners if they found fault, to point out that with which they found fault. The Commissioners were there as public men to discharge a public duty, and to vote the payment of public money, and he thought they had only one course to consider, and that was to do their duty to those whom they represented, and appoint the best Man they could find for the office. Dr. Watkins WAS a tried man, Who had been with them from the commencement, and he believed he had faithfully and fearlessly discharged his duty. He hoped they would be unwilling to part with a willing and faithful servant.—Mr. WOOD seconded the proposition.—Mr. Ben- LET, with much diffidence, proposed an amendment. He had known Dr. Watkins as long as Colonel McCorquodale had—that was ever since Dr. Watkins had been in Newton— and he did not for one moment impugn his abilities as a medical officer, but as the medical officer of health for that Board he thought he deserved some rebuke of some sort. [Mr. PENNINGTON: Hear, hear.] Dr. Watkins had been present several times with his report, and when he had been spoken to about it he had said, "I will not alter one single word of this. You, gentlemen, can do what von like. This is a copy of what, has gone to Lon-don, and I will not alter one single word.' He did not think that was a respectful way for any paid officer to address a Board like that.—[Mr. PENNINGTON : Hear, bear] —lt was for that reason and that reason only that he felt it his duty to oppose the election of Dr. Wat- kins, and he therefore begged to propose the appointment of Dr. Handyside, whom he believed to be equally as clever as Dr. Watkins.—Mr. FoasvEn. seconded the proposition.—Mr. PENNINGTON proposed the appointment of Dr. Hannah, but did not find a seconder.—The amen4m9t MS then put, and two members voted for it, four hands being held up for the proposition. Dr. Watkins sails therefor? re-elected.—The Cumgattar said he had much pleasure in supporting the nomination of Dr. Watkins, although be thought he had been a little indiscreet in the way that had been referred to very properly, and as to his conduct to the Board. He had no doubt been an energetic and good officer. He understood thoroughly the sanitary duties of .the district; and he (the chairman) did not like to tern aside an old officer if they could possibly avoid it. He did not think the ground WAS quite sufficient to do that in his opinion, but he trusted the doctor would in the future see that his report was in more moderate terms, and th it he would give satisfaction.— Mr. WINSTINLEY, while voting for the proposition, agreed with what Mr. Birlev had said, and said no one had pro- tested more strongly against it than he had himself. He was pleased the present course had been taken of advertising for a medical officer, because it would show Dr. Watkins that he could not treat the Board in the cavalier manner he had done on several occasions. The meeting then terminated.

div.head: LkTEST NEWS.
div.p: LkTEST NEWS.

A public meeting was held at the Fishmongers' Hall yes- terday in furtherance of the decision of a recent meeting of noblemen and gentlemen to hold an International Fisheries ! Exhibition in London during 1883.. Prince Biaden, Shoe- ! bridge, said the fishmongers, too, would give .£5OO towards ' the expenses, and guarantee £2,000. Ile moved a resolution declining it was desirable to hold the exhibition. Mr. Bir- beck seconded, and said lie had authority for saying the Prince of Wales highly approved of the project. Lord Abinger, Sir John McDon tld, and others supported the motion for the appointment of a general committee, which was carried.

Mr. Bradlaugh attended yesterday before Mr. Justice Grove, and psoduceel a telegram sent to a club by a news agency on the 21d July, 1880, giving the result of the division on which the prosecution in the case of Clarke t. Bradlaugh was based. Ile also produced an affidavit and sub- mitted that the documents, though conclusive as to time were strongly in favour of his contention that the writ must have been issued before the vote was given. Mr. Justice Groves said he would consult with Mr. Justice Lindlay, and give their judgment on Monday mornine. At the Westminster Police Court, yesterday, Mabel Wil- berforce was charged with having committed wilful perjury during the hearing of the case of Wilberforce v. Philip. Mr. St. John Wontner prosecuted for the treasury, and said he should content himself with providing five assignments of perjury. Several witnesses were called, who supported the case for the Crown, and the prisoner, who briefly cross- examined the witnesses, was remanded.

At Limerick City Sessions, yesterday, John Moran was sentenced to six months imprisonment for highway robbery and assault. The Chairman said there were about 70 other similar cases, and until the city was better protected lawless- ness and crime would continue to reign supreme with nothing to check them.

div.head: WIDNES WIND )W PLANT ASSOCIATION,
div.p: WIDNES WIND )W PLANT ASSOCIATION,

The fourth exhibition of this flourishing society was keld in the Market Hall, Widnes, on 'Thursday afternoon, in splendid weather. The Ladies' Visiting Committee are Mesdames Bingant, Carey, Cross, Colley, Cooper, Deacon, Holloway, Williams, McClellan, James White, S. Robinson, and Misses McClellan, and Meacock. The names of the General Committee are as follow :—Messrs. T. Atherton, P. Blinstone, V. C. Driffield, I. Hunt, C. Jones, T. Lancastert J. Latchford, J. Morrison, J. Shepherd, S. Muspratt, W. E. Oakden, J. Rawlinson, and T. Reay. Mr. Eustace Carey acted as chairman, and Mr. T. Atherton as hon. secretary. There was a very fair attendance at the show, which was arrayed in a manner similar to those of previous years, and the members of the Ditton Brass Band provided the specta- tors with music. We understand that in past years there has been a little laxity in regard to making careful en- quiries as to whether the exhibits were really the bona fide property of those by whom they were shown; but a month previous to Thursday's gathering the houses of the intend- ing competitors were visited and a seal placed upon the various plants. This strictness may account for a slight falling of in the number of the exhibits, which were, nevertheless, very numerous for a district so peculiarly situated as Widnes for the culture of floral and horticul- tural productions. The exhibitors numbered about 60. The judges were :—Mr. John Glover, Leigh Hall, Gateacre; Mr. John Drysdale, gardener to Sir A. B. Walker, Gateacre; and Mr. Green, of Bank Park, Warrington. The liliums and fuschias were exceptionally good, and there were also some capital musks. The following is a list of the prizes : Class I.—For the best collection of window plants, any number, but not fewer than six, any variety: 1, Mrs. Allam; 2, Mrs. Vose ;3, Mr. J. Broome. . _

elass 2 (A).—Ten prizes of 7s. 6d. for any collection of not fewer than three plants, any variety: 1, Mrs. Brad- shaw; 2, Mrs. Taylor; 3, Mr. J. Hesketh ; 4, Mr. J. Lightfoot; 5, Mr. P. Denham; 6, Mr. Wm. Blinston ; 7, Mrs. Rathbone ; 8, Mrs. Hart; 9, Mrs. Lomax; 10, Mrs. Barnett.

Class 2 (B).—Ten prizes of ss. each for any collection of not fewer than three plants: 1, Mrs. Broome; 2, Mrs. .1. Broome; 3, Mr. George Proffitt; 4, Mr. Joseph Sparks; 5, Mrs. Young; 6, Mr. John Dainty; 7, Mr. John Lunt: 8, Mrs. W. Parker; 9, Mr. Pammant; 10, Mr. John Cooley. Class 3.—Best fuschia : 1, Mrs. Voss; 2, Mrs. Allman; 3, Mr. S. Lightfoot. Class 4.—Geraniums: 1, Mrs. Horrabin ; 2, Mrs. Joseph Brown; 3, Mrs. Haddock. Class s.—Petunias: 1, Mr. J. Dainty; 2, Mr. J. Lunt ; 3, Mrs. Joseph Broome. Class 6.—Lilium : 1, Mrs. Jos. Broome; 2, Mrs. Rigby. Class 7.—French nettle: Ist, Mrs. J. Brooms; 2, Mr. John Dainty; 3, Mr. Joseph Spitks. Class B.—Plant of any description: 1, Mr. Lawrence; 2, Mrs. Lawrence; 3, Mrs. Lomas. Class 9.—Musk: 1, Mr. John Hesketh ; 2, George Merkell; 8, Mrs. Rigby. The following were awarded extra prizes :—Mrs. Barnett, Mrs. T. Atherton, Mrs. A. Showan, Mrs. Mallon, Mrs. James Broome ,Mr. James Burns, Mrs. Baskerville, Mrs. Bann, Mrs. McEvoy, and Messrs. Baskerville, W. Calland, W. Horrabin, and Joseph Lunt.

THE REV. S. P. GREEN'S Immusowscsmr.—The Rev. S. F. Green from his residence in Lancaster Castle, has addressed a letter to the Secretary of the Church of Englaud Working Men's Society, which held its annual meeting in London, on Saturday. Mr. Green writes that they who are "fighting for the Church "are met by the portentous fact that vast masses of their fellow-countrymen knew nothing wltatever of the Church, its origin, or its essential I characteristics. In his opinion there is now in existence I one law for the bishops and laymen, and another for the I priests, the latter being administered solely for the purpose of crushing a section of the priesthood—that section who receive the "whole Prayer-book as it was." He trusts that Archbishop Tait will " live to repent" his remarks the other day on "freaks of .conscience," and adds that the Primate's expression respecting the "keys of his prison being in the hands of the prosecution," was the most perfect imaginable satire upon the Public Worship Regulation Act, under which the proceedings at Miles Platting—" an outrage under the guise of the law "—had been taken. A letter from Dr. Pusey was also read to the meeting. It strongly encouraged the society to persevere in their work, and asserted that Mr. Greer' is confined "in a prison boilt for felons," because he refuses to disregard a plain direction in the Book of Common Prayer. Dr. Franey claims for the Church the " rights " which even Henry VIII. affirmed. He desires that spiritual causes shall be decided by spiritual courts, but .Ines not remind his correspondents that in cases of con- tilmacy the secular arm would still have to be called in, as now. The further hearing of the appeal of the Bev. S. F. I Green, Miles Platting, Manchester, against the writ under which he is now imprisoned, took place on Tuesday, beim- the Lord Chancellor, who dismissed the appeal Lotdi Blackburn and Watson concurred.

Ihe mevon s.tid he was sorry to say he had had a letter from Mr. Roger Iliad, a member of the Council, resigning his office. It was as folluwsz— Warrington, July 19th, len—Deer Mr. Mayor,—Rinally I accept my resignation as Town Coutelilof of the bJrough ot Warrington, and also me to thank it and the other members of the.Coancir for the courtesy an., kindness I have Invariably received trom —Youts truly, I:OGFEC Hien. He (the Mayer) Was sa:e it was a source of regret to them all that Mr. Hind should be placed in such a position as to send in his resienation He move ~. (Hear, hear.) d " That this Council accept with regret the resignation of Roger Hind, Esquire, as Councillor for the \ orth-East Ward, without payment of the fine of £25 imposel by the bye-law of the Council, dated I.4th June, 1847. made under the Ist section of the A ct, 5 and 6 William IV., ch. 76." Alderman Davus seconded the motion. The Council could only echo that it was with exi rattle regret that they took that course. Everybody had very great regard for Mr. Hind, and especially at the present moment. (Hear, hear.) The motion was carried unanimously. STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE. At a meeting of this committee on the 7th July, an amended plan of 21 houses and stables, in Latchford, for Mr. Sylvanus Reyn-olds, was approved; Also plan of six cottages in Wellfield-street, for Mr. It. Hewitt; plan of a bottling warehouse in Aiken-street, for Mr. Jos. Mounfteld. The surveyor submitted the apportionment and cost of form- ing and paving Pierpoint-street, which wts approved, and he was instructed to give notice of the apportionment to the owners of property adjoining such street and to demand and recover payment thereof. The committee rec entnended that the plan for the forming of a foot% ay on the west side of Wilderspool-causeway, from Mr. Brown's premises to the south side of the house belonging to Miss Picton, be ap- proved. The tender of Mr. Charles Andeews for the form- ing and puttine: in of the found aion of Victoria-street, was accepted. Alderman BIIBGESS said he noticed that the lamp at Towa's-end, opposite the Lord Rodney, had been removed for some purpose. He should like to know the reason. Councillor PLATT seid it ad probably been removed fora similar reason that one was taken from another part of the town some time ago—repairs or improvement. The minutes were contiened. MUSEUM COMMITTEE. - A meeting of the Museum, Library, ands Arts Committee was held oo the 18th ult., when the curator presented his report for the month of June, which was as follows:— Visitors to the museum, 2,252, an increase of 26 compared with June, 1880; volumes ksued to subscribers, 2,330, an increase of 1 compared with Juice, 1880; volumes issued to readers, 575, a decrease of 62 compared with June, 1880. There were also le ported the following gifts, for which the thanks of the committee were ordered to be sent to the donors : From Mr. William Fell, plaster casts, made and painted by himself, of two species of fishes—turbot and mackerel; Mr. James Bate, a lobster and four coins; Mr. P. Pearse, a lobster; the Smithsonian Institution, their annual report • the Local Books Fund, two volumes; Mr. John Peers, report; Spherical Astronomy ; the Author, Tul- loch's Crimean Commission and Mr. Kinglake; the British Museum, Catalogue of Birds (vol. 5), Illustrations of Lepi- doptera (part 5); Mr. Sherratt, Works of Josephs, to. 1794; Mr. W. Fell and Mr. John D. Turner, of Stromness, specimens of fossil fish from Stromness ; the Liverpool Free Library Committee, catalogue of the lending library. On the motion of Councillor GREENING, seconded by Councillor MILNER, the minutes were agreed to. TOWN HALL, PARE AND BATHS COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee comprised a recommenda- tion that a pair of light iron eatesbe purchased and put up, and the hurdles extended on the far side of the west entrance to the Town Hall from Sankey-street, to complete the en- closing of the recreation ground. The report of the bath- keeper showed that the income from the Baths for the past four weeks was £36 14s. 6d., and for the corresponding period last year £35 us. 10d. The MAYOR moved, awl Councillor RIDGWAY seconded, the adoption of the minutes, and the motion was carried. INFANTILE DIARUHCEA. ' The Sanitary Committee's minutes stated that a letter Ins received from the Local Government Board informing them that their Inspector, Dr. Ballard, had been instructed to make a general inquiry into the causes of the annually- recurring prevalence of infantile diarrhcea, and that Dr. Ballard prouosedto include this borough, and requesting the committee to afford him any assistance it was able to give. it was resolved that Dr. Gornall and other officials afford such assistance. The medical officer reported as follows as to houses built on chemical waste, and it wes ordered that a copy of the report be sent to the Paving and Sewerage Com- mittee —"I: am of opinion that houses built on chemical Waste are not necessarily unwholesome, and as long as the foundations do not give way, and they are properly thained, they are fit Per human habitation, though I would recom- mend that any proposal for building on such a site should be only entertained with very great caution." Recommenda- tion that at the reqaest of Dre!Ballard certain meteorological instruments be provided for the making of observations to assist him in his inquiry as to the causes of the annually- recurring prevalence of infantile diarrhcea at the estimated

, cost of £1.5. A!derman BI7EGESS movedatandaConncillor MONKS seconded, the adoption of the minutes. Councillor WHITTLE said he saw an item of £l5 for appar- atus for Dr. Ballard. He thought that gentleman ought to bring his own apparatus. - A Volcut He's a member of theicommittee, too. (Laugh.

ter.) Alderman HOLMES : Do we buy this machine ourselves? Alderman DAVIES: It is not a machine. (Laughter.) The MAYOR: I don't know what this means. A Mstsuna : It is a machine. Alderman DAvms : No; it is infantile;diarrhoea—(load laughter),—at a coat of £l5. Alderman BURGESS, in reply, :protested against having to reply to anything a member of the Sanitary Committee mabt have to say. If that member attended the cftmittee be could there take objection. [Councillor Wittrrtn: It would have no effect--(laughter) ;3 but be must at once give up the idea of answering members of the committee in that room. The minutes were adopted.

GM &OMITTED: APPOINTMENT OE ASSISTANT MANAGER. The minutes of the Gas Committee stated that the average illuminating power of the gas for the fortnight ended let July was equal to. 19, candles, and for the fortnight ended lath July 10.13 candles; that the Manager reported damage to pipes at Birchdale, and loss of gas occasioned by sewer- age works, and he was instructed to see the Town Clerk and be advised what course to adopt; and that on the re- commendation of the sub-committee, Mr. William Spence Haddock be appointed assistant gas manager, at a salary of £l3O per annum, to commence on the Ist of July instant, on condition that he undertakes to reside at the:new works as soon as a house can be built for him. Alderman Horacits, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said in reference to the assistant gas manager, this was not an increase in the number of officials, as previously to him they had a man whose business it was to see to the buildingof the gas works. That man had now left and it was proposedltherappoint Mr. Haddock as assistant to Mr. Paterson, 31r. Haddock had been in the, service of the Gas Committee. for a , considerable time at a salary of £lOO a year, and as the new office was one of more responsibility they proposed te give him £l3O a year. Alderman DAVIES seconded. Councillor _SqTrox said, in the absence of Councillor Dixon, he begged to ask when they were likely to have a redaction in the price 'Again (Loud laughter.) Alderman limax wan afraid the members of the Council were not paying much attention to the increase in the number of street lamps. If they looked at the amount the Corporation paid now and compared it with the amount they paid to a private company for the lighting of the street lamps, they would see that already the public are reaping an advantage. _ • CounclllOr IplaMos asked how soon the committee expected the new, gas works to be in working order. Alderman HoTmEs, replying to CGuncillor Sutton, said the committee did not anticipate that kr the present they would be able to make any reduction in the price of gas. Let them get into the new w6rIT., see -what their expenditure would be there, and then they would consider the question of a reduction of the price of gas. According to Act of Parliament the committee had to pay the cost of the new gas works out of the profits Of the new concern—(hear, hear)— and even if they were not reducing the price of gas, the ratepayers were getting hold of a very valuable property at no expense to themselves. (Hear, hear.) He hoped they would be at work at the new gas works in about six weeks. The minutes were confirmed. smfoor. ATTENDANCE OOMMITTRE.—TEE STANDARD FOR HALF-TEVERS.--42EPORT OF TEE DEPTJTATION. At a meeting of the School Attendance Committee the inspector reported that 16 cases had been inquired into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed for 33 children; that 9 cases had been taken before the magis- trates, when fines were inflicted in 8 cases and 1 adjourned. Eighteen cases were brought before the committee and dealt with. The deputation appointed by the School Attendance Committee to wait upon the Lord President of the Educa- tion Department reported as follows --We have to report that in pursuance of the resolution of the committee we at- tended the deputationhteo.Lbicoerat oSpencer h tat de anduta Mr. Mundella on the 11th July. T the members attending it other than ourselves, was as fa as solely confined to the subject of payment of the school fees by the Guardians: We, with the consent of the Educational De- e partment, introduced the further subject of conferring upon school attendance committees the powers of school boards for providing, as we called it a ragged school or in- dustrial day school. The Chairman and, Mr. Alderman Harrison both explained their views on both subjects to thei vice-president, Mr. Mundella, but with regard to the latteii point we were informed by the Vice-Pres4dent that be word not fora moment hear of a refusal on the part of any echo° manager to receive a child on the ground of its want of proper clothing and cleanliness to attend that school, and that if any such case came to his knowledge he woald at

...re grant to that school be refused. He at ~.ne strongly objected to the use of the expression ‘,..1 school, and would not admit the propriety of the existence of any such schools. On the subject of payment of school fees the Vice-President informed the deputation that they must not expect any alteration of the law, and that nothing in that direction would be done. He at the same time suggested that the objection on the ground of pau- perizing the parents might be overcome by appointing members of the Board of Guardians to sit with the School Attendance Committee, and there and then to adjudicate upon the cases instead of taking them before the Guardians at the Workhouse. This we were some time since advised by the Clerk to the Guardians could not be done with pro- priety. Mr. Mundell a, hlwever,. assured us that it could be legally done, and that the remedy for thevil of which we complained was accordingly in our own hands. Minute, that the applicatioa to the Education Department for their consent to the proposed reduction from the 3rd to the 2nd standard for half-timers had been refused. Councillor WALLINGTON moved the confirmation of the minutes. •

Alderman KEAN seconded the motion. Councillor Peen said the minutes seemed to be very im- portant, and he was hoping to hear some explanation from the members of the committee. (Hear, hear.) But the chairman was not present, and perhaps that accounted for the silence of the other members. He might say, in regard to the latter part of the minutes, the Education Department had refused their consent to the proposed reduction of the standard for half-timers. He was sorry that was the case, as he thought under the present circumstances, in Warring- ton, at all events, it would have been wise to have allowed the reduction of the standard, not as a measure which was to take effect altogether, but as a termiorary expedient, There were a good many children in Warrington who were not up to the third standard, and whom it would take some time to gat up to that standard. The parents of very large families were sometimes very hard pressed to pay the school fees and provide for their families. If the standard had been reduced so that some portion of their families could have been at work it would have been much better. As to the payment of school fees, he theueht the suggestion made by the vice- president of the Education Department was a very valuable one, and one which ought to be carried out if possible. It was that members of the School Attendance Committee should see if they could not get the School Attendance Com- mittee of the Board of Guardians to sit along with them and hear the cases, and then and there decide upon them. He thought that was a workable expedient, and one that should be adopted. The clerk to the Guardians slid it could not be done with propriety, but against that they had the experi- ence of Mr. Mandella that it could be done. He hoped the committee would see if they could net bring about that reform. In reference to reducing the standarl for half- timers, he thought the difficulty might be met by the com- mittee giving instructions to their officers that, when children were attending school half-time, and were in beneficial employment, there should not be any prose- cution. ' Councillor MoNES was sorry the chairman of the com- mittee was not present, as be had hoped the committee would state what they proposed to do in reference to the education question. He thought a very reasonable time had been given to the opponents of a School Board to organise a scheme, or to attempt to do what they could to carry out the ideas they had as to the working of the question of educa- tion in Warrington. So far it had resulted iff nothing but delay, but he hoped- at the next meeting that the chairman would be prepared to state how he proposed to deal with the difficulty and let the Council have some well considered plan which would meet the acknowledged difficulty. He thought those who had read the report of the discussion on the question at the Board of Guardians, and what Mr. Winstanley said as to the ' contact of the people who applied for fees with the work- house, would admit that there was a grave defect in the ' existing arrangements; and he for one would like to see a way out of it. He did not wish to create any difficulty for the School Attendance Committee of the Council or any other public body, but he might say that this matter woeld not be allowed to rest where it was. At the same time, as far as be was concerned, he would like the present ideas to have a fair chance because he believed it would be by far the best way of dealing with tire question as people, after having had their way, could not complain of being forced to adopt a better system. He hoped the question would not be allowed to drift on month after month and nothing be done. Councillor BURGESS thought Councillor Monks had mixed matters too Much. As to the paymeot of school fees he thought Mr. Maniella's recommendathm should be acted upon at once. It was all very well to say people were not paupers because they accepted schoot fees, but Mr. Win- stanley said it lcd to pauperism. He lemed Some members of the Board of Guardians would sit w,rit the School At- , tendance Committee and adjudicate upon the cases. Councillor WOOLFALL said he had had a conversation with the chairman of the Board of Guardians on the sub- ject, and he was of opinion there could hot be any difficulty. The MAYOR said the primary objection of Mr. Mandel la was to allow education committees to pay the fees. He thought he very properly said as the education committees were on the same footing as school boards if the Guardians were to attend the committees the difficulty might be got over. In reference to the last paragraph in the minutes, and what Councillor Platt said about the refusal to reduce the standard from the 3rd to the 2nd, he did not see himself how they could do it. The law must be made for all. It had no doubt been well talked over in the House of Commons when the Act was passed, and there was no doubt there were! certain points about it the Council did not know of, but which recommended themselves to the gentlemen who spoke at the time. In reference to the Education Committee and the Guardians, Mr. Mundella said it was a matter he dared not bring intb the Rouse of Commons as it raised the re- ligious question again. How it did so they could not tell, but they were bound to believe him. The only difficulty was in allowing the poor people to get the school fees from a committee instead of going to the Board of Guardians. Councillor Moults: The education of the waifs and strays. There are about a thousand. •.The MAYOR said they acted as a school board; they ap- point officers to go round and get these waifs and strays in. Mr. Mundella'very properly said that if a waif or stray was denied admission he would stop the grant, and' he quite agreed wait him. He hoped when a child was sent to school in Warrington it would not be refused admission except on goad grounds. As to there being any difficulty in the way, he'did not see any at all. Alderman BURGESS said it appeared to him by whatever arrangements they strove to make this payment of school fees they must be paid by the Board of Guardians' and by! 'mixing the menibers of the Council with the Board ofi 'Grfardiaiiirthe result would be the same. The Board Of, . Guardians would pay the money, and the people would- know it. The matter must remain precisely in the same position. The MAYOR: It is exactly the same with the School Board. , Alderman BURGESS said as it seemed to be determined that theaducation Act should not be altered to meet the views of _Warrington, he knew the time was coming when Warrington would have to adoptthe Education Act whether It met their views or not. He would call the attention of the Council, and of the School Attendance Committee more especially, to the very rapid growth of the town. They certainly could not (without largely increasing the present school accommodation) go on more than two or three years with their growth of population without being compelled to have a School Board. The accommodation at the present ' time was insufficient, and how they were going to meet the increasing demand arising from the increasing popula- tion of the borough he could not comprehend. He-did not think they were going to get it through the instrumentality of voluntary subscnptions ; and, if they did not get it that way, as soon as n Was known to the authorities in London who were in charge of the department, that there was not accommodation in Warrington for the admission of the children, and that the education of those children wag being neglected, whether they liked it or not, they would have to have a School Board. The MAYOR: You are departing from the question. Councillor SUTTON: It is not question whether we are to have a School Board or whether we are not. That question has been discussed on two occasions, and on the last occa- sion, at all events, it was decided by a large majority that. there was no necessity for a School Board. If Alderman Burgess desires to bring it forward again I think it should be done in the regular way by a motion. (Rear, hear.) Councillor Witnworow said in regard to the payment of school fees, he could not see any difficulty at all under their present arrangements. When parents came before the committee some times they said the reason they did not send the children to school was that they could not pay the fees. The committee recommended them to go to the enquiry officer Who would enquire into their case and recommend it to the committee appointed by the Board, of Guardians. They went before that committee who granted the fees. They were not made paupers; they lost none of their privi- leges or rights, and that was impressed upon their minds. The only advantage that would be gained by the guardians sitting on the School Attendance Committee would be the saving of a week's time Alderman Harrison, as chairman of the Board, had been requested to arrange with the-Guar- dians to meet with the committee. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were then agreed to. RIVERS COMMITTEE. A meeting of this committee was held on the 22nd ult. when it was resolved that a deputation of the committee wait, upon the:Salford Corporation with the object of obtaining their joint opposition to clause 37 of the Rivers Conservancy and Floods Prevention Bill (which had been inserted on behalf, or through the instrumentality of the Manchester Corpora-' tion), and to confer with them upon the other provisions of the bill. On the proposition of Councillor Caoserieue, seconded by tlderman DAVIES, the minute was approved. GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE. The minutes comprised recommendations that the tender of Mr. Josiah Whittle for painting Trinity Church clock tower be accepted; and that the permission to erect posts for telephonic purposes asked for by the secretary to the General Post Office, be granted on the understanding' that facilities will be afforded to Warrington for the use of the telephonic communication if required. The MAYO7I moved, and Councillor WOOLFALL seconded, the adoption of the minutes, and the motion was carried. THE BYE-Laws FOR MARINE STORE DEALERS. A portion of this plan was adopted, and it would be made use of in the new cutting, which would be made by the sanction of the Council, whereby these sewers might be kept clean and answer their purpose as well. He believed that when the work was completed it would be satisfactory to everybody in Latchford and Warrington. (Hear, hear.) They must have sympathised with the people of Latchford in their sufferings. From the report they would see that there were large numbers of houses in Latchford which had no proper means of drainage, the sewage being drained into cesspools and ditches was a real nuisance and dangerous. It was time that such a state of things was done away with ; and if the plane were adopted by the Town Council they would get rid of the complaints they had heard about so long. The number of the inhabitants of Latchford was increasing, and it was desirable that the recommendations named in the report should be adopted. One of the schemes proposed by Mr. Vawser could scarcely be carried out, as he intended to carry the sewage under the canal at Black Bear Bridge, the depth required would have been of such a character that it 40ould have caused the sewers in a great measure to be below the bed of the river. That would have created some difficulty. But Mr. Vawser had not the assistance of either the air compressor or the sewage ejector. Mr. Longdin had. and that was the great advantage he had in bringing out his scheme. The plan proposed by the Borough Surveyor reflected great credit on him, and all who had studied the matter were of the same opinion—that the scheme would be an effectual one for the drainage of Latchford. Councillor WOOLFALL seconded the motion. Councillor PERCIVAL called attention to the condition of the main sewer in Church-street. It was not sufficient for the purpose, especially in times of heavy .afins. On two occasions during the last month the street had b:(..11 flooded, and it appeared to be the general wish of the inhabitants and Property owners that the matter should at once be con- sidered by the Town Council and the nuisance re- moved The floods had a tendency to produce ill-health, and also caused bad smells. No doubt the Surveyor could devise means to remedy the nuisance. , Councillor WALLINGTON considered the Borough Sur- veyor had submitted a very effectual and economical plan for the drainage of Latchford. He was one of the deputa- tion who went to see the ejector at work, and it appeared to Ihim a very effective machine, and quite capable of doing the work it was intended to do. There was very little wear ,upon it and it would last a long time. It was also a very simple machine. He had great confidence in the scheme proposed by Mr. Longdin, and he hoped the Council twould adopt it. , Councillor BURGESS: If the scheme is agreed to, how soon will the committee be prepared to go on with the work? As all the members of the Council are aware, Latchford suffered a great deal last winter for want of a good drainage scheme. I hope the chairman of the com- mittee Will he able to tell us they will be able to go on with the work at once. • Councillor GREENALL made a complaint of the condition ,of Bridge-street. The sets were very slippery and were the cause of many accidents in that part of the town. He !hoped it was not intended to pave the road over the bridge with setts, as it would then be most difficult for horses to mount, and be very dangerous. Alderman HOLMES said there was one part of the scheme to which he must take exception. There was a paragraph on page three which was to the effect that the steam required could be got at the Gas Works, where there was an abundance of reserve boiler power, for the purpose of work- ing the air-compressing plant, which would be fixed at these works. The matter had never been discussed by the Gas Works Committee, although he learnt from a conversation he had just had with the Borough Surveyor that Mr. Paterson approved of the scheme. Councillor MONKS: There will not be any objection to it I think. Alderman BURGESS said he should like to ask if the ejector had been introduced anywhere else and had worked satisfactorily. Councillor WALLINGTON: It is working at Wrexham. Alderman BURGESS: I know that, but that is only on a small sewage farm. I dare say it may be a useful thing, but I cannot help thinking that we are making an experi- ment which we are not justified in making. I think it would be better to deal with Latchford as we know it can be dealt with, that is by adopting the principle Mr. Vawser laid down for pumping the sewage and carrying it through the main under Bank Quay, and discharging it at one point. Sanitary engineers were good at devising schemes of a very costly character, but be doubted whether the machine would work satisfactorily unless Mr. Shone, the inventor, could always be present. He could not support the motion. Alderman DAVIES well understood the anxiety of Alder- man Burgess as to undertaking any experiment. (Laughter.) He had had considerable experien:e so as to know that it was a serious matter. The scheme proposed was an im- portant one, and if he thought it would end in disappoint- ment. he should of course be one of the first to vote against it. But the explanations he had heard had caused him in a great measure to decide how he should vote. He was perhaps more anxious than any one to see something done in Latchford to improve the sewage arrangements, because the sewage of nearly all the outer parts of the township within the borough went through his own property. If he had not been a member of the Corporation he should have taken proceedings against that body to cause them to obviate the nuisance. What could be done on a small scale could be equally well done on a large one. The same system was being used for colliery purposes at the Westminster col- lieries, where water was raised in greater quantities and at a much greater elevation. He was prepared to vote for the carrying out of the scheme. Councillor MILNER asked what proportion in size did the Wrexham machine bear to the one required in Latchford. Although many of these machines worked beautifully with small quantities, with larger ones they did not do so well.

WARRINGTON POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Councillor Fairclough and Mr. John White. INCREASE OF SCARLET FEVER.—Application was made by Mr. Whittle, the deputy town clerk, for the removal of Edith, aged three years, the daughter of Edward C. Jones, to the Infectious Diseases Hospital.—Mr. Whittle said Mr. jones occupied a provision shop at 176, Manchester-road, , and the child had been suffering from scarlatina since Mon- day, the 20th July. The business of the shop had been conducted in the ordinary way, and in addition there were five or six cases of the disease in the same neighbourhood, all having sprung from one cause, though he could not say from the ease in question. At 172, Manchester-road—two doors from Jones's house-there were two cases, and at No. - 178 there were also two cases. . Notice had been propstly served. As their worship's were aware the town was just recovering from an epidemic of scarlet fever; and as it appeared to be again breaking oat, :they wished to Put a check to it. The . committee were certain that there were several cases that were hidden from them, and they pressed for an order in this case. It was really dangerous to leave the ,child where it was. Dr Joseph, the doctor in attendance, had advised the parents to have it removed, and had told Dr. Gornall it should be re- Moved.—Dr. Gornall, the medical officer of health, said he had received the usual certificate from Dr. Joseph, and he visited the house on Friday morning, when be found the provision shop open for the usual conducting of business. It was a well marked case of scarlet fever, and one of those cases most likely to extend the disease in the neighbour- hood. The mother asked him if she should be allowed to hurse the child if it was removed to the hospital and he had granted her that privelege. It would be dangerous to the heighbourhood if the case was left in the house.—Mr. Jones o ented that the business was being carried on, and said the hild was recovering, He handed hr a certificate from Dr. seph stating that the case was sufficiently isolated—Mr. Whittle said Dr. Joseph had changed his opinion since the previous day. He observed that the medical officer having IS ta te d the case to be dangerous, the bench had no option but Ito make the order.—Mr. Jones: There is no occasion to fear the disease; the child is getting better. -- Dr. ,Gornall: For another four weeks the case will be h-centre for the spreading of the disease.—ln answer to Mr. Fairclough, Dr. Gornall said Mr. Jones had no more chil- dren, but they had a shop.—Mr. Jones: The shop is shut up. 1--Mrs. Jones, who appeared greatly distressed, said She had a nurse who never left the child, and . the room was thoroughly disinfected and isolated. She had followed im- plicitly the directions of Dr. Joseph, and had closed the shop. IMr. White said it would no doubt be very distressing to her, ut every precaution ought to be taken for preventing the 'spread of the disease.—Mr, Jones: It is the only child, and it is three years old, and Dr. Joseph says that with the least fright it might "pop" off at any minute. Mr. Whittle said they would grant Mrs. Jones a separate ward in which to nurse the child, and she would be able to do everything for it as if she was at home.-Mrs. Jones said in an excited manner the child should not go.—Mr. White said every con- sideration would be shown to the child, and the Bench made the order for its removal. VARIETY IN BEDGARS.-H tall young DUD named Michael Keeney was charged with obtaining 6d. from Sergeant- Major Chubb, by false pretences. On Thursday, the 21st ult., prisoner went to the Barracks, and representing that he wished to enlist, was given 6d. by the Sergeant-Major with which to buy food. The charge was altered to one of vagrancy,: and prisoner was sent to gaol for seven days.— For begging in Manchester-road, on the previous afternoon, Lawrence Craney was.comnaitted to gaol for 14 days.. MEETING HIS DESERTS.—Wm. Bolton was charged with having, on Thursday, unlawfully assaulted his wife Alice.— Prisoner" believed ',! be was guilty.—About 8 o'clock on the day named prisoner went home drunk, and commenced to call his wife foul names. Having concluded this "pas- time," he went into the street and created a row there. Again returning to the house he kicked and struck his wife about the legs and.body ; he: daughter in attempting to pro- tect her receiving some ugly blows about the head and face. Prisoner was already under bail for six months for an assault upon his wife, and Mr. Hunt said his surety applied to be released on Thursday. On that afternoon Mr. Hunt remonstrated with prisoner about his conduct, but it ap- peared he afterwards went home and abused his wife.—Pro- secutrix said the prisoner had done the family no good for several years, and she asked for a judicial separation. He was in receipt of' 31s. per week.—The Bench sentenced the prisoner to three months' imprisonanent, and granted a judicial separation; prisoner oh his release to contribute 10s. per week tojyards his wife's maintenance. YOUTHFUL GARDEN ROBBERS.—Two ,boys named Then.l Geo. Cooper and Henry Barton were charged with being in , the garden of George Ferry, for the purpose of stealing 1 garden produce, on the previous morning. Prosecutor had I had a large quantity of vegetables stolen, and in consequence each night during the week had net a watch. On Friday morning the prisoners jumped on the wall, but seeing him ran away. A HOMELESS YooTH.—Frederick Brown, a boy 15 years of age was charged with being found on the premises of Mr. Frederick Monks, Atherton's Quay Forge, at 4 o'clock that (Saturday) morning, for an unlawful purpose.—Thos. Woolley, a foreman, deposed to the prisoner picking iron from the ground, and said he was in the habit of sleeping on the workS, bet he could not -discover where. It waabe- cause the boy had no home, and was likely to come to ~" no good," that he had brought him up,—The Bench, ordered the prisoner to the Workhouse. A HORRIBLE ATROCITY.-ISOBIG day ago Russian letters reported that 117 persons had been burnt in a barn. Naturally the story was received with incredulity, but the St. Petersburg Gobs declares that it is only too true. Ac- cording to this journal 119 women and girls employed in a large turnip faxen in the district of Putinol, in the govern- ment of Koursk (Southern Russia), were much dissatisfied with the bread supplied by the farm steward, alleging that it was unfit for food, and threatening to leave off work. After dinner they all withdrew to a barn to rest during the hottest period of the afternoon. The steward locked them in and went away: butlour farm labourers came and set fire to the barn. The fire spread rapidly through the build- ing, which was like tinder, and soon the whole barn was in flames. The shrieks of the unfortunate prisoners 80011 brought some people to the spot They could not be helped because the doors opened inwards, and atready the mass of frmtic women so jammed the doors from within as to make an,. effort to open them fruitless. Five women were taken out alive, but so fearfully burnt that they died almost im- mediately. All the remaining 114 perished on the spot. One of the incendiaries went off and drowned himself straight away; the other three are in prison. div.head: PUSCOT- HIGHWAY BOARD
div.p: PUSCOT- HIGHWAY BOARD

the Maydeck Colliery Club.—Charles Maurice Stuart said he was relieving officer for the St. Helens No. 1 district, and resided at 88, Bickerstaffe- street, St. Helens. On Saturday, the 9th July, the prisoner came to his house and made application for relief. This was about half-past one o'clock in the afternoon. Prisoner brought a letter with him from Mr. Buckley, requesting him to give him some relief. He had previously relieved the prisoner on the sth ult., to the ex- tent of 55., owing to his inability to work in consequence of a broken arm. Prisoner, at the time, said he had nothing coming in; he had only been working a short time at the colliery, and did not know whether he would be entitled to any allowance from the funds of the club. When prisoner applied to him on the 9th, he told him he could not give him any further relief until he had visited his house. Prisoner said his wife had been confined and there was no meat in the house, and he did not know what to do. Believing the prisoner's statement to be true' he went with him to the office in George-street, and gave him a ticket for food to the extent of 63., and told him what sort of food to get for his wife. After he had received the ticket the prisoner appeared anxious that he (witness) should not visit Ids house, and made a statement to the effect that Mr. Buckley had been to his house, that all was right, and that the officer need not go till Monday. Prisoner then left the office with the ticket. He (witness) decided to im- mediately visit the case, and went to the house, No. 130, Park-road, Parr, reaching here about half-an-hour after he had received Mr. Buckley's letter. On going into the house he found the prisoner's wife and four children. He asked her whether she had been confined that morning, and she replied "No." She appeared to be in good health. A girl about 15 or 16 years of age (daughter of the prisoner) was cooking some eggs and bacon at the time. He afterwards met the prisoner and asked him if he had got his things from Mrs. Middlehurst's, and he-replied that he had not got them all, bur that he was going to send for the remainder in the afternoon. He told him he need not trouble himself to send for the remainder of his goods as he would probably hear something mere about it. He (witness) then went to Mr. Middlehurst's shop in Parr-street, and obtained from her the ticket which he gave to the prisoner, and by her per- mission altered the ticket to 3s. 3d., so that the defendant could not get any more on it.—Other evidence in support of the charge having been given, the prisoner Was committed for trial at the next Kirkdale Quarter Sessions, bail being accepted, himself in £2O and two sureties of £5 each. ST, FIELES POLICE CO TRl`. FRlDAY.—Before the Ex-Mayor (Alderman Johnson.)

The monthly meeting of this Board was called for Tues- day, but the only members present were Messrs. Tyrer and Whitfield.—Mr. GOLDSWORTH (surveyor), submitted his statement of expenditure for the four weeks ending, July 28th, from which it appeared that he had expended in the , township of Bold, £l6 3s. 01; Knowsley, £7 18s. Oct.; Rain- hill, £2B Is. 41.; Whiston, £ll Ils. 01.; team labour, £59 15s. 311; new materials, £ll9 3s. 91; incidentals, £2O Is. 81d.; total, £262 14s. Id., against £215 12s. Od. expended in the four weeks ending June 30th.—From statement submitted by the Clerk, it appeared that the total amount owing on the last call was £435; Knowsley owed £135; Rainhill, £200; and Whiston, £100; Bold had paid up. The balance against the Board was £lBB 2s. 7d. PRESCOT POLICE COURT.

TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. W. Pilkington and A. R. Gladstone. A CONSCIENCE-STRICKEN DESERTER—John McKay, a respectably-attired young man, was charged with deserting from the Royal Artillery, Clonmel, Ireland, in October, 1878.—P.C. Prior deposed that on the night of the 28th July, as he was proceeding along Derby-street, the prisoner came up to him and said he was a deserter and wished to give himself up. He therefore took him into custody and locked him up.—Prisoner was remanded to Walton to await an escort. GAME TRESPASS AT ROBY.—John Brown was charged with using a dog for the purpose of taking game at Roby, on the 27th July.—Mr. T. Swift appeared to prosecute, and in opening the case said the information was laid by the game- keeper of Mr. Brocklebank, of Childwall Hall, who preserved game in Huyton and Roby. Upon Wednesday morning in the previous week a cowman in the employ of Mr. Frederick Earle, J.P.,Edenhurst, was going down to the park to the cows about half-past five o'clock, when he Saw three men with a dog at the bottom part of the park. The men after- wards left that part of the park, and went into one of Mr. Earle's fields, and the dog chased a hare. As soon as the men saw the cowman they endeavoured to get away, one running off towards Childwall, and the other two down Carr- lane. The cowman went round and met them, and asked what they had been doing, and they replied that they had not been doing anything. He, however, noticed that one of them had something- bulky about his person, and he at once put his hand into the man's pocket and took out a hare ; so that at the time the cowman saw them they had got ens hare, and the dog was chasing another. The man was taken to Prescot, where his name and address were taken, and he had been served with a summons. As the defendant did not choose to appear, he asked their worships to inflict a sub- stantial penalty. The defendant stated that he had been in the employ of the Liverpool Corporation, and lived at Fair- field, but that he had removed to Gateacre. Whatever the defendant might have been before, he seemed to have got into bad company, or else he had made the company bad; he did not know which.—Henry Beesley, cowman to Mr. Earle, then stated the facts of the case, the majority of which are contained in Mr. Swift's statement. When he met the defendant and one of his companions in Carr-lane after they had left the field, he asked them what they were doing there, and they replied, "Nothing." Witness noticed the bead of a hare protruding from the defendant's coat pocket and got hold of it, and, pulling it out of his pocket, said, "What do you call this?" Defendant never answered.— Mr. Swift remarked that they had not been able to serve summonses on the other two men as yet, but there was no reason why the defendant should not be dealt with then.— A fine of £3 and costs was inflicted, in default, one month's imprisonment. STEALING CORN AT WHISTON AN IMPUDENT THIEF. —Thomas Forrester, a middle-aged man, was chargee with stealing a sack, containing 931bs. of Indian corn, from Quarry Bank Farm, Whiston, on the 20th July, the property of Mr. Wm. Lougton ; also with having, between the Ist and the 13th, stolen a sack from the same farm.—Edward Hughes, a labourer, in the employ of Mr. Longton, and re- siding at Bickerstaff-street, St. Helens, stated that on Wed- nesday morning the 20th July, about three o'clock in the morning he saw a man with a sack on his back going out of the farm-yard. He followed the man, and on coming up with him found it was the prisoner. He took the bag off his back and put it on the ground. Prisoner said "Ned, don't split." Witness replied "Hold on a bit, I will call Rimtner up about that." Witness then went and called Rimmer, but on returnmg the prisoner had decamped, leav- ing the sack behind him.—Mr. Rimmer, the farm bailiff, stated that he had missed corn for the last eight weeks. Two sacks had been taken away with small quantities. Prisoner was formerly employed on the farm—lnspector Barnett said there was no doubt the prisoner had systemati- cally robbed Mr. Longton for some time.—Prisoner, who pleaded guilty, was sent to gaol for two months with hard labour.

OBTAINING RELIEF BY FALSE PRETENCES AT Sr. HELENS—James Taylor, St. Helens, was charged with hav- ing, by a certain false pretence, obtained from Charles Maurice Stuart, relieving-officer of St. Helens, an order for food to the value of Os., one relief ticket, and one piece of paper, the property of the Guardians of the Poor of the Prescot Union, with intent to cheat and defraud the same; . . . . . . . _ ..
and also with haying obtained from Emma Middlehurst the sum of 33. 3d. in money, the moneys of Thomas Wilcock, . . . . _
with intent to cheat ana'defraud hiin and the Guardians of
the same.—Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Guardians,

appeared to prosecute, and stated that on the 9th of July the prisoner obtained from one of the relieving officers of the Guardians a ticket for food to the value of es. Prisoner made his first application for relief _ _ . . . .

on the sth of July, when he stated to the officer that he had met with an injury to his arm, and was in consequence un- able to-work, and he had a wife and six children. The officer relieved him to the extent of ss. Four days afterwards the prisoner, it appeared, went to Mr. Buckley, one of the guar- dians, who sent a letter by the 'prisoner to Mr. Stuart, in which he advised a further ticket to be given to the extent of 65., inasmuch as he (the prisoner) represented that his wife was near her confinement. The officer, upon the recom- mendation of Mr. Buckley, gave the prisoner a ticket for food to the value of 6s. 6d. Prisoner then went to a shop kept by Mrs. Emma Middlehurst, to whom he represented that his wife had been confined, and asked her to advance . . .

him money on the ticket, and he actually received the sum of 3s. 3d. He (Mr. Hartley) would call evidence to show that during the whole of the time the prisoner had been out of work. He had been receiving from two colliery clubs the sum of 185. per week, less Sd. for weekly subscriptions. He had been in receipt of 108. per week from the Lancashire and Cheskire Miners' Permanent Relie' Fund, and Sa. from

DRUNKENNESS —Hettry Ince- ma‘de his eight appearance, after a lapsa of eleven years, and was fined 3s. and costs for . .
being drink.

USING OBSCENE LANGUAGE.—Thomas Ford, a young roan, with six convictions recorded against him, was fined 10s. and costs for using obscene language in Liverpool-st.— Kate McDermot, for a similar offence on Friday night, was fined ss. and costs.

CROSBY'S SIXTY-FOCRTH APPEARANCE.—John Crosby, formerly a butcher, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Water-street, on Friday night.—The case having been proved, Superintendent Johnston said the defendant had been up 63 times before.—The Magistrate: What have you got to say for yourself. I thought you promised the last time I saw you here that the thing would never occur again. But I find you have been up here since then. It appears there is no reclamation.—Defendant : I could not pay a fine, because I have not had any work to do lately.— Magistrate: Then why do you get drunk? What do you do for a living ?—Defendant: Butchering what bit I have had to do for the last 6 or 8 months; sometimesl make some- thing on a Saturday.—Magistrate: I suppose nobody will employ you because you are so fond of drink. Defendant : Oh yes, plenty get drunk besides me.—Magistrate : You will be fined IN. and costs. Defendant: If you will give me a fortnight I will pay it.—Superintendent Johnston : No, I'll give you no time ; you have plenty of friends who can pay if they will. . _

SHOPKEEPERS' Fanurs.—Michael Bohn, provision dealer, Bridge-street, was summoned for causing an obstruction in Bridge-street, in front of his shop, by leaving fourteen full boxes and three empty ones from a quarter to one until a I quarter past one three feet in the road.—P.C. Peebles proved the case, and a coachman said that he was driving up Bridge. Street, when a passing vehicle took off the cap of one of his carriage wheels. This was owing to the boxes being in the road.—PC. Peebles said he had cautioned the defendant several times before that date.—The magistrate said it was an unpleasant thing for him to fine a shopkeeper like him- self. He would like to have seen the defendant put in an appearance.—Fined 2s. Od. and costs.

STRIKING A HORSE WITH. A PIECE Ow WOOD.—JOhR Roberts, a youth, was charged with ill.treating a horse by striking it on the leg with a piece of wood.—Sergeant Robinson said that at five minutes to three on Friday after- noon, 22nd inst., the defendant was in charge of one of Messrs. Pilkington's horses' in the Alexandria Colliery yard, Sutton. The defendant, holding the horse by the bridle, called out to it, and struck it on the left fore-leg with part of an old coal box three times. The horse lifted its leg, and appeared to be in great pain. Defendant was about to strike it again. when he (witnesß) intorfored.—Defcndant said he did not wish to be cruel to the horse, but it was very stupid. —Sergeant Robinson said the horse was going the wrong way when the defendant struck it—The magistrate said ill- treating the horse was not the way to make it any better • besides, it was somebody elses property.—Fined 2s. 6d. and costs. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. H. S. Hall, and W. Blinkhorn. DAMAGING GRASS.—William Henry and Hugh Logan, boys residing in Windle, were charged with wilfully damaging grass in a field belonging to Mr. John Littler, near Denton' s Green.—Superintendent Johnston said the boys were caught that morning by Mr. Littler, who was very much annoyed by persons from St. Helens, who kept rabbits, going into the field, which was now growing for a second crop. The boys were brothers and had two rabbits, and a little bag filled with grass was found upon them.—Mr. Littler deposed to arresting the boys in his field, and he assessed the damage at 11—The boys' mother, in answer to the magistrates, said her husband was a plasterer' and was at present working at Mr. Robinson's place at Crank.— The boys were each fined ss. id., or seven days' imprison- ment. MARIA "PUTS HER Four iw tr."—Maria Callagan, well known on Greenbank, was charged with being drunk in I Liverpool-road, Eccleston, on the previous night.—Super- intend Johnston said the prisoner had been 29 times before the court, and was a very bad character.—Prisoner: Oh, but I was four years and never put my foot in it.—Superin- tendent Johnston said the prisoner had been convicted three times this year.—She was fined 13s. 6d. and costs, altogether 205., or, ,1.4 days' imprisonment.
