div.head: TRAVELS UTIIE EAST.
div.p: TRAVELS UTIIE EAST.
BY A SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE GENTLEMAN. tSrzclAL.] No. X. CAIRO AND THE PYRAMIDS.

(Cosmxinen.) From the Mission House we drove to the site of Heliopolis, the ancient city of On, mentioned in Genesis. It is five miles from Cairo, through a country richly cultivated. At this once famous seat of learning I suppose it is quite certain Plato studied, and almost equally certain that Moses received his brilliant education. It was from this city thet Joseph married " Asenath, the daughter of Potipkerah, priest of On." A splendid granite obelisk, perhaps the largest monolith in the world, is the only relic above ground of the once illustrious city. Its hieroglypalcs are still in beautiful character, almost as clear as the day they were carved. It is said to bear the name of Osertesan, who was the Pharoah of Joseph's time. There it stands, a solitary monument the tombstone of a buried city, whose site-and name, but for this memento, would have been swept out of all remembrance. Not far from the obelisk is a well, in 'which it is said Mary, the mother of Jesus, washed, when she and Joseph fled with the young child into Egypt. We drank of the water which, it is further said, was made sweet and sett by Mary's ablution, although previously salt or bitter. Then, close by, is the tree under which the Holy F l sted,—a tree quite old enough, I should say, to amiy re have bad the honour of giving them shelter. To have seen so noble a sycamore was worth the five miles' journey. Its trunk is about twenty-two feet in diameter one way, and nine Sr ten feet the other, sound and gnarled, and with the foilage quite heavy upon its branches. To indulge the desire after immortality, which se Often finds vent in the carving of initials on all such oh- the owner, with bitter irony, has put up a notice re- questing visitare to carve their names on the palings, by . which the tree is now protected. We had a conversation with our dragomaucn domestic or married life in Egypt. We ventured to ask him about his own home, a point upon which most Moslems are very tenacious, being exceedingly jealous of any intrusion into their family circle. He said nothing would purchase an introduction into his house; it would be a disgrace to take a stranger over his threshold, or to be seen himself, with his wife on the street. With the exception of going once or twice a week to the baths with one of her own family, his wife, he said, never went over the doorstep ; and no respectable woman would. • His jealously-guarded treasure was considerably under twenty years of age, and had five children, which corroborated Miss Whately's statement that she could not keep the girls after the age of twelve. On the way we bad on each side of the road long rows of orange trees, laden with their rich ripe fruit. Large orchards, too, of olives lined the way. It seems the olives are ripe when the Nile is at its height, and boats have to be used to gather the fruit. So it is with the date palm. We were told that a single data palm some- times yielded £lOO worth of fruit—a most difficult thin ato believe. It was much less difficult to believe, with all the evidences of lavish expenditure, and consequent ppverty around us, that every date-palm and every fig-tree, every donkey and even every fowl, are taxed by Egypt's rapacious government. For not only is the land, to a very great ex- tent, held under copy-hold from the Crown, and tithed to the hilt, and loaded, moreover, with fines on every change of proprietorship; but every article the poor farmer grows, as well as every tree it grows upon, is taxed to the very utter- most. It is no uncommon thing for the land itself, as well as its produce, to be sold for the payment of taxes. The people themselves do not run away, as families, friends, and even villages are held responsible for unpaid taxes. As far as regards the poor fellah, or farm labourer, if he cannot satisfy the shirk, or tax-gatherer, he is t astinadoed. It makes one's heart bleed to recount the wrongs and sorrows of Egypt's degraded and down-trodden people. CAIRO TO PORT SAID. It was not without regret we drove to the station through the busy thoroughfares of Cairo on Friday, March 3, a 9 I a.m. Its street scenes to which we were now bidding adieu, had, like so many illuminated pictures, been alternating during our stay with visions of Egypt's anc:ent glory, as seen in her colossal monuments, upon which we had loosed and pondered. We felt we neither understood the one, nor had had sufficiently gathered into our souls the impress of the other. Still we were reconciled to depart, for had we not the sacred hand before us? Were not our feet to stand within the gates of Jerusalem ? The prospect softened our regrets. Besides, we had not yet done with Egypt ' • its most sacred fields had to bless our eyes! The land of Goshen lay along the road bttween Cairo and the Suez Canal, to which we were bound. Soon after leaving Zagazig, we saw the old country, rendered holy by the long residence of Jacob and his family, stretching before us—a good and beautiful land! We had expected to find it to a much greater extent swept over by the sands of the desert. Considerable tracts are so as you draw near to Ismailia; but for miles end miles the fields were garmented with their first annual crop, and smiling in all the beauty and freshness of spring. Unlike most other parts of Egypt, Goshen is divided into well- defined plots, with hedge-rows or regularly built fences ornamenting the landscape. Had it not been for the palm trees everywhere visible we might have thought we were passing through England in the early summer. If, as Mr. Sharp says, the land is neither moistened by rain from heaven, nor by the overflow of the Nile, its present condition speaks well for the industry of its cultivators, as its former luxuriance in the hands of the Israelites spoke well for them. Pharoah pointed out Goshen as "the best of the lard." He must have meant it was the best of the pasture land. Unceasing industry is required to keep it fruitful. The desert is ever ready to encroach when the labour if man's hand is relaxed. On the other band, the means of irriga- tion are not far to seek. Robinson says—" The water of the Nile soaks through the earth under the sandy tracts, and is everywhere found 18 or 20 feet from the surface." As we drew near to Lamella, fertility ceased, and large tracts of sand covered the soil; but we saw in many places where the surface of the earth had been disturbed in cutting for the railway, that six or eight inches of sand brought you down to the dark soil, which is usually of great depth. May we not, therefore, justly conclude that, with deep plougaing and irrigation, by the sinking of wells, the land, even in this desolate region, might be brought into still higher cul- tivation than ever? After very carefully observing every cutting as we rode along, I believe the remark as to the shallowness of the sand will apply to nearly the whole of the land between Zagazig and Ismailia, over which the sand has swept.. lam glad to know that the waters of the Suez Canal are gradually bringing the desert through which they flow into a state of cultivation. A.recent writer says —"Before the canal was opened there was scarcely a blade of grass in the region, except on the borders of the bitter lakes, and about the oasis of Ismailia. But now the whole face of the country is becoming changed. Everywhere along the line of the canal herbage of various kinds is springing up. It is, of course, known to everyone that the water of the canal is salt ; but, as it filtrates through the sand, it becomes capable of affording nourishment to vegetation. The large influx of water into the desert has affected the atmosphere. The rapid evaporation which takes place during the day descends in thick dews at night. • Captains of Suez Canal steamers declare that, even in the case of such a rarity, as rain, the rainfall is every year markedly increasing." The testimony here given as to the effect of the moisture upon the earth's surface, proves, I 1 think, that the soil capable of cultivation, covered with but a thin layer of sand, extends far beyond the borders of Goshen to Eastern Egypt. The ruins of the treasure cities—Python and Raamses—built by the children of Israel towards the end of their sojourn in Egypt, when Pharoah set over them taskmasters, were objects of great interest to us. These ruins occupy elevated sites not far from the line of railway, and are about two miles apart. From Raamses the children of Israel took their departure fo7 Canaan. From these low hills and fertile plains the multitudes (with women and children probably numbering two million persons) went forth with their flocks And herds. At the command of Jehovah, they went forth to seek a home in the land He had prepared for them, and to which we were now bound. Associations such as these we felt were a most natural and pleasing preparation for those more solemn scenes which Palestine should present for oor contemplation. I say in my note book: "Have not I seen the land in which the children of Israel fed their flocks, over which, probably, the good old Jacob travelled, staff in hand, and from which he was borne with high funeral honours, when they carried his eml?almed body to lay it in the cave of Machpelah ? And might not Joseph in his old age, re-united to his own people, have wandered along these hedgerows with his great great grand-children, the seed of Ephraim by his side, or have sat within the boundaries of yonder city with the grand-children of Manasseh upon his knees? (Gen. 1,23.) Oh, how dear I feel Egypt to be, in spite of all her present degradation; and how gladly should I hail the day of her political and spiritual emancipation. May the Lord hasten it in His own time." We reached Ismailia about half-past five p.m., and, although our guide had telegraphed to arrange for our accommodation, not a bed was to be had on our arrival. Having laid in a hasty supply of bread and oranges, we embarked in one of the little steamers which ply on the canal, and which had been specially engaged to convey us at once to Port Said. The moonlight favoured our trip, throwing quite a joyousness over a jour- ney which, otherwise, would have been dull enough, owing to the sand banks on each side of the canal standing high above the line of vision. With the moon globular in its silvery clearness, and the stars blazing out with amazing brilliancy, we sat for six delightful hours talking over our adventures, and singing to the ceaseless pratter of the screw. So we made the desert to rejoice, if not to blossom as the rose.

div.head: PORT SAID.
div.p: PORT SAID.

Port Said, having sprung rapidly into existence, to meet the passenger and trade requirements of the canal, has all the characteristics of mushroom growth written large upon It. Its buildings are ricketty; its streets are wide, but un- finished; and its social life, not only raw and unsettled, but exceedingly low in its moral tone. The singing cafés are its most prominent feature, and in these gambling ar.d licentiousness abound. Being principally in the hands of the French, who, as a rule, care nothing tar religion, the town is with out any counteracting influences of a moral and religious kind to stem the torrent of profligacy that surges through it. There is a sad future for Port Said, if Chris- tian phil irthrophy, aided by a kind Providence, does not i n terpo,e. We were detained from Saturday morning until rnesdav cvening awaiting the arrival of the steamer, which
was delayed by the storm in Alezandria.l now bid fare- well to the land of the Phmaohs, In the hope of meeting my rmders on the shores of Palestine. (To be continued next week.)

RUNCORN ImpRovENIENT COMMISSIONERS. The monthly meeting of this body was held on Wednes- day (by arrangement, owing to the ordinary day of meet- ing being Bank Holiday). Dr. Steele presided, and there were also present Messrs. Norman, Dobson, Lyon, McDou- gall, J. J. Speakman, Meadowcroft, Briscoe, Marshall, blandley, Frith, Linaker (law clerk), Brookes (secretary), Barker (surveyor), and Mouritz (medical officer). MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. The report of Dr. Mouritz stated that the number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the past month amounted to 18, representing a death rate of about 14 per 1,000 per annum. Of the deaths five were due to diseases of the nervous system, three to pulmonary organs, three whooping cough, two to exhaustion, two plithisis, two diseases of the heart, and one to hepatic disease. Ten of the deaths occurred amongst children of two years and under, and eight under one year. Four inquests had been held, making the total deaths 22. THE INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL QUESTION. THE BRIDGE SLOPE. The following letter was read :—" The Street, Lincoln, let August, 1881. Dear Sir,—l sent up the Runcorn In- fections Diseases Hospital plans to the architect of the Local Government Board for his observations. He says there are a good many things about them that require alteration, and he thinks it would save a good deal of time if the Run- corn Commissioners could appoint one or two of their mem- bers with the person who drew out the plans, to confer with the Local Government architect and the medical officersali the Local Government Board on the subject. Will you kindly inform the Commissioners to this effect 7—Believe me, dear sir, yours faithfully Richard I. DANCEY.—Mr.Nort..I MAN said that if the Local Government Board were not carefully watched, they might put the Commissioners to considerable expense. The London Board wished the Run- corn Ghardians to go to• an expense of about £4,000 in a similar matter, but they declined to enter upon such a serious expenditure.—Mr. P. SPEAKMAN said that the matter of the bridge slope was in the hands of a solicitor, and it was in an advanced state. As to the other matter, he moved that Mr. Norman, Mr. Handley, Mr. Taylor, and the Surveyor be appointed a committee for the purpose of considering the plans, and that two of their number, together with the surveyor, be appointed a deputa- tion for the purpose of going to London and conferring with the architect and medical officers of the Local Government Board with reference to the hospital plans.—The resolution was passed unanimously. MORE TALK ABOUT MR. CLIFF'S CONTRACT. Mr. CURZON, a well known ratepayer, appeared before the Board, and read a petition signed by about 270 ratepayers, asking them to reconsider the contract they were about to sign with Mr. Thomas Cliff for cleansing the streets of th- town. The petitioners were of opinion the Board ought not to let the cleansing of the streets to any one, but carry on the work as usual under the jurisdiction of the Board. They felt that by the letting of the street cleansing, as pro- posed, the Commissioners would be doing the ratepayers a great injustice and increasing rates. They understood that the contract was to be £450 per year, and that this was £3O per year more that it had cost for the last 3 years. They also were of opinion that the Board had not got,,proper value for the horse, watercarts and other things which have been sold, considering that the horse cost the ratepayers over £9O. In presenting the petition Mr. Curzon got into a somewhat excited state, and remarked that some of the supporters of Mr. Cliff had spoken on this question as if the ratepayers were in future to walk the town in silver slippers, as it would be so clean but he was inclined to think that instead of such being the case, they would each have to order a pair of top boots. (Langhter.)—The CHAIRMAN said the petition should receive consideration, but it was a pity it had not been brought under the notice of the Board weeks ago.—The subject came up again on the reading of the minutes of the Highway and Sanitary Committee, which stated that the committee had given in- structions to the law-clerk to write to Messrs. Grundy, Kershaw and Co., that the Commissioners would not give an undertaking to pay their costs in connection with the land in Algernon-street. A letter had been received from the London and North-Western Railway Company with refer- ence to the railway bridge slope, stating that the company must have an assurance that their powers for the compul- sory purchase of the property would be exercised at the Commissioners' expense. A motion had, .been passed approv- ing the reply of the law-clerk, stating that he could not advise the Commissioners to pay any costs in putting in force compulsory powers.—Mr. NORMAN moved that the minutes be confirmed wiih the exception of that part relat- ing to Algernon-street, and the proceedings of the committee as to Mr. Cliff's contract. He considered that the Alger- non-street matter had better be left over, as Mr. Statham had submitted plans for several lurge houses which he proposed 1 to erect in a line with Leinster gardens. The contract matter would be better referred back to the committee. The Surveyor had had to put three men on to sweep Regent- street one day lately, and he proposed to charge the cost to the contractor.—Mr. P. SPEAKMAN seconded the motion; and a discussion followed as to the contract, which has now been before the Board on several occasion% when the re- marks of the members have been fully reported in the Examiner.—Dr. MCDOUGALL said the question of the con- tract had been thoroughly thrashed out. He, however, thought that such a respectably signed petition as they had received that day ought not to be ignored. Either they 'taught to at once accept or reject Mr. Cliff's contract. —Mr. MEADOWCROFT considered the Commissioners were boundl by consistency and principle to carry out the contract.—Mr. Donsole said that the proposal to let the contract to Mr. Cliff had given great dissatisfaction to the ratepayers. He suggested that the proper course to adopt in order to main- tain the honour and dignity of the Board was to reconsider the matter, and he gave notice that at the next.meeting he should propose that a committee be appointed to arrange with Mr. Cliff as to what terms he would accept to cancel the agreement. (Hear, bear.)—Mr. HANDLEY thought the petition which bad been sent to the Board ought to have the attention it deserved, but he felt sure that the position of the Commissioners as to the tender had not been properly understood by some of the ratepavers.—Mr. Lem moved an amendment which Was seconded by Dr. McDotrow, in favour of the minutes passing, with the exception of that part in them which related to Algernon-street.—Messrs. Lyon, McDougall, Meadowcroft, and Frith 'voted for the amendment. and Messrs. Norman, Dobson, Williams, J. J. Speakman, P. Speakman, Briscoe, Marshall, and Handley, for the original motion, which was declared carried.—The minutes were then approved. EDUCATIONAL MATTERS. The Canal Boats and Hospital Committee's minutes stated that the Canal Boats Amendment Act, of 1877 had been con- sidered, and a resolution passed that the Runcorn School Board be requested to co-operate with the Commissioners in considering the educational clauses of the bill.—The minutes were passed. - -

...... _ THE FREEHOLDERS' RIGHTS. Mr. DortsoN reported that no proper meeting of the com- mittee appointed to consider the rights of the freeholders had been held, but information wal being got together upon the matter. A PUBLIC LIBRARY FORESHADOWED. Mr. HANDLEY moved that a committee be appointed to open up communications with the Literary In- stitute with a view to acquiring the public library connected with that body for the use of town. He understood the committee of the institute would welcome any proposal which would tend to the advancement of the intellectual position of Runcorn. Of course this proposition might be said to foreshadow what he should be very glad to see, viz., a public library and museum for the town.—Mr. MEADOW- CROFT seconded the proposal, which was supported by Mr. Marshall—Messrs. Norman, McDougall, Briscoe, Shaw, and G. S. Hazlehurst were appoiated a committee to carry out the negotiations. GAS MATTERS. Dr. McDorGALL moved that the minutes of the General Purposes Committee should be approved. They recom- mended that Mr. Richard Hampson's tender to repair the street lamps for three years from September let be accepted, at the following rates :—First year, £3O; second year, £2B; and third £26. The committee recommended that a letter should be sent to the secretary of the Gas Company, praying for a further reduction in the price of gas supplied to the street lamps.—The resolution was seconded by Mr. Dobson, and the minutes were passed. ADJOURNMENT OF THE MEETING. On the proposition of Mr. Frith, seconded by Mr. Nor- man, it was resolved unanimously, that the meeting should stand adjourned to the 11th inst., for the purpose of receiv- ing and considering the report of the Highway and Sanitary Committee with reference to the contract for street cleansing and the memorial of the ratepayers thereon. This terminated the business.

ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT ST. HELENS THROUGH LOVE DISAPPOINTRIENT.—A determined attempt to commit suicide was made on Monday night by Thomas Henry Pilkington (24), residing with his father at a beerhouso at the junction of Nerth-road and Duke-street. The young man has for some time been paying his addresses to a young woman in service on Cropper's Hill, but of late not finding a reciprocity of feeling on the part of the young lady, who appeared to bestow her smiles upon some one else, be became depressed, and on 11,Iongay night seems to have arranged a plan for doing away with himself, and rumour says not only himself but the young lady also. On Monday night he went to where the object of his affections resided, and threatened to kill her, when she ran out of the house. He then swallowed some c.rbolic acid which he had taken with him, and was found in a state of unconsciousness lying in the road, by two policemen, who took charge of him. Or. Griffiths attended the man shortly after, and be is now in a fair way towards recorery. The carbolic acid, it appears, , was thrown back, being taken in too large a quantity. He will be brought before the magistrates. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY AUGUST 6,188 L
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY AUGUST 6,188 L

WIDNES POLICE COURT. WEDNEsnAv.—Before Messrs. E. Gibbon (chairman), H. S. Hall, and A. R. Gladstone. AN ADVENTURE WITH A POLICE INSPECTOR.—Thomas Herbert Orrett, barman at the Cressington Hotel, Aigburtb, Liverpool, was summoned for having at Farnworth, on the. 21st tilt., committed a breach of the peace by shouting andi making a great noise and disturbance.—The police were ' represented by Mr. Swift, sen., St. Helens; and Mr. Bart- lett, Liverpool, appeared for defendant, a respectably. dressed young man, slightly built, of middle height, and apparently of a somewhat ,mild disposition. The inspector is a tall, bony north countryman.—Mr. Bartlett made an ap- plication to the Bench to permit of the case being postponed. There was certainly a charge before them, preferred by the inspector, but defendant alleged that instead of his being the offender, Barnett had committed a elms and wanton as- sault upon him. Mr. Bartlett had advised defendant to take action against Barnett in the County Court at St. Helens for assault. However, before any action could be commenced against a police inspector a month's notice must be given to him. The offence with which defendant was charged was alleged to have been committed on the 21st ult. On the 26th ult. Barnett was served with a notice as to the County Court proceedings, and on the same day the summons in the present case was served upon defendant requesting him to appear on the 27th of the same month to answer the charge of disturbance. Under these circumstances, he asked that the case might be adjourned until the one now pending in] ithe St. Helens County Court, and which would be tried by I a jury, had been decided. The Bench would observe that I ' no action was taken against the defendant until Barnett got his summons.—Mr. Swift opposed the application, and maintained that the proceedings of the police were perfectly regular. Summonses were frequently issued in batches, and the defendant's was one of a number.—After some further discussion between the legal gentlemen, the magi- strates decided to proceed with the case that day.—Mr. Swift, in his opening address, said that on the 21st ult. the Widnes Athletic Sorts took place at Farnworth, and the Inspector and a number of policemen were present for the purpose of preserving order. After the sports had ter- minated, the Inspector sent two officers into Derby-road, in consequence of a complaint about certain proceedings there. Later on he received a further message, and then went to the place himself. He found a considerable crowd had assem- bled, and it was principally composed of gambling men. The police had taken possession of some boards which bpi during the day been used as gambling tables. They broke one of these in order to prevent its being employed a second time for a similar purpose. The crowd then became very excitedand defendant, who happened to be present, cried out "Shame, shame," and incited the people to assault the officers. Barnett, seeing what was going on, tried to get amongst the crowd, and succeeded at last in pushing his way through it. Whilst doing so, he carried a stick in his hand. He held it in an upright position to prevent it hurting any- one. However, as Barnett was going through the crowd, the stick "did touch the defendant on the cheek or eyelid," but the blow merely caused a scratch ard was not worth taking any notice about. Defendant told Barnett what he had done, on which the Inspector told him it was a pure ac- cident and that he had brought it upon himself by his own disorderly behaviour. One of defendant's friends then came up, told bin that he was in the wrong, asked him to go away, and said he had better be quiet and say nothing.— Inspector Barnett was called and gave evidence in support of Mr. Swift's opening statement.—ln cross-examination, wit- ness stated that he did not see any nuts or cakes about the place where the row occurred, nor was any inquiry made for the boards by any old women.--P.C.'s Strickland and Brydges corroborated, as did also a civilian named Henry Wyman, who stated that defendant was in drink at the time. —Mr. Swift was about to call Sergeant Robinson when the magistratessaid they did not consider it necessary to have any further evidence placed before them in Support of thecharge. Mr. hartlett said that defendant was perfectly sober at the time. Defendant's version of the affair was that having missed the train he, went into Derby-road, where he saw some women will) had tables on which they were selling cakes and nuts. The police came on the scene, seized the tables, and commenced breaking them up. This the police did in rather a violent manner, and some of the crowd cried "Shame" several times. Defendant shouted out " Shame" twice. As he was saying this, Inspector Barnett came up behind him—perhaps he dare not come up in front—and struck him a violent blew with his fist. Subsequently be struck him across the eye with a stick, causing it to bleed. He would calla medical man who would state that he saw defendant shortly after the affair, and he was sober. He (the speaker) did not believe in the police striking right and left simply because they wore blue clothes and white gloves. If defendant had acted improperly the proper course for them to adopt was to summon him before the Magistrates, and not take the law into their own hands.—Mr. Bartlett then called Dr. R. A. Morris, of Oarston, who said that on the 21st ult., between nine and ten at night, he saw the defendant, who was then quite sober. He had a small wound over the right eyelid, about one-third of an inch long, and there was a considerable contusion.—Defendant was called to corroborate theatatement of Mr. Bartlett. In the course of his evidence, he stated that the Inspector hit him with his open hand at first, and knocked his bat off. As he was getting up , from picking up his hat, Barnett hit him again with his stick. The discolouration upon one of his eyes was where the In- spector struck him. The blow caused him to feel stunned for a. minute, and he said to Barnett "Yon see what you have done?" He said "Yes," on which witness asked "Will you give me your name and address?* He then at- tempted to write it down but he could not do so owing to the blood running down his face. Previous to the assault he had just been on a sick bed for six months, suffering from fever.—Thomas Cross, a young man, who said he lived in Aigburth-road, stated that he was present at the time of the assault. He saw the Inspector strike defendant three or four times on the face, hut the blows were not given with a stick.—This concluded the evidence for the defence.—The Chairman: We shall deal with this case as we should with any, ordinary case of the same kind, and it is a very or- dinary one, after all. This man will be bound over, him- self in £lO and one surety in Z. Mr. Bartlett objected to his client paying the costs, but Mr. Blackwell, deputy magistrates' clerk, said the practice of that court in such cases was that the costs always followed the verdict. ASSACLTING AN OLD MAN.—James Duffy Was charged with threatening, and John Duffy with assaulting an old man named Edwarl Duffy.—Cemplainant said that on the afternoon of the 31st ult., he was coming out of a public- house, when the two defendants met him and wanted to fight. John. Duffy said he would make him fight or be would have his life, and the other that "be would hang for him." One of the defendants hit him over the mouth.— The Inspector said that James Duffy had been up at the court before for breach of the peace, assault on the police, and common assault; and the other defendant bad been be- fore the Bench six times.—The Bench discharged defendants .;on each of them paying 63. 6d. costs. A! WEAN CAsE.—Edwird Duffy, the complainant in the previous case, was then charged by one of the witnesses who had appeared on behalf of the last-named defendants, named Sarah Ann Duffy, with indecent exposure on Monday after- noon, on the door step of his hence—Defendant denied the charge, and said it was only brought because he had pro- ceeded against the two men.—A woman was called who gave evidence on his behalf, and the case was dismissed. STEALING PIGEONS.—James Dillon, aged 16, who had been previously canvicted, was ordered to receive 12 strokes with the birch rod, and afterwards be sent to gaol 14 days with hard labour, for stealing two pigeons, the property of a couple of lads named Barrett and Nickton; who live with their parents in Elizabeth-street, on Sunday evening.

THE ATTEMPT TO BLOW UP LIVER- POOL TOWN HALL. The two men, M'Grath and M'Kevitt, who were arrested on the 10th of June for the outrage at the Liverpool Town Hall, were on Tuesday put upon their trial the assizes in that city before Mr. Justice Lopes. Two charges were brought against them—first, that of doing damage to the building by means of an explosive, whereby the lives of certain persons were endangered; and secondly, of placing an explosive near t'le building with intent to do damage Both the prisoners were found guilty of the first and graver sffence. M'Grath was afterwards indicted for causing an explosion at the Central Police Station, Hattod Garden, a short time prior to the Town Hall outrage. Amongst the witnesses called by the prosecution in this case was one Edward Wilkinson, keeper of a refreshment-house at Mid- dlesborough, who said that M'Grath visited his house on five different occasions between the months 'of April and June. Believing that he had met Wilkinson at a Land League meeting at Dublin M'Grath became communicative and said that he was a letter-carrier in the service of "the organisation," and that his district was an extensive one, including Manchester. He stated further that he had had "two failures"—presumably referring to explosions which had failed of their purpose—and on one of his visits he carried an iron or tin box, which he said contained "some- thing that would blow up the biggest ship that ever swam on the seas." For the defence it was stated that the prisoner had never been in Middlesborough, and that Wilkinson's , story was fictitious. The Jury found the prisoner guilty of being an acsessory before the fact as regarded the Hatton Garden outrage, proof having been given that he had got plugs made for the explosive instruments used dn that occa- sion. M'Grath was sentesced to penal servitude for life and 111‘Kevitt to penal servitude for 15 years.

On Tuesday, a young married couple were in the Ship Inn, Raven-street, St. Helens, when some cross words were spoken. The wife declared that if her husband took another mug of beer, she would go and jump into the canal, which runs past the house. The husband took up the vessel, and was raising it to his mouth, when she seized it and rushed to the canal. Throwing it in, she either jumped or fell in herself, but, repenting of her rash threat, shouted loudly for help. Her husband got the assistance of another man, and she n as rescued, not much the worse for her immersion. I.IOLT MISSION Room, RAINIIILL.—On Monday, about 55 Sunday scholars and congregation in connection with the above room, had a pic-nic to Frodsham, Cheshire. The party left Rainhill station in the morning, and after a very enjoyable ride, reached Frodsham about ten o'clock, and proceeded to Mersey View, where a variety of games were indulged in. Tea was partaken of about four o'clock, at one of the numerous refreshment bosses, and after rambling about for three or :our hours, the party returned, much pleased and satisfied w3th their day's outing.

WARRINGTON CLERGY INSTITUTIONS. The anniversary of the Warrington Institutions for Clergy Widows and Orphans, and Clergy Daughters' School, was held in the Clergy School, Warrington, on Thursday. The chair was occupied by Sir R. A. Cross, G.C.8., M.P., presi- dent for the year; and there were also present the Lord Bishop of Liverpool, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bishop Kelly, Archdeacons Darby and Anion, Canons Barclay, Heron, Appleton, McClure, Stowell, Gore, Stanton, Pitcairn, Hop- wood, Blackburn, Fielder, Penrhin ; Rev. Sparks, Byrth,. Jones, Barnes, Deacle, Wilkinson' Atkinson, Quekett (rector of Warrington) Greenall, Toft ;and Messrs. Wilson, Watson, 'Linsley, Birley (Newton), Smith (Chester), Jones (Dares- bury), R. Livingstone, Buckton, and G. S. Marsden, (Man- chester.) The SECRETARY (the Rev. Canon Greenall) said that he had received letters of apology for non- attendance from the Bishop of Chester, Bishop of Manchester, Rev. Chancellor Espin, and. 66 others, including the Rev. Canon Wilson, Macclesfield; Rev. Canon Fergie, Wigan; Rev. Canon Grey, Durham; Canon Stewart, Liverpool; Canon Gibson, Manchester; Canon Hornby, Bury; Rev. A. C. Adams, Knntsford : Colonel Gamble, St. Helens; Colonel Ireland Blackburne, M.P.; Rev. Foster Rogers, Chester; Rev. W. J. Knox-Little, Alderman Pickmere (Mayor of Warrington), Mr. P. Stubs, Mr. J. C. Parr, Mr. T. B. Forwood, dm. THE WIDOWS AND ORPHANS' FUND. The SECRETARY read the following. report :—This is the 184th anniversary, of the present institution. Founded in 1697 for the undiVided diocese of Chester, it belongs now in 1881 iu the 3 dioceses into which the old See has been divided, and working under the presidency of the Bishops of Chester, Manchester, and Liverpool, endeavours to supply the wants tbat arise within the respective dioceses, except that for Manchester, which only includes the archdeaconries of Manchester and Blackburn. The committee venture to express the earnest hope that the dioceses will always be one together in doing all they can to promote the interests and increase the usefulness of a charity which has for so many years ministered to the wants of the fatherless and the widow, and which must continue to be needed more and more each year, as the number of the married clergy. increases, if their incomes remain as at present so miserably small. Three urgent cases ot distress have been relieved during the year to the, amount of £25. Four of the old pensioners, one belonging to Chester diocese, and three to Manchester, have died. Three ladies (all belonging to Man- chester diocese) not requiring assistance any longer, or rather honourably trying to do without it, have withdrawn their names from the list. There are twelve new applicants, three widows and one orphan from Chester diocese, four widows and four orphans from Manchester. The numbers now on the list are: 22 Chester widows and 5 orphans, 29 Manchester widows and 15 orphans, 11 Liverpool widows and 4 orphans, making a total of 62 widows and 24 orphans Two widows from Chester and one from Manchester apply for grants to give their daughters free board and education at the clergy daughters' school. Two orphans from Chester diocese and four from Manchester seek a renewal of grant for the same purpose. You will be asked to-day to sanction pensions, donations, and payments to the clergy daughters' school to the amount of 42,280. The treasurer reports that he has £1,909 in hand to meet this demand. There has been one legacy since the last anniversary of £lO3 16s. Od. from the late Miss Mary Lupton, of Manchester, and dona- tions amounting to £59 12s. Od. The subscriptions (repre- senting 234 subscribers in Chester, 222 in the archdeacon- rise in Manchester and Blackburn, and 185 in Liverpool) amount to £855 ss. The offertories plus the grants from the unappropriated funds of Chester and Liverpool dioceses amount to £717 10s. 4d. The coin- mitte desire to call particular attention to the last two items (subscriptions and offertories), and to say that in their judgment considering the wealth and extent of the three dioceses, they are far from satisfactory. These are the soarces of income that they have claiefly to rely on in pro- viding for their heavy expenditure, the invested capital only being £7lB Bs. 11d. The following statement will sufficiently explain how it is that the annual income from church offertories is so small. In Chester there are 252 parishes, ecclesiastical districts and chapelries. In the arch- deaconries of Manchester and Blackburn 373, in Liverpool 201, making a total of 826 separate sources from which some animal sum might reasonably be expected. Li from each would have brought up the amount to £lOB more than was received. But in Chester 102 churches, in the arch- deimonries of Manchester and Blackburn 320 churches, and in Liverpool 105, total 527, out of the 826 sent nothing. The committee grieve to have to report such apparent cold- ness. They are well aware that local calls are many and pressing, but surely as long as these touching appeals for help come to us from so many Imor widows and fatherless children, it is the duty of every clergyman whose parish is within the operations of this institution on one Sunday every year at least, to publish its existence and afford his people the opportunity of supporting it. They earnestly invite all the gytnor. to do trice 11 in this or in some other way the charity cannot secure more general support (especially in the districts which reap the largest benefit from it) the com- mittee foresee difficulties in the way of maintaining the present course of distributing tile grants. They hope that each of .the three dioceses will rite to its duty and send in its fair share of contributions. They call upon all, their friends to help them to stir up a general and united effort to secure for this valuable institution a more generous support. The report was adopted. THE CLERGY DAUGHTERS' SCHOOL. Rev. E. L. Y. DrecLE (secretary) read the report, which was as follows :—The committee, since issuing their report of the Clergy Daughters' School, at the meeting of sub- scribers last year, have had every reason to continue their confidence in the energy and ability of the head mistress and her staff of teachers. At the close of last term there were 63 pupils in the school-12 from the diocese of Chester, 30 from that of Manchester, 14 from that of Liver- pool, seven extra diocesan and one student teacher. The report of the Oxford and Cambridge Local Board in the examination held by them last Christmas was encouraging and satisfactory,'and the committee have under their con- sideration the desirability of yet further stimulating the energies of the teachers and pupils of more publicly testing the value of the education given here. The committee with thankfulness report that during the past year the health of the school has been excellent. The clerical principal has most regularly and efficiently discharged the duties of his Office, and in his last report the principal states that which he believes that an increasing interest is being taken in the religious lemons. He yet hopes to be able to arrange a scheme for giving more individual attention to the pupils. The question of an infirmary remains to be settled owing in part to the delay in getting the necessary plans ireared and, mainly to the fact that to carry out the plans which have been approved a larger sum will be required than is at the disposal of the committee. On this point the committee of yesterday passed the following resolution : 'That this com— mittee h .ving decided that it is most desirable to carry out the larger of the two schemes for the erection of the hospital directs that an appeal be made at the annual meeting of the friends of the charity to provide the additional funds which may be required.' The committee earnestly , appeal for Contributions towards building an infirmary and providing a covered play-room and additional play-grounds, The pre.; sent provision being quite inadequate, and to the latter of these points the Oxford Examiner calls the special attention of the committee."

AssauvriNG A YOUNG WOMAN WITH A BRIM—Ann Parry was summoned for assaulting Sarah Jane Owen, a young woman, on the 18th ult. Complainant said that defendant came to her mother's house at twelve o'clock at night and wanted her to fight, but she would have nothing to do with ' her. Parry then bit complainant on the bead with a brick. —The Chairman said the assault seemed to have been a most brutal one, and defendant would probably learn to behave herself better after she had paid a fine of 10s., and the expenses 12s. (including 28.6 d. charged for attendance by Dr. McDougall). or in default of payment, be committed 14 days, with hard labour. PROSECUTIONS BY TRE BOARD OF GUARDIANS.—Isaac Nichols, of Appleton, was summoned by the Runcorn Board of Guardians, for leaving his father chargeable to the com- mon fund of the Runcorn Union. Mr, Thomas Houghton, collector to the guardians, said that formerly defendant paid Is. 3d., per week to the support of his father, but since the guardians had reduced the amount to is. per week, he had paid nothing. Defendant drove a horse and cart for Messrs. Walker, brewers, of Warrington* and was paid a weekly wages of 208. It was quite true that defendant had not been well for some time.—ln reply to the Bench, defendant said he had three children, and very, often did .not work more than.half his time. He waswilling to pay.—The Bench said that if defendant was ill at any time and would apply to the guardians and state the time which he bad been incapaci- tated, they would allow for the period. An order would be made upon him to pay Is. weekly. Taking into account that he had been ill, he would not be charged the expenses Incident to the proceedings.—Samuel Mercer, lately a wheel- wright at Mews. Hutchinson's works, Widnes, was charged with leaving his mother, who lives at Overton, chargeable I to the union. The defendant was represented by a friend, who said he did not dispute his liability to pay the amount, which the guardians said be ought to contribute, and he was wil- ling to pay it —Mr. Houghton said the guardians asked for is. 6d. per week from the defendant, upon whom the Bench made an order to contribute that sum weekly and 14s. 61 enQts.—A similar summons had been issued against Richard Ree.. Ne'-Ari is employed at Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele's at a weekly wage of 18s., for arrears in contributing to the maintenance of his mother, who belongs to the township of Weston. Mr. Houghton said that two brothers of defendant contributed is. 6d. and is. per week respectively to the old woman. All they asked defendant to pay was 6d. per week. Rees said he should have been quite willing to pay the money. but Mr. Houghton had not left his address with him. On calling upon his brother, Mr. Charles Houghton, shoe- maker, arid asking for the address, he simply said it was Duke's-fleM ; and on asking whereabouts in that somewhat wide neighbourhood, he said "You must go and see." When a man did not know where he was to take the money what was he to do? Mr. Houghton said he had a certain day allotted for collecting such sums in Runcorn, and if he did not find the people in they were required to wait upon him. Defendant owed arrears amounting to about 335. The Chairman said he did not believe the defendant's excuse was a truthful one, and an order would he made upon him to pay 6d. per week, and the costs lie. 6d., which had been in- curred through the man's carelessness in not taking the money to the collector. Mr. Houghton said he would have o take other steps to recover the arrears

F RODSHAM. BANE HOLIDAT.—A large number of excursionists visited Frodsham on Monday, and were favoured with beautiful weather. The Belle Monte pleasure grounds were well patronised and the streets presented quite a lively apcear- ance, while the railway station was crowded in the nay part of the day and evening. The Birkenhead Conservatives mustered, to the number of upwards of 1,500, at Mersey View, Overton, when speeches in the Conservative interest were delivered by Mr, Laird, M.D., Mr. Mclver, M.P., the 1 Hon. Wilbraham F. Tollemache, M.P., Mr. Henry J. Tolle- i mache, M.P., and others. VOLUNTEER MANCEUTRES.—The Frodsham volunteer corps had a march out on Saturday afternoon, anal visited, by invitation, the residence of Mr. Charles Reynolds, J.P. A sham attack had been decided upon, and each man was supplied with 20 rounds of ammunition. They advanced in skirmishing order up the field on the south-west side of Mr. Reynolds' mansion, and then charged in a body, a parting volley being fired, which roused the echoes. Refreshments were kindly provided by Mr. Repeolds, and the amateur brass band and Victoria drum and fife band played a selec- tion of music. The officers present were Captain Hammers - ley (adjutant), Lieut.-Col. Ashton, Captain Robert Ashton, and Lieut. Henry. . RECHABITES' Fesriver.,.—The annual festival of the Delight of Frodsham Tentand Hope of Frodsham (Juvenile) Tent, which have about 100 members, was held on Monday. The members assembled at the Primitive Methodist school- room, and proceeded in procession through the town, accom- petaled by the Halton brass band and the Frodsham Victoria drum and fife hand. They afterwards visited the residences \of Mn. dohn Heyes and the Misses Crosfield, Revs. H. B. Blogct aud A. P. Reynolds, Messrs. E. A. Wright (Castle Park), John Simpson, Charles Reynolds, J. C. Sutton, Hy. Liwker, C. E. Linaker, John Robinson, John Ashton, and Thomas Hough. Tea was provided in the school-room at five o'clock, to which about 150 members and friends sat ' down, the tables being presided over by Mesdames Dixon and Chapman, Misses Jackeon, Walker, Trelfa, Booth, ' Thomas, Atherton, and HulEe. A public meeting was held ' in the Town Hall in the evening, when the Vicar (Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A.) presided, and addresses were delivered by ' the Chairman, Rev. A. P. Reynolds, senior curate, Mr. W. King, of the Chester temperance society, and Mr. William Dutton, of Norley. A vote of thanks to the chairman, pro- posed by Mr. Hough, seconded by Mr. King, and supported by Mr. Dutton, brought the meeting to a close. --.........--

NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN. 1.0.G.T., HOPE OF EARLESTOWN LODOR.-011 Monday, the usual quarterly session of the above lodge was held, and after the reports of the various officers had been tendered and adopted, and arrangements made for visiting the Temperance Mission Lodge, Warrington, and Ebenezer Lodge Golborne, during the month of September, the officers for the ensuing quarter were installed by Bro. John Warburton, lodge deputy. W.C.T. Sister M. Allison, W. Sec. Bro. Edward Newman, W.F. Sec. Bro. John Taylor, W. Treasurer Bro. , Henry Warburton, &c. ' MINERS' DEMONSTRATION AT NEWTON COMMON. A demonstration of the miners of the St. Helens and Haydock district, which it is hoped to make an annual evert, took place on Monday on the grounds adjoining Newton Com- mon. The weather was favourable, and there was a large gathering of miners, the attendance being estimated at some 2,000. Four members of Parliament, Mr. Burt, Mr. Mac- donald, Mr. Broadhurst, and Mr. Bradlaugh had been an- nounced as speakers on the occasion, but upon the chair !being taken about two o'clock by Mr. John Cross, miners' I agent, St. Helms, it transpired that none of those gentlemen was present, and from three of them, Mr. Burt, Mr. Broad- hurst, and Mr. Bradlaugh, letters explaining non-attendance were read.—The Chairman, in a brief address, stated that the Tories had put out placards announcing other sports, with a view to keeping miners away from that meeting— (cries of " No "1 —and a great many of the clergy had in their churches warned people against attending it. It was, however, never intended to make the gathering a political affair. He urged the miners to have faith in one another, ' and to combine in order that their present low rate of wages, laveraging in ntany cases only 12s. a week, might be im- proved.—On the motion of Mr. L. H. Riley (St. Helens), seconded by Mr. James Beech (miners' agent, Oldham), it was resolved by acclamation that the exclution of Mr. Brad- laugh from Parliament was subversive of the rights of the whole body of the electors of the kingdom—Thanks were voted to the chairman for presiding, after which a pro- gramme of athletic sports was gone through. BAND OF HOPE GALA AT ASHTON.—On Saturday last, the Bands of Hope in the Ashton Union held their annual gala. The Ashton Baud of Hope walked in procession to Stub- shaw Cross, where they were joined by the Stubshaw Cross, Edge Green, Park-lane, and Newton-le-Willows Bands of Hops; also a goodly number of Good Templars in regalia, from the Ashton Excelsior, Hope of Earlestown, Golborne, and Wigan Lodges. The whole party, to the number of about 700, were headed by the famberhead Green tem- perance brass band, and, after parading the principal streets in the town, causing "no small stir" with their flags and banners waving, and the happy faces of the children pro- ceeded to the Haydock Lodge Park, which had been kindly lent by Dr. Beaman for the occasion. Here tea or milk, and cakes and buns, were indulged in. After a short tinpri rports and games of the usual kinds were participated in. A choir contest was held between the Ashton, Newton-le- Willows, and Park-lane choirs, the prize being a neat banner, which was eventually won by the Ashton Band of Hope cimir, who sung "Resurrection" from the " Messiah," and "Bear on the temperance banner." Recitation contests were held for boys and girls; the first prize was won by Eliza Winstanley, of the Ashton Band of Hope, and three other prizes won by Isabella Hardy, Arthur Jones, and Robert H. Hardy, of the Newton-le-Willows Band of Hope. Altogether, a most enjoyable half-day was spent. During the day there was an attendance of about 800, in addition to those in the procession, which made a total of about 1,500 persons in the park.

As, GOOD TERTIARY IN Si'. HELENS.—The St. Helens Ebenezer Lodge, No. 752, held its usual quarterly meeting at King's Coffee Tavern, Westfield-street, St. Helens, on Wednesday evening last, Bro. C. F. Haddy, W.C.T. , pre- siding. There was a good attendance of members and visitors, among the latter being Brother A. Newall, P.W.D.S.,and Bro. B. Preston, P.W.D.A.S., both of Bed- fordshire. At the request of Bro. Haddy, Bro. Newall took the chair, and conducted the business of the lodge very effi- ciently during the remainder of the. evening. The officers for the ensuing term were impressively installed by Bro. Newall, assisted by Bro. Preston as G.W.S , and Bro. Gore as GM. Officers :—Bro. C. F. Haddy, W.G.T. ; Sister M. King, W.V.T.; Sister Lindon, sen., W.S.; Bro. J. Glover, W.F. sec.; Bro. W. King, W.T.; Sister E. King, W. chap.; Bro. Thompson, W.1.G.; Sister M. J. Lihdon, W.M. ; Bro. R. Skaife, W.D.M. ; Bro. J. Lindon, P.W.C.T. Bio. R. Skaife was unanimously elected as lodge deputy in the place of Bro. I'. Hewitt, resigned. Earnest addresses on the good of the order were delivered by Bros. Newall and Preston, and attentively listened to and highly appreciated, and votes of thanks accorded these brethren for their visit and for the addresOes The lodge closed at 10 p.m., and was one of the l.):st meetings held for some time.

The SECRETARY, previous to reading the list of grants, said in consequence of the comparatively small sum in the hands of the treasurer, £l9O, and as there were 12 new applica- tions the committee were very reluctantly obliged to dis- pense altogether this year with the bonuses which it was usual to give. The summary of grants dm., was as follows —22 Chester widows the on list, pensions £415, donations £140; 6 Chester orphans, pensions £65, donations £3O; 4 girls, clergy daughters, £180; total for Chester £830; 11 Liverpool widows, pensions £235, donations £6O; 4 Liver- pool orphans, pensions £lO, donations £55, total, £360. COMMITTEE OF MANAGEMENT. The following gentlemen, who retired by rotation, were re-elected members of the above committee :—Canon Bar- ' clay, and Rev. A. J. Blencowe, Chester; Canons Birch and Birley, Manchester; Canons Bridgeman and Clarke, Liver- pool; Lord Egerton, of Tatton ; and Sir Gilbert Greenall, Chester; Mr. Herbert Birley and Mr. Hugh Birley, M.P., Manchester ; Colonel Ireland Blackburne, M.P., and the Earl of Lathom, Liverpool There were two other vacancies to fill which Mr. E. Banner, of Roby, and Mr. Pair, of Haigh, near Wigan, were elected. FUNDS WANTED. Archdeacon ANsoN moved, Canon PENRIIIN seconded, and it was carried :—" That an effort be made to raise funds for the erection of a separate infirmary in accordance with plans approved by the Committee."

A procession of some 60 clergy entered the Cathedral, singing Psalm cl., with the Bishops of Nova Scotia, Quebec, Maine, and Albany, a chaplain followin; each, the Rev. Canon Medley, the Metropolitan's chaplain, bearing a magnificent pastoral staff of silver, the Metropoli- tan himself (the Bishop of Frederickton) wearing a white and gold mitre. The sermon was preached by the Bishop of Albany. An immenge congregation was present, including one old lady who had been walking a day and a half to reac") the Cathedral. Rev. Mr. BERTH (Ashton-under-Lyne) proposed the fol- lowing motion, in the absence of the Rev. W. J. Kidd (Didsbury), "That in future the anniversary meetings of this institution be held by I otatiou within the diocese of Chester, the diocese of Manchester, and the diocese of Liver- pool." The motion, however, was not seconded. Rev. Caatort STOWELL then moved "that the annual meet- ing be held as heretofore at Warrington, and that steps be taken by the Committee to hold influential public meet- ings in the large centres such as Manchester and Liverpool in order to excite more public interest in the charity." Fine Ranges of VINERIEi AND PLANT HOUSES Excellent MUSEUM of Natural History, Geology, Coins, Medals, and Curiosities. Street tramway cars run between the Botanic Gardens, Southport, and Birkdale, every seven minutes in summer.

LIVERPOOL TO YORK. The revival of the Stage Coach, with its bounding steeds and fansounding bugle, was a pleasant reminder of the good old days when railways were not, although there are few who would care to recall the times when " George the the Third was King ; " yet the remembrance of bye-gone days, with slow means of transit, and difficulty in reaching distant towns no penny post; no gas; no telegraph, has a charm for the busy people of the latter half of the nine- teenth century. In those days the existence of large firms like THE GRAND CLOTHING HALL COMPANY would have been an impossibility. A Coat purchased at a very large outlay had to last a man's lifetime, and descend from father to son, as a valued acquisition. With the Introductiou of railways and machinery, commercial enterprise In the manufacture of Clothing, as In other branches of trade, effected a complete revolution. "Our Boys" of the present day are clothed in a manner our grandfathers would not have dreamed of. Talented artists are engaged In designing, and thousands of specially trained workpeople in making up, dress for the Boys. A quarter of a century ago THE GRAND CLOTHING HALL COMPANY com- menced their operations, starting with a thorough know- ledge of the trade, and large capital at command. They soon became known in the commercial world for the uni- form excellence of their Men's, Youths, and Boys' Clothing; and probably at the present time they are the largest Manufacturers of Clothing in the World. They reject all but the most reliable material in their manufacture; and, by constant supervision in the minutest details, maintain the pre-eminence they have obtained as producers of Clothing for all Classes. THE GRAND CLOTHING HALL COMPANY, 28, 30, & 82, BRIDGE-STREET, WARRINGTON; ROCHDALE, PRESTON, SHEFFIELD, DERBY. ,
